Title: Opening remarks at the Governors' Symposium on financial inclusion in Africa
text: BANK OF ALGERIA Opening remarks by Mr. Mohammed Laksaci, Governor of the Bank of Algeria, President of the Association of Banks Central African Governors' Symposium on "Financial Inclusion in Africa: Challenges to Monetary Policy and Financial Stability posed by Financial Innovations" Port Louis, Mauritius, 22 August 2013 1 First of all, I would like to thank Mr Rundheersing BHEENICK, Governor of the Bank of Mauritius, for the hospitality and excellent organisation of the annual meetings of our association. Today's event is dedicated to the Governors' Symposium, which this year addresses a theme that is particularly important for the economic and social development of the continent, namely financial inclusion. It is entirely legitimate for African central banks to take an increased role in scaling up financial inclusion, in line with their monetary policy and financial stability missions. 1. Africa, which had adopted prudent macroeconomic policies and experienced a period of macroeconomic stability and sustained growth, suffered since 2009 the effects of the global economic crisis. Due to deterioration of accounts Monetary policies are weak and have little fiscal room for manoeuvre. became relatively accommodating. However, access to credit remains below of the potential, especially for small and newly created firms. Uncertainties about the prospects for a short-term recovery in the global economy, and in particular those related to the state of public finances in developed countries with high unemployment rates, are likely to affect growth in several African countries, even though the continent as a whole is on a relatively more sustained recovery path than the global economy. It is in this context that the necessary improvement of financial intermediation must continue in a situation of preservation or return to macroeconomic stability, as financial stability alone is not a sufficient factor to ensure the best financial inclusion in Africa. 2. I would like, through the example of my country, to outline recent developments on financial inclusion, in interaction with the reform of the policy framework monetary and progress in financial stability. The inflation target was established as an explicit monetary policy objective in 2010 as part of the revision of the Money and Credit Act, after the effectiveness of monetary policy in reducing the structural excess liquidity in the money market could be established over the past eleven years (2002-2012). Prior to this important reform of the monetary policy framework, the update in 2009 of the regulatory framework for the conduct of monetary policy (liquidity recovery, interest-bearing deposit facilities and minimum reserves) and the introduction of short-term inflation forecasting instruments enabled the Bank of Algeria to refine the conduct of monetary policy and keep inflation at target (4%). However, while inflation has been under control at this level for fourteen consecutive years, its rate exceeded the medium-term target rate in 2012, reflecting the acuteness of endogenous inflation. Data from the first half of 2013 show that 2 the forward-looking approach to monetary policy supports the return of the inflation rate to the target set by the Monetary and Credit Council (4%) in 2013, especially as fiscal consolidation contributes to this. The contribution of monetary policy to financial stability remains decisive in Algeria, given the predominance of banks in the financial system. With the advent of the international financial crisis, the Algerian banking sector remains solid, anchored on a high capital adequacy ratio and a very appreciable profitability. Indeed, the minimum capital of banks was significantly increased in 2009, four times its pre-crisis level, while the operational framework of banking activity was consolidated in 20102011 (accounting rules, interbank risk management standards, compliance and internal control, risks on the interbank foreign exchange market, etc.). At the same time, recent years have been marked by a strengthening of the supervisory system, from a risk perspective, while the controls carried out by the Bank of Algeria on the basis of documents and on the spot have been intensified. Indeed, the Bank of Algeria must constantly ensure the safety and soundness of the banking system, as its tasks in banking supervision and supervision have been strengthened as part of its new prerogatives in the field of financial stability, including the supervision of new financial products and systemic risks. Since 2010, the Bank of Algeria has had a monetary and financial stability objective of equal importance with the objective of price stability, even if the contribution of monetary policy to financial stability is important in Algeria. In addition, the Banque d'Alg8erie's interventions in the interbank foreign exchange market, with the objective of stabilizing the real effective exchange rate at its equilibrium level, underpin the monetary policy objective. From the point of view of the objective of developing financial inclusion, the revision of the law on money and credit of August 2010 made it possible to establish the right to the account, the effective implementation of which was organized by an instruction of the Bank of Algeria of December 2012. The aim is to facilitate the opening of bank accounts for households regardless of gender. Also, the information relating to this device has been widely disseminated for the benefit of households and the 48 branches and branches of the Bank of Algeria, throughout the national territory, are fully invested with the mission of facilitating the opening of bank accounts for households at the local level. The results for the first half of 2013 are substantial and allow households to take advantage of the potential in basic banking services, especially since the modern mass payment system, to international standards, has been operational since May 2006. Since then, interbank telecompany clearing at national level has been functional, but its potential is poorly used. This makes it possible to largely support the operations related to the new accounts opened from the beginning of January 2013, while the preference of households for fiat currency characterizes the demand for currency in Algeria. At the same time, the network of banks is experiencing densification, particularly outside the major cities, which is helping to increase the use of 3 the modern infrastructure of payment systems available that covers the entire national territory and this, for the benefit of the necessary development of mass payments and therefore financial inclusion. As for the new banking conditions enacted in June 2013 by the Currency and Credit Council, they have substantially reduced the cost of access to banking services for both businesses and households. These new banking conditions introduced free basic banking services. From the point of view of access to credit, the potential for developing financial inclusion remains significant for households. While mortgage loans to households are growing in line with the supply of promotional housing, consumer credit (excluding mortgage credit) has been banned to avoid a "bubble" in this area and therefore the over-indebtedness of households, while the modernization of risk centres is being completed. However, the financial savings accumulated by households represent an increasingly important source for banks in terms of means of action. As for loans to private sector enterprises, and for the last eleven years (2002-2012), their average growth rate is estimated at 20% against an average overall growth of lending of 16.1%. As a result, the share of credit to the private sector reached 52.3% of the total credit distributed by banks at the end of 2012, compared to 43.5% at the end of 2002. Moreover, compared to several emerging and developing countries, credit growth continued at the pace before the global financial crisis (2008) and even at a higher rate from 2009 onwards. This confirms the sustained expansion of credit to the private sector, supported by increasingly favourable financial conditions and guarantee mechanisms. In this regard, 2012 saw the effect of the significant financial support provided by the State from 2011 onwards to stimulate medium-term loans to SMEs. In addition, as of January 2013, measures to facilitate access to credit were taken by banks, including the limitation of administrative documentation, the deadline for the study of files reduced to one month and the implementation of the new legal provisions of August 2010 relating to money and credit. In addition, some so-called microfinance institutions and institutions managing financing support schemes contribute, to a certain extent, to inclusion through credit. Finally, the deepening of the reform of the financial sector in Algeria takes charge in a more sustained way, from 2013, of the important aspect of financial inclusion, that is to say better access for households and SMEs to bank credit as well as to quality basic banking services. A Financial Sector Assessment (EFSAP) scheduled for September-October of the current year will identify areas for further consolidation of financial stability and deepening of the banking sector aimed at the benefits of financial inclusion better disseminated between SMEs and households. 4 In conclusion, I wish every success to the work of our symposium. The density of the programme and the quality of the interventions will undoubtedly stimulate exchanges of experience beneficial to all of us. Thank you for your attention. 5

Title: Speech during a video-conference of the International Monetary and Financial Committee (IMFC)
text: BANK OF ALGERIA Speech by the Governor of the Bank of Algeria at a video-conference of the International Monetary and Financial Committee (IMFC) held on March 27, 2020 Let me begin by thanking the Chairman and Managing Director for their opening remarks. I also take this opportunity to offer my sincere condolences to all the families who have lost a loved one during this coronavirus pandemic. In this very difficult global environment characterized by a rapid and bruised pandemic, we welcome this opportunity to demonstrate the willingness of the global financial community, with the IMF at the center, to stand ready to rapidly implement a comprehensive strategy to help members reduce the impact of the pandemic covid19. In this respect, we note with satisfaction the support provided by the Executive Board to the Director-General for the implementation of the crisis response strategy. For today's conference, let me briefly address the two issues on the agenda. Firstly, with regard to the countries in our constituency. - Like the rest of the world, they are gradually affected by COVID19 PANDEMIC. In each country, the authorities are sparing no effort to contain its spread, taking measures drastic health in the clear hope that its impact on growth will not be devastating. However, many of them may need immediate support from the Fund. In fact, Ghana, the Pakistan, lran, ! Afghan istan and Tunisia have already applied to the Fund for emergency financial support. Second, the political response to global liquidity and funding needs. To support the final recovery, the global community should focus on containment and reversal of the pandemic and promote urgent cooperation in the health sector. For its part, the IMF should devote its human and financial resources to meeting the immediate needs of emerging markets and developing countries, through emergency financing and adequate to the world economy, by providing additional liquidity. essential. In this regard, we welcome the IMF's response to the crisis, including !' temporary increase in access limits to emergency facilites. It is important to note that beyond the be Financing associated with the pandemic, many emerging markets and developing countries are now exposed to a significant outflow of foreign financial investments and some are facing !' Impact of the sharp drop in oil prices, adding pressure additional balance of payments. In this context, we invite the Fund to remain vigilant and to consider, after six months and if necessary. a suoolementary increase in Access limits. We also encourage FENDS to show the necessary flexibility when countries participating in programmes have difficulties in applying pre-conditionality. In addition to upgrading the facilities of the Fends, we also support the proposal for a significant new general allocation of SDRs in view of the continued massive outflows of foreign financial investment from emerging market economies. Finally, let me stress that we are facing a humanitarian crisis. The current pandemic is not selective, affecting all countries, rich, poor and the poorest. That is why global cooperation is essential. In this respect, it is important that Fends applies with the greatest importance the principle of impartiality when deciding on its support to member countries. Thank you for your attention.

Title: Communication on macroeconomic stability and bank financing of growth
text: Algiers, 11 June 2015 Macroeconomic stability and bank financing Growth 1. Macroeconomic and financial stability Unlike the 1990s marked by structural adjustment (1991 and 19941998), the Algerian economy was characterized during the years 2000 to 2013 by an excess of savings over investment, i.e. fourteen consecutive years of current account surpluses in the balance of payments, and a strengthened macro-financial stability, anchored on an appreciable stock of savings of the Treasury (stabilization fund) and a solid external financial position. During this period, despite the external shock of 2009, the net external financial position remained strong. The sustained accumulation of official foreign exchange reserves between 2000 and 2008 and the early repayment of external debt mainly in 2006, so that at the onset of the international financial and economic crisis, external debt was already at a historically low level (3.5% of GDP in 2008), have placed Algeria in a position of net creditor to the rest of the world. The net international investment position reached 91% of GDP in 2013, following the continued prudent management of official foreign exchange reserves by the Bank of Algeria. This degree of external financial stability is supported by the flexible management of the exchange rate by the Bank of Algeria through its interventions in the interbank foreign exchange market. These interventions aim to stabilize the dinar's real effective exchange rate around its medium-term fundamental equilibrium level, although in 2013 the dinar's real effective exchange rate remained slightly appreciated, in a context of disinflation. Between 2002 and 2013, monetary stability in Algeria was based on a good inflation performance (4% on average), despite the structural excess of liquidity in the money market. After an inflationary "peak" in 2012, disinflation that began in February 2013 continued during that year (3.26%). After nine consecutive years of surplus in Treasury operations, the impact of the external shock of 2009 resulted in a deficit in Treasury operations from that same year onwards, driven by the sharp contraction in oil taxation and the expansion of budgetary expenditures, even though 2013 saw fiscal consolidation. 1/8 However, the financing capacity of the Treasury built up between 2000 and 2008 made it possible to cope with the impact of the external shock on public finances, while remaining significant (34% of GDP at the end of 2013), in a situation of very low domestic public debt (8% of GDP at the end of 2013). Prior to the credit expansion phase from 2013 onwards, the revision of the 2003 Banking Law by the Currency and Credit Ordinance of August 2010 broadened the central bank's tasks, explicitly assigning it the objective of financial stability in addition to the price stability mandate. The contribution of monetary policy to monetary and financial stability remains decisive, given the predominance of banks in the financial system in Algeria and their potentially important role in the development of financial intermediation. This contribution is all the more important in view of the persistence of excess liquidity on the money market since 2002. Key elements for financial stability, the monetary policy framework and instruments were strengthened during the years 2008 to 2010, particularly with the explicit inflation target enshrined in the 2010 Banking Law. The Bank of Algeria's conduct of monetary policy remained prudent, contributing to the good performance of inflation (4% between 2002 and 2013, 2.92% in 2014). The banking law of 2010 highlighted more particularly the role of the Bank of Algeria in the field of the stability of the banking sector since it must ensure its security and solidity. To this end, since 2010 it has been endowed with broader prerogatives to carry out any investigation at the level of banks and financial institutions allowing a greater capacity for early detection of vulnerabilities. This has led the Bank of Algeria to intensify micro-prudential controls and improve their effectiveness. To ensure that the stability of the banking sector is generally managed, the Bank of Algeria periodically assesses the soundness of this sector by means of stress tests, developed from 2007 onwards and reinforced in 2013-2014. The results of these tests make it possible to anticipate the possible risks of weakening the sector. At the macro-prudential level and in the context of excess liquidity, existing instruments that are part of microprudential regulation, such as the level of mortgage credit in relation to the value of the property given as collateral by individuals, minimum reserves - moreover, an instrument of monetary policy - and the debt service ratio to the income of mortgage applicants, can be modulated according to the possible systemic risk. In addition, a strengthening of macro-prudential tools was initiated at the beginning of 2013, in particular through the introduction of new tools for horizontal risk analyses and stress tests. To further develop the operational framework for financial stability, regulations on the identification, measurement, management and control of liquidity risk were enacted by the Currency and Credit Council in May 2011. A minimum short-term liquidity ratio than banks and institutions 2/8 financial must respect at all times has been instituted; and a system of internal supervision and counterparty limitation of outstanding interbank loans and borrowings, in particular those on the money market, has been set up. As an indication, the assessment carried out by the Bank of Algeria for the year 2013 shows that the banks of the place meet the requirement in terms of liquidity coefficient (169.87% at the end of 2013), even if the year 2013 recorded a relative stabilization of bank liquidity. From the point of view of the depth of the banking sector, it is worth noting that the ratio of resources collected (demand and term deposits excluding hydrocarbon deposits) to non-hydrocarbon GDP increased between 2012 (62.39%) and 2014 (66.48%), after stabilizing at 61.44% in 2011. The upward trend in the ratio of bank loans to the private sector to private sector dinar deposits between 2008 and 2014, in the context of increased financial transformation, is another relevant indicator of the depth of the banking system. In addition, the ratio of total credits to non-hydrocarbon GDP, which remained stable between 2011 and 2012, increased to 44.77% in 2013 and 52.47% in 2014; loans to the private sector increased to 25.33% in 2014, relative to non-hydrocarbon GDP, compared to 23.76% in 2013 and 21.50% in 2012. Despite the strong expansion of credit to the economy during 2013 and 2014, and while continuing their efforts in provisioning, banks have consolidated their indicators of financial soundness. An assessment of the banking and financial sector in 2013, carried out by the International Monetary Fund and the World Bank, helped to identify areas for deepening the reform of the banking sector and further consolidating financial stability in Algeria, with effective implementation from the first quarter of 2014. In this context, the prudential regulatory framework has been reformed to bring prudential rules into line with the new standards and norms of the Basel Committee. Indeed, three regulations were issued by the Currency and Credit Council in the first quarter of 2014, with effect from October, on solvency ratios, large risks and participations, and classification and provisioning of receivables and commitments by signature. In this new regulation, the minimum solvency ratio to tier one is set at 9.5%, i.e. a ratio higher than the minimum recommended by the Basel Committee, and that to regulatory capital around 12%. An estimate of financial strength indicators at the end of 2013 shows that the soundness of the banking sector is anchored in high solvency ratios, relative to credit risks, around 14% to core capital and 20% to regulatory capital in 2013, comfortable profitability and appreciable liquidity. In addition, with a ratio of non-performing loans net of provisions constituted at 3.36% in 2013, the decline in non-performing loans continues more resolutely. These indicators of financial soundness are in line with those of comparable emerging countries. At the end of 2014, these indicators would be lower, as the new prudential regulation also covers the coverage of operational and market risks. In addition, as part of broader prerogatives established in 2010, encompassing the operation, supervision and security of payment systems, the Bank of Algeria completed in 2014, the update of the modern infrastructure of 3/8 payment (real-time payment system for large amounts and urgent payments and tele-compensation system), meeting international standards and implemented in 2006. This action to modernise payment systems further promotes financial inclusion for the benefit of households, in particular by allowing a smooth application of the system in this area put in place in December 2012. 2. Structure of the banking sector At the end of 2014, the banking system consists of twenty (20) banks including six (6) public banks and fourteen (14) private banks, subsidiaries or branches of major international banks. It also includes nine (9) financial institutions, six of which are public. The overall indicators show that the level of bank intermediation is gradually improving in terms of network development, the number of accounts, the level of deposits collected and credits distributed, although it remains below the levels reached by some neighbouring Mediterranean countries. The pace of establishment of branches of private banks has accelerated in recent years, contributing to the development of competition, both in terms of the collection of resources and in the distribution of credit and the offer of basic banking services to customers. However, the potential for financial inclusion remains significant, whether it is basic banking services to household customers or the distribution of credit to small and medium-sized enterprises. This means the scope of financial inclusion for the development of bank intermediation in Algeria. The activity of banks in terms of resource collection and credit distribution is growing steadily, while the credit distribution activity of financial institutions remains very weak. A significant part of the loans granted by the latter are for leasing operations (85.9% compared to 78% in 2013), while they are not allowed to collect deposits and manage means of payment. The year 2014 recorded a strong increase in bank assets (16.5% compared to 6.8% in 2013), while the assets of financial institutions are up more moderately (7.4% against 9.2% in 2013) and represent only 0.6% of total assets in the banking sector. In the total assets of banks, public banks remain predominant with a relative share of 86.8% at the end of 2014 against 13.2% for private banks. The growth of the latter's assets was less sustained in 2014, both in terms of the distribution of credits and the mobilization of resources. The ratio of gross assets in the banking sector (banks and financial institutions) to gross domestic product reached 69.6% in 2014 compared to 62.5% in 2013. The ratio of gross assets in the banking sector (excluding deposits in the hydrocarbon sector) to non-hydrocarbon gross domestic product also increased in 2014 to 89.9% from 84.8% in 2013. The activity of collecting bank resources from residents (dinars and currencies) increased significantly at a rate of 17.2% in 2014 against 7.6% in 2013 and 7.5% in 2012. Market penetration indicator, the ratio of deposits excluding 4/8 hydrocarbons/non-hydrocarbon gross domestic product stood at 66.5% at the end of 2014 compared to 62.7% at the end of 2013. Banks' credit distribution activity also rose sharply in 2014 (26.3%), after the high rates recorded in 2013 (20.3%) and 2012 (15.1%). The credit distribution activity (loans to residents) of banks and financial institutions, including non-performing loans repurchased by the Treasury by issuing securities (unmatured securities), represents 55.4% of gross domestic product excluding hydrocarbons compared to 48.9% in 2013. 3. Bank intermediation and growth financing prospects excluding hydrocarbons In the context of the structural excess of savings over investment, the structure of investment financing in Algeria, for the last nine years, shows a very high level of self-financing (84%) and this, mainly due to the self-financing of investments by the State and the national hydrocarbon company. Investment in the national economy (excluding the hydrocarbon sector) has also been strongly self-financing, at 59.7% over the last nine years, while the financial savings of private enterprises and households have risen sharply. In particular, the years 2010 and 2011 recorded strong growth in self-financing, at rates of 71.4% and 24.1% respectively, which certainly contributed to the significant recovery in investment in non-hydrocarbon sectors. As for medium- and long-term domestic bank loans, which have increased significantly over the last three years, their share relating to the financing of investments in non-hydrocarbon productive sectors reached 45.2% in 2014 against 38.4% in 2012. The share of medium- and long-term loans distributed to the energy and water sector at the end of 2014 represented 47% of total loans distributed to companies compared to 44% in 2013. In particular, the distribution of long-term loans to these sectors is very important, accounting for 65% of total long-term loans distributed to companies compared to 63% in 2013. These medium- and long-term credits allocated to the energy and water sectors aim to accelerate the development of investments in these strategic sectors, decided by the public authorities, in order to meet the demand of productive enterprises and households. Driven by the dynamism of medium- and long-term loans, loans to the economy recorded a strong growth rate in 2013 (20.3% against 15.1% in 2012) and 2014 (26.3%). The improvement in credit conditions combined with the State's credit support scheme for SMEs, which further improved their access to bank credit from 2011 onwards, has consolidated credit to the private sector, whose average growth rate is 19.4% for the last thirteen years (2001-2013). In the context of strong credit expansion to the economy over the past two years, especially in real terms, the net flow of credit distributed to private enterprises has more 5/8 focused on medium- and long-term loans distributed to finance investments than on operating credits. Overall and excluding loans repurchased by the Treasury, bank loans to the private sector (private companies and households) reached an outstanding amount of 3120.1 billion dinars at the end of 2014, in a situation of increase in the relative share of medium- and long-term loans to 64.3% against 62.3% at the end of 2013 and 61.3% at the end of 2012. The dynamism of bank loans to the economy, particularly for the benefit of private companies, clearly reflects the improvement in the structure and conditions of financing (interest rates and maturity), as a result of the measures taken by the public authorities (financial support) to stimulate medium- and long-term credit to SMEs, in particular the measures to facilitate SMEs' access to bank credit implemented in 2013. Six years after the beginning of the international economic and financial crisis, the Algerian economy suffered, like other oil-exporting countries, the drastic drop in barrel prices from the second half of 2014. Despite the recovery in growth, estimated at 4% in 2014 against 2.8% in 2013. This is a source of vulnerability for the balance of payments and public finances. After fourteen years of surpluses, the external balance of payments recorded a deficit in 2014, leading to a decline in official foreign exchange reserves in the second half of 2014, after a long period of sustained accumulation. However, their level remains adequate, standing at more than 30 months of imports of goods and services at the end of 2014. Similarly, given the historically low level of external debt (3.735 billion at the end of December 2014), the net external financial position remains strong at the end of 2014. This should help mitigate the effect of the external shock in 2015. In addition, the very low foreign currency indebtedness of companies in the hydrocarbon sector and banks helps to limit the financial consequences of the external shock. However, it is now necessary to control the level of absorption in order to preserve the long-term sustainability of the balance of payments. The impact of the fall in oil prices also resulted in a contraction in the Treasury's financing capacity during 2014, after several consecutive years of accumulation of budgetary savings. However, the widening of the budget deficit in 2014, driven by the upward profile of disbursements for budgetary expenditure, particularly capital expenditure, in the context of lower oil tax revenues, did not thwart the objective of controlling inflation. In addition, and despite this external shock, the expansion of credit to the economy continued during 2014 at a high pace in real terms, particularly towards private companies, reflecting the dynamism of financial intermediation and the promotion of financial inclusion towards SMEs. Anchored on the relatively stable nature of banks' resources, in a situation of persistent excess liquidity on the money market and the prospects for 6/8 Reactivation of refinancing by the Bank of Algeria, the bank credit channel remains potentially important in terms of financing productive investment and non-hydrocarbon growth potential. Hence the scope of effective bank intermediation in favour of inclusive non-hydrocarbon growth, with the objective of achieving a target ratio of investment and SME loans relative to non-hydrocarbon GDP over the medium term. To this end, banks will need to diversify their financing instruments, while effectively pursuing improvements in the analysis, measurement, monitoring and control of credit risks. At the same time, and in this new context marked by the external shock of a sustainable nature that could quickly affect their resources, banks must develop their means of action in the long term by promoting attractive financial products, particularly in terms of real returns. The realization of the non-hydrocarbon growth potential will have to be driven by productive investments, in particular from the private sector, in a situation of continuation of the public investment programme at an appropriate pace. A sustained improvement in the business climate is needed to boost the private sector's contribution to strong and inclusive non-hydrocarbon growth. In the new context of the gap between savings and investment from 2014 onwards, it is expected that net exports will make a sustained contribution to the acceleration of growth, in particular through the valuation, from 2015, of the significant potential for export diversification. Depending on the evolution of fundamentals, the Bank of Algeria will pursue an exchange rate policy that promotes external competitiveness and stability. After the measures to support non-hydrocarbon exports taken in 2011, the Bank of Algeria will take new measures in 2015 to develop the interbank foreign exchange market and promote forward hedging by local banks for the benefit of operators. The reactivation of operations on the interbank money market, with a view to the banks' return to refinancing with the lender of last resort in 2015, will contribute to this dynamic. At the same time, the monetary policy conducted by the Bank of Algeria will remain prudent to contribute to the good performance of absorption. The entry into force in the fourth quarter of 2014 of the new prudential framework, in line with the risk orientation of supervision, will help to better calibrate the credit channel, as it is important to preserve credit quality. In addition, as part of the development of control and supervision tools, a micro and macro stress testing model, taking into account credit, liquidity and interest rate risks, has been operational since the beginning of 2015 at the Banque d'Algerie. The macro-prudential aspect of this model is particularly relevant in this context of a large-scale external shock. The establishment of the new risk centre before the end of 2015 will be another risk management tool aimed at strengthening the stability of the banking sector in Algeria. 7/8 Preserving the stability and soundness of the banking system remains a priority. In view of the development of the financial market, the mobilization by banks of domestic savings resources is of particular importance. In this regard, and in order to better establish the resilience of the Algerian economy to external shocks, the development of financial savings in the long term by banks remains potentially important and must be the basis of the new financing scheme for non-hydrocarbon growth. The development of non-hydrocarbon productive sectors, in particular the activity of SMEs, now requires larger loanable funds for investment. As part of the necessary economic diversification, this will contribute to the development of the potential for non-hydrocarbon exports. 8/8

Title: Statement in the videoconference of April 22, 2020
text: BANK OF ALGERIA Responding to the COVID-19 Pandemic in the Middle East and Central Asia: Regional Economic Outlook Video conference on Wednesday, April 22, 2020 Statement by the Governor of the Bank of Algeria What are the key challenges you see for the payback period? First of all, let me bow to the memory of all those who have been swept away by this pandemic in our countries and pay tribute to the men and women who face it every day with courage and bravery. Madam Director of the International Monetary Fund, dear colleagues and friends; As you know, this unprecedented global health crisis has resulted in the emergence of emergencies, not only economic, but also social. These emergencies have necessitated the rapid implementation of responses combining both unconventional monetary and prudential policies, as well as expansive fiscal policies. These emergency cyclical policies will certainly lead to widening budget deficits, the financing of which will lead to an increase in both internal public debt and external debt for a significant number of countries in our region. Also, the emergence of twin deficits (fiscal and balance of payments) for oil countries in the context of falling oil prices, will be a great challenge for the future. Also, the drop in demand and the effects of the lockdown would lead to the emergence of new upside risks for the banking system in terms of non-performing loans. Thus, four major challenges are emerging before us for the post-crisis period: 1- the return to inclusive and sustainable growth allowing the creation of wealth and employment. 2- the implementation of monetary, budgetary and exchange rate policies capable of responding gradually and in the medium term to the problems of budgetary and balance of payments deficits. 3- the establishment of debt treatment mechanisms. 4- safeguarding monetary and financial stability. Madam Director, dear governor friends, it is understandable that the challenges that lie ahead require the collaboration and solidarity of everyone. We are now at a crossroads and this crisis has shown us our limits, making sure to face it together without dogmatism and for the well-being of all. Thank you for your attention.

Title: Speech by Governor Salah Eddine TALEB on the occasion of the 46th meeting of the International Monetary and Financial Committee  18 and 19 September 2022
text: INTERNATIONAL MONETARY AND FINANCIAL COMMITTEE Forty-Fifth Meeting April 21, 2022 Statement No. 45-8 Statement by Mr. Fadli Algeria On behalf of Islamic Republic of Afghanistan, Algeria, Ghana, Islamic Republic of Iran, Libya, Morocco, Pakistan, and Tunisia Statement by Mr. Rosthom Fadli Governor of the Bank of Algeria On behalf of Islamic Republic of Afghanistan, Algeria, Ghana, Islamic Republic of Iran, Libya, Morocco, Pakistan, and Tunisia At the outset, we would like to express our sincere hope for an early, peaceful and durable resolution of the war in Ukraine. The war has confronted the world economy with a serious crisis just as it had begun to recover from the COVID-19 pandemic shock and its aftermath. The adverse spillovers of the war have already been felt far and wide, through a set of direct and indirect channels and with different degrees of intensity across countries. Most prominently, the war and associated sanctions on Russia, self-imposed sanctions, and disruptions in energy and grain trade have been manifested in steep increases in energy and food prices hitting the vulnerable groups worldwide the hardest. Food insecurity has emerged as a global crisis. The plight of the Ukrainian refugees and internally displaced peoples in Europe is a sad reminder of the plight of all refugees and displaced populations from other conflicts in other regions. Compounding the scarring effects of the pandemic, the war in Europe could substantially weakenif not permanently rupturethe trade, financial and technology links that have been developed and strengthened over the past decades. The war in Ukraine should not distract us, however, from the COVID-19 pandemic that is still there to be defeatedwe have won the early battles but not yet the war. The recent mutations and spread of new variants of the virus should be of great concern, especially for the unvaccinated population. It is very disappointing that more than half of the Fund members will not be able to meet the Fund vaccination targets, and that the vaccination rates in many LICs, mostly in Africa, are still in single digits. Improving vaccine access and strengthening healthcare measures, particularly in regions and countries lagging in vaccine coverage, should remain in focus until the pandemic is over. Faced with a new set of challenges, it is crucial for policymakers to clearly identify policy priorities and design well measured policies to safeguard macroeconomic stability and address the scarring effects of the two overlapping crises. Policies should be tailor-made and country-specific for full effectiveness. Supporting the recovery, in the context of limited fiscal space, calls for a careful calibration of withdrawal of pandemic-related emergency measures, while protecting low-income households through targeted subsidies and income transfers. The war, and its consequent impact on prices, has also accelerated the tightening of global financial conditions that was already underway in response to rising inflation before the war. With inflation now expected to remain higher for longer and be less transitory than expected only a few months ago, a protracted period of tight financial market conditions would be placing the highly indebted EMDCs at elevated risk through capital outflows, currency depreciation, higher debt service costs, and constrained access to international financial markets. The IMF played a pivotal role in successfully helping members to cope with the economic and financial fallout of the pandemic and is now expected to rise to the challenge again and help members address the negative spillovers of the new global crisis. We welcome the IMFs recognition of acute vulnerabilities of fragile and conflict-affected states (FCS) and its intention to customize financial and CD support to country circumstances and step-up partnership with other development partners and institutions, in the context of the new FCS Strategy. The welfare gains of the past few decades, and our more recent successful collective effort in fighting a common enemythe COVID-19 pandemicare testaments to shared benefits of multilateralism. Strong multilateral cooperation is crucial now more than ever to protect the rules- based multilateral trade system, safeguard global financial stability and meet new challenges. The rapid growth of digitalization presents opportunities but also risks to financial stability and even to the international monetary system. We welcome Funds deepening of its expertise for assessing the potential risks of digitalization and developing guideless to mitigate such risks through a multilateral effort. Swift and coordinated international action is needed to prevent food insecurity becoming a full- blown humanitarian crisis. In this connection, we welcome the proposed joint action of the Fund, the World Bank, the World Food Program and World Trade Organization to help provide emergency food supplies and financial support to vulnerable countries through grants; facilitate unhindered trade; and invest in sustainable food production. We encourage other IFIs, UN agencies and NGOs to join and strengthen the initiative to prevent a new humanitarian disaster. The famines in Afghanistan, Yemen and pockets in Africa must not be forgotten. We note with deep concern that the rising food and energy prices are fueling social tensions and threatening political stability. As in other parts of the world, the shock of the war in Ukraine is reverberating across countries in our constituency. Higher food prices have pushed the poor into deeper poverty and have made parts of the middle class vulnerable to food insecurity, while the tightening of global financial markets is placing some countries in our constituency at the serious risk of constrained access to external financing. The Fund should be attentive to the difficult trade-offs and competing challenges that our authorities are facing. The Fund's policy advice should be even more pragmatic and country-specific than ever, considering the delicate socio-political balance in many countries. The higher oil prices have provided a temporary respite for the oil and gas exporters in our constituency for sure, but it is important to keep in mind that these countries are also facing costly transitional challenges of their own. They recognize that their long-term efforts towards economic diversifications should not be side-lined by temporary windfall gains and that diversification is necessary to avoid boom-bust cycles of the past. As always, they continue to be committed to the stability of the international oil and gas markets. The low-income countries (LIC) that have been hit hard by the double shocks need sustained international financial support at concessional terms and generous debt relief. The LICs emerged from the pandemic with little or no policy space, significant financing constraints and elevated 2 debt levels, and with their fragilities aggravated by the pandemic and now by the crisis in Europe. We note with serious concern that 60 percent of LICs are already in debt distress or at high risk of distress. For them, their daunting challenges, including longstanding structural problems and fragilities, pose significant impediment to their financial stability and sustainable growth. The Fund policy advice and financial and CD support will be critical. IMF facilitiesparticularly the PRGT and the newly established Resilience and Sustainability Trust (RST)would need to continue to address their imbalances and financing needs that are likely to rise in the aftermath of the two crises. The RST particularly will be expected to play a fundamental role in helping members to address structural shortcomings and to build resilience to external shocks by providing long-term financing. We extend our appreciation to countries that have expressed their intentions to support the PRGT and the RST by rechanneling their SDR allocations. We are all committed to a greener world and attach great importance to transformational reforms required to address the existential threats of climate change. Unfortunately, LIDCs and small island economies with negligible carbon footprints are bearing the brunt of a problem essentially created and perpetuated by large carbon emitters over the past few decades. The RST will be expected to play an important role in helping the developing countries and small island economies vulnerable to climate change to build resilience. We also feel it is important that the Fund and other IFIs take a holistic approach to decarbonization addressing the concerns of energy importers and exporters alike during the transition. It is also important to recognize that the same green objectives could be achieved through different means and on different tracks depending on individual countries circumstances. Finally, we reiterate our call for a strong, quota-based, and adequately resourced IMF at the center of the global financial safety net. We support the ongoing work on the 16th General Review of Quotas with the aim of completing it by December 2023, while protecting the shares of the poorest members. As before, we call for a revised quota formula and for an increase in the IMFs quota resources that is less dependent on temporary borrowed resources. 3

Title: Message from the Governor of the Bank of Algeria
text: Statement by Mr. Mohammed Laksaci, Governor of the Bank of Algeria, to the banking and financial community on financial inclusion I would like to say a few words about the growing importance of financial inclusion around the world, with financial inclusion understood as making quality financial services available to as many citizens and businesses as possible, including the unbanked or underserved segments. It also works to encourage the availability of finance, in particular to small and medium-sized enterprises and micro-enterprises, and to improve the protection of beneficiaries of financial services, including by improving their knowledge of their rights. As such, financial inclusion is an essential factor for financial stability, promoting sustainable and inclusive economic growth, job creation and the reduction of inequalities. In this regard, a regional working group, composed of representatives of Arab central banks and working under the aegis of the Arab Monetary Fund, is responsible for making all proposals and recommendations to Arab central banks that can promote the achievement of this objective. In order to support these efforts and contribute to a better dissemination of information on the financial inclusion approach and its objectives, the Governors of the Arab central banks, in coordination with the Arab Monetary Fund, agreed to establish april 27, financial inclusion day. A joint declaration and a jointly prepared information brochure will be posted on the electronic websites of all Arab central banks. I invite you to consult them. I would like to recall that in terms of financial inclusion, the Bank of Algeria is constantly taking action to promote banking and financial accessibility. I would mention in particular the system implemented in 2012 ensuring the right to the account and the basic banking services associated with it as well as the free provision of a certain number of operations. In the area of credit, banks have been instructed to ensure compliance with the processing of credit applications, to provide an information service at each counter for the benefit of customers and to respond to their complaints. Further action will be taken in the coming weeks. In particular: - An instruction is being prepared to better frame the general and minimum conditions of the deposit account agreement, thus conferring better transparency in the bank-customer relationship. - another instruction will strengthen measures to facilitate the provision of banking services. The Bank of Algeria will continue to work towards sustained financial inclusion, taking into account regional efforts, but also by taking advantage of successful experiences in other countries, particularly emerging countries. Thank you.

Title: Message from the Governor of the Bank of Algeria
text: MESSAGE FROM THE GOVERNOR OF THE BANK OF ALGERIA ON THE OCCASION OF THE ARAB DAY ON FINANCIAL INCLUSION APRIL 27, 2021 It is with great pleasure and honor that I speak, on this date of April 27, 2021, marking the commemoration of the Arab Day of Financial Inclusion, proclaimed by the Council of Arab Central Banks and Monetary Institutions. This year's commemorative day is placed under the theme "Role of digital transformation in improving financial inclusion", which we are celebrating for the third consecutive year, in a difficult context of exceptional global health crisis that tends to last over time. It puts us in front of a situation that requires an increasingly rapid degree of responsiveness, in terms of resilience and adaptation, paying more attention to supporting the use of Financial Technologies, and the establishment of accompanying regulatory mechanisms, aimed at improving access to banking products for all categories of customers. The theme chosen this year, for the celebration of the day of the promotion of financial inclusion in the Arab countries, is in line with the approach adopted through a legislative and regulatory system by the public authorities and the Bank of Algeria in terms of support and encouragement of banks. The main lines of the latter are essentially focused on: - The popularization of digital banking services, - The development of products and services for startups and SMEs; - The implementation of products in line with the needs of the clientele. 1 This is all the more so since the pooling and coherence of recent efforts have stimulated the implementation of a certain dynamic, taking advantage of existing new technologies and according to their availability, and according to the convenience of customers throughout the national territory. In fact, banks and financial institutions have put on the market, in a relatively short time, digital banking services that are beginning to spread to the public, such as the use of payment cards, the endowment of VSEs for the benefit of merchants, the generalized online payment for large billers as well as mobile payment when it is backed by a bank or postal account. Also, the banking landscape has been enriched, because banks and a certain fringe of customers have shown a real enthusiasm, following the intervention of the new regulatory system put in place, specially dedicated to the "Islamic window". In the sense that the latter innovates, in addition to traditional products and encourages banks and financial institutions that wish to do so, to expand their network and establish themselves in the most remote regions. Much more recently, a new step has been taken by the promulgation of measures to relax foreign exchange regulations, aimed at capturing startups operating in the export of digital services and online services in particular, with a view to encouraging them to bank their activities. 2

Title: Arab Central Banks Governors' Common Statement
text: THE COUNCIL OF ARAB CENTRAL BANKS GOVERNORS SUPPORTS THE DEVELOPMENT OF FINANCIAL INCLUSION IN THE ARAB COUNTRIES Considering the transformative impact of financial inclusion and its critical importance in fostering sustainable growth, creating employment opportunities, reducing inequality and maintaining financial stability, the Council of Arab Central Banks Governors reaffirms its commitment to continue improving financial inclusion within the framework of national and regional economic policies to ensure access to a full range of quality, cost-effective and appropriate financial services to unbanked and/or under-served populations and businesses, particularly for youth and women. In this context, the Council recalls its continued efforts to put in place comprehensive and proportional regulatory frameworks that achieve the goals of financial inclusion, financial stability and financial integrity in a complementary manner, while recognizing consumer protection and empowerment as key pillars of financial inclusion efforts. Moreover, the Council highlights the benefit of knowledge exchange and peer-to-peer learning among regional and international financial regulators and policymakers for the design and implementation of regionally relevant financial inclusion policies. In this context, the council recognizes the effort being undertaking by the regional financial inclusion task force, established under the umbrella of the Council of Arab Central Banks Governors and the coordination of the Arab Monetary Fund and welcomes its contributions and recommendations to improve financial inclusion indicators and to promote financial education and awareness among the Arab region as well as fostering consumers protection. Likewise, the Council supports the international efforts aimed at improving access to financial services, stressing the importance of the international cooperation and deepen partnerships between the public and private sectors to contribute achieving 2020 Universal Access. In this context, and in order to contribute to raise awareness of the importance of financial inclusion amongst all stakeholders in the Arab countries, the Council decides to adopt an Arab Day of Financial Inclusion. Finally, the Council reiterates its commitment to continue working to provide an appropriate environment for achieving the universality of financial services in the Arab countries. On this occasion, the Council expresses also its appreciation for the results achieved by the Arab Monetary Fund, the Regional Financial Inclusion Task Force and their international partners in promoting financial inclusion in the region, calling to follow up and to intensify efforts to build capacity among Arab countries and provide technical assistance, where needed, in order to serve financial inclusion strategic directions and development. April 27th, 2016

Title: Joint statement by the Board of Governors of Arab Central Banks
text: THE BOARD OF GOVERNORS OF THE ARAB CENTRAL BANKS SUPPORTS THE DEVELOPMENT OF FINANCIAL INCLUSION IN ARAB COUNTRIES Given the transformative impact of financial inclusion and its importance in sustainable economic growth, job creation, reducing inequality, and maintaining financial stability, the Board of Governors of Arab Central Banks reaffirms its continued commitment to supporting improving financial inclusion in national and regional economic policies to ensure access to a full range of financial services. quality with a sustainable cost structure and adapted to unbanked and/or underserved populations and businesses, especially young people and women. In this context, the Council reiterates its efforts to put in place coherent and proportionate regulatory frameworks that complement the objectives of financial inclusion, financial stability and financial integrity, while recognising consumer protection and empowerment as key pillars of financial inclusion. In addition, the Council underlines the important benefits of knowledge sharing and networking of Arab regulators and policymakers for the design and implementation of regional financial inclusion policies and strategies. In this context, the Council notes with satisfaction the efforts undertaken by the Working Group on Financial Inclusion in the Arab World, established under the aegis of the Board of Governors of arab Central Banks and the coordination of the Arab Monetary Fund and welcomes its contributions and recommendations for the improvement of financial inclusion indicators, the promotion of financial education and consumer protection. Similarly, the Council supports international efforts to support inclusive finance, stressing the importance of international cooperation and public-private partnerships to achieve the goals of universal access to financial services by 2020. In this context, and with the aim of contributing to raising awareness of the importance of financial inclusion among all stakeholders in Arab countries, the Council decides to adopt an Arab Day of Financial Inclusion. Finally, the Council reiterates its commitment to continue working to provide an appropriate environment to achieve the universality of financial services in Arab countries and on this occasion welcomes the efforts made by the Arab Monetary Fund and the Regional Working Group as well as their international partners in promoting financial inclusion in the region and calls for the intensification of efforts to strengthen the capacities of Arab countries through a appropriate technical assistance to support the strategic directions of inclusive finance. April 27, 2016

Enfin, le Conseil ritre son engagement de continuer  travailler pour offrir un environnement appropri pour parvenir  l'universalit des services financiers dans les pays arabes et  cette occasion, il salue les efforts fournis par le Fonds Montaire Arabe et le groupe rgional de travail ainsi que leurs partenaires internationaux dans la promotion de l'inclusion financire dans la rgion et appelle  l'intensification des efforts pour renforcer les capacits des pays arabes par une assistance technique approprie afin de soutenir les orientations stratgiques de la finance inclusive. Title: Understanding financial inclusion
text: BROCHURE ON FINANCIAL INCLUSION This brochure aims to make known to as many providers and users of financial services in Arab countries as possible the approach to financial inclusion, its objectives and its role in achieving financial stability and economic growth in countries, in addition to its social contribution by including the categories marginalized by the official financial system and protecting them financially through the knowledge of their rights. In addition to this, it pays particular attention to the availability of financing for small and medium-sized enterprises and micro-enterprises, while emphasizing the role of states, governments and financial service providers in supporting this approach and in particular the role that central banks play in this regard, identifying the essential pillars and components that constitute the main characteristics for the development of strategies. national financial inclusion (1). First: the definition of financial inclusion Financial inclusion means the availability and use of all financial services by different segments of society, including institutions and individuals, especially those who are marginalized, through official channels, including current and savings accounts, payment and transfer services, insurance services, financing and credit services and innovations in more suitable financial services with competitive and reasonable prices. It also works to protect the rights of consumers of financial services by supporting them so that they can properly manage their funds and savings in order to prevent some consumers from using informal channels and tools, which are not subject to any supervision by the supervisory bodies and which charge relatively high prices leading to the non-satisfaction of the needs for financial and banking services through these channels. Financial inclusion is measured by the availability in terms of supply of financial services and their uses in terms of demand, as well as the quality of these services. (1) The legislation of each State must be taken into account when applying the financial inclusion approach 1 Second: the importance of financial inclusion and its objectives  Financial inclusion has become the focus of many governments and financial regulators, especially central banks. This demonstrates a close relationship between financial inclusion, financial stability and economic growth. It is difficult to conceive of a sustainability of financial stability while a large part of the population and businesses remain financially excluded from the economic system. Financial inclusion fosters competition among financial institutions by working on the diversity and quality of their products in order to attract the largest number of customers and transactions, and the entry into legality of certain informal channels. - On another level, financial inclusion is achieved at the social level by increasing interest in low-income populations, paying particular attention to women, the accessibility of individuals, small, medium and micro enterprises and their integration into the official financial sector through the provision of financial services, making them available to marginalized categories, in the public interest of job creation, which contributes to economic growth and thus to the reduction of poverty, the improvement of income distribution, and the raising of living standards. Third: Financial Inclusion Modus operandi It is recommended that the conduct of the financial inclusion process take place after the States have prepared a study on supply and demand gaps, a cornerstone of from which, they can either set future goals with priorities, or consider that the gap study is the first step in preparing a national strategy involving all parties concerned (2). In all cases, the objectives of the strategy must be defined and measurable and can be achieved on time, working to unify the efforts in the same direction and to realize the objectives set to achieve the greatest number of possible segments of the targeted sectors. (2) For more information, see the document prepared by the Working Group on Financial Inclusion approved by the Board of Governors of the Arab Central Banks under the title: The Requirements for the Adoption of a Comprehensive National Strategy to Promote Financial Inclusion in the Arab States. 2 Fourth: the role of central banks and supervisory bodies in consolidating financial inclusion Central banks play an important role in consolidating financial inclusion through: The development of regulations to facilitate banking transactions in all its forms, and to overcome supply and demand barriers to ensure access to financial services for its users. Work for the entry of informal channels into legality by subjecting them to their control and supervision. Work to promote the creation and development of alternative channels to conventional financial services, using modern technologies. Improve the financial infrastructure through the creation of credit information offices and the development of payment and settlement systems and financial intermediation. Stimulate the financial sector to generalize financial education. Fifth: the main pillars to promote the approach to financial inclusion 1.Strengthening the financial infrastructure The availability of a sound financial infrastructure to meet the requirements of financial inclusion is one of the fundamental pillars for creating an enabling environment. Priorities should also be set for the construction of this infrastructure in order to consolidate economic growth and facilitate citizens' access to financial services. These priorities are: Legislative environment: Establish an appropriate legislative framework to support the approach to financial inclusion through the development and amendment of instructions and resolutions that address priorities as set; The establishment of the network: promote geographical location by facilitating the extension of the network of agencies of financial service providers and support the creation of agencies or small offices for service providers, in particular, for microfinance. It is also a question of encouraging the creation of access points for financial services such as banking agents, points of sale, counters 3 automatic, insurance, securities and others, in accordance with the legislation of the State. The development of payment and settlement systems: the development of national payment and settlement systems with a view to facilitating the implementation of financial transactions and their settlement between providers in a timely manner to ensure the continuous provision of financial services. Take advantage of technological advances: work to develop and improve communication and exchange of information through the expansion of the offer of digital financial services, as well as payment by technological means in order to facilitate access to financial services at the lowest cost and greater efficiency. Provide a comprehensive database: work to activate the role of credit information bureaus, and create comprehensive databases that record credit history for individuals and small and medium-sized enterprises as well as movable property, and take the necessary steps to ensure that service providers and customers have access to the information they need to ensure transparency and protection the rights of all. 2. Financial protection for consumers Given the growth and development of the financial sector and the complexity of financial products and services offered to customers as well as the evolution of electronic financial instruments and the expansion of these services, the concept of financial consumer protection has been the focus of recent times. The aim of the rules laid down in this regard is to increase confidence in the banking and financial sector with a view to promoting the approach to financial inclusion and financial stability through: Ensure that the client receives fair and transparent treatment of financial services and products, with ease at a reasonable cost and quality. Provide the necessary and accurate information at all stages of the customer's relationship with financial service providers, through the transparent disclosure of data to customers ensuring that they are informed about the benefits and risks associated with the product while developing a mechanism 4 to keep customers regularly informed of all updates and changes in products and services. The ability to give advice based on customer needs and the complexity of the products and services provided to them. Protect customers' financial data and develop appropriate mechanisms to monitor and defend their rights. Establish mechanisms to deal with customer complaints in a timely manner, and ensure that they are independent, impartial, accountable, effective and in line with international best practices. Inform and sensitize customers and marginalized groups, in particular, and financial service providers to the principles of consumer financial protection for the understanding of their rights and responsibilities so that they fulfil their obligations. 3. Developing financial services and products that meet the needs of all social categories This point is considered one of the most important pillars to achieve financial inclusion through the facilitation of access to financial services for the benefit of individuals and small and medium-sized and micro enterprises, it follows that this requirement of financial products and services is the responsibility of financial service providers, taking into account: The needs and requirements of customers targeted when designing products and services for them before they are put on the market, as well as the innovation of new savings products, insurance, and means of payment, other than loans. Promote competition between providers of financial products and services, to offer more options to customers and improve competitiveness between financial institutions, to maintain a high level of quality of services, allowing customers to easily choose in full transparency, products with reasonable costs. The reduction of unjustified taxes and commissions imposed on customers, as well as the reduction of inappropriate financial services in return for the payment of commissions by the customer. 5 Take into consideration the situation of customers during the relationship in order to prevent them from being exploited by financial service providers by over-indebting them. The reduction of financing needs through the revision of the instructions in force by the supervisory authorities. Provide training to the staff of financial service providers, dedicated to this activity. 4. Financial education - Every state must be concerned with financial education and awareness through the development of a national strategy to promote education and financial literacy. The development of this strategy by government agencies and the private sector, in order to improve the financial knowledge of citizens, especially vulnerable groups such as small and medium-sized enterprises, young people and women. - The objective of financial education is to establish an integrated financial education system with a view to building a financially cultivated society and works to promote and develop the awareness of all segments of society, which will possess the skills that will enable it to be able to understand and assimilate financial products and services, knowing that financial literacy helps citizens to make healthy and studied investment decisions in their various financial transactions with the lowest degree of risk. - A balance should also be struck between the information available to consumers and financial service providers, in particular new consumers, taking into account their lack of experience in the consumption of financial services to help them understand their rights and responsibilities. Consumer awareness programs are often implemented through public awareness campaigns aimed at enabling consumers to make financial decisions tailored to their needs. 6
