Title: Common statement of the Council of Arab Central Banks and Monetary Authorities' Governors
text: Press Release issued by: The Secretariat of the Council of Arab Central Banks and Monetary Authorities Governors Arab Day for Financial Inclusion - April 27, 2021 Under the theme of Role of Digital Transformation in Increasing Financial Inclusion Enhancing and accelerating the transition to digital financial services, and importance of raising awareness Call on to: Alignment with the priorities of the Group of Twenty (G20) Promoting digital financial inclusion for young people, women and MSMEs Giving great importance to the applications and issues of Fintech Importance of building a strategy to move to a digital banking system to enhance financial inclusion Spread the digital financial literacy to all community categories The issue of promoting access to financing and financial services in the Arab countries is receiving great attention from the Council of Arab Central Banks and Monetary Authorities Governors, in recognition of the potential and great opportunities that can be achieved through enhancing financial inclusion to support inclusive and sustainable economic development, address unemployment challenges, and achieve social justice. There is no doubt that the current developments and the negative repercussions of the COVID-19 pandemic have clearly highlighted the great importance of deploying Fintech for the purposes of financial inclusion, and the need to enhance digital financial services and familiarize users with them. The pandemic has increased the demand for digital financial services and made the need to accelerated digital transformation and improved digital financial services a critical issue in economic policies in the Arab region. The available statistics highlight the great opportunities inherent in the development of digital services, as nearly 85 percent of adults in the Arab region have a mobile phone, 48 percent have a mobile phone and can access the Internet at the same time, 7 percent own mobile money account, and 33 percent made or received digital payments in the previous year, compared to nearly 44 percent globally. In this context, the Council of Arab Central Banks and Monetary Authorities Governors, considering the growing need to intensify awareness of the importance of financial inclusion among all community categories in the Arab countries, endorsed in 2016 the 27th of April as the Arab Day for Financial Inclusion, celebrated this year under the theme of Role of Digital Transformation in Increasing Financial Inclusion. It is important on this occasion to emphasize support for the efforts of the international community in enhancing financial inclusion, which was adopted by the G20 as one of the main aspects to support the sustainable development goals and enhance financial stability. The G20 pays special attention to supporting the access by young people, women and micro, small, and mediumsized enterprises (MSMEs) to digital financial services using Fintech, in addition to paying attention to digital community awareness and education, which increases the chances of success of efforts and policies in this regard. The Council is keen to give a great importance to the issues of financial inclusion in the Arab countries, as it welcomed the launch of the Financial Inclusion for the Arab Region Initiative (FIARI) by the Arab Monetary Fund in cooperation with several regional and international organisations, to empower capabilities that aim to overcome the challenges of enhancing the financial inclusion indicators in the Arab countries. In this regard, the Council values the FIARI activities that focus on digital financial transformation. The Council calls on the partner organisations to pay more attention to supporting the use of Fintech in enhancing the access of young people, women, and MSMEs to financial services, and welcomes the Digital Financial Transformation Framework in the Arab region issued in the framework of FIARI initiative in September 2020, as a roadmap to help develop domestic policies and action plans to create inclusive and secure Fintech ecosystem. The framework is based on a few primary goals to enhance access and expand usage and quality, and discusses Fintech sandboxes, consumer protection and financial literacy, financial and technical infrastructure, competition, data and cybersecurity, monitoring and cooperation. In this regard, it is important to mention measures and actions taken by the Arab countries to enhance digital financial literacy. Arab countries can also work on developing country action plans that contribute to digitally transforming financial systems and supporting economic development to achieve sustainable growth and poverty alleviation. The Council also reaffirms the need to integrate all community categories into the formal financial system, especially young people, women, entrepreneurs and MSMEs, to benefit from Fintech and follow-up efforts to raise the awareness of all these categories, protect their financial rights, and improve their knowledge of digital financial issues, so that they can make sound investment decisions. In this context, the ministries of education, culture, and higher education in the Arab region can contribute to strengthening efforts to spread and deepen education and digital financial literacy. In the context of the increasing importance of using Fintech in the financial and banking sector and the great and rapid growth witnessed by Fintech and related services, the Council commended the role of the Arab Regional Fintech Working Group launched by the Arab Monetary Fund in sharing expertise and knowledge about Fintech issues and crystallising different visions on the best way to regulate and put technologies into effect in the Arab countries. In this context, it is worth noting that the Fund issued in 2020 guiding principles to enhance the requirements of digital transformation, specifically the frameworks on digital identity and e-KYC, principles for building national strategies for Fintech, and Open banking operations. Arab countries can adopt these guiding principles within the framework of needs and procedures of each country. On the other hand, the Council values the increasing interest in Fintech issues in the activities of the Arab Financial Inclusion Task Force, and its role through developing policies and procedures related to enhancing financial inclusion, ways to improve financial inclusion indicators, working to help Arab countries implement relevant international standards and principles, and strengthening cooperation between various national institutions concerned with financial inclusion issues and between them and the relevant international organisations. Furthermore, the Council looks forward to pursuing the improvement of financial inclusion indicators, as recent statistics reflect the efforts made by the Arab countries to enhance access to financial services. These statistics reveal that the percentage of the adult population in the Arab countries who have access to formal financing and financial services has risen, on average, to 37 percent, 26 percent for women, and 28 percent for low-income groups. Although these statistics conceal disparities in this regard among Arab countries, they still highlight the great potential opportunities  especially for private financial and banking institutions  that can be exploited to enhance access to financial services in the Arab communities. In this context, it is worth noting the efforts of the Arab countries that have implemented the statistical surveys, and to emphasize the importance of following up its implementation by the rest of the countries, in order to help improve the quality of financial inclusion indicators according to the circumstances of each country. Before concluding, the Council values the efforts made by the Arab central banks and monetary authorities, the commercial banks and the official financial institutions in the past years to celebrate the Arab Day for Financial Inclusion and the related activities and events that contributed to spreading financial literacy among people. Accordingly, the Council calls on all member countries to celebrate the Arab Day for Financial Inclusion and encourage large community participation through the implementation of activities and events that enhance knowledge of financial inclusion. On this occasion, the Director General Chairman of the Board of the Arab Monetary Fund, H.E. Dr. Abdulrahman Al-Hamidy, stressed the importance and the role of financial inclusion in addressing the economic challenges that affect economic growth. He added that this goal could be achieved by mobilising resources to increase investments and create new job opportunities. Director General also praised the increasing attention being paid to issues related to enhancing financial inclusion by policymakers in the Arab countries, which would help to address the challenges of poverty, unemployment and social justice. He then referred to the efforts made by the Arab central banks and monetary authorities and the increasing attention paid to issues of improving financial inclusion and access to quality financial services at reasonable costs. Director General also lauded governors for giving appropriate importance and priority to such issues as part of their economic policies, spreading the culture of responsible finance in the banking sector, making use of Fintech in providing financial services, developing legislation, regulations and supervisory frameworks that help improve the spread of financial and banking services, following up efforts to develop sound financial and banking infrastructure systems, encouraging the expansion of non-banking financial services, as well as developing policies and programs that enhance transparency in the financial and banking transactions. Director General praised the Buna Arab payments platform, which was launched recently by the Arab Monetary Fund, and its role in providing innovative services in accordance with international standards and the best practices and technologies. He is looking forward to the platform's role in encouraging the development of digital financial services in the Arab region and linking Arab countries with their main global trading partners.

Title: Financial stability and banking sector developments in Algeria: lessons from the international financial crisis
text: BANK OF ALGERIA Istanbul, Turkey, Sunday, 4 October 2009 SPEECH BY MR MOHAMMED LAKSACI, GOVERNOR OF THE BANQUE D'ALGERIE AT THE INTERNATIONAL MONETARY AND FINANCIAL COMMITTEE AT THE NAME OF THE ISLAMIC REPUBLIC OF AFGHANISTAN, ALGERIA, GHANA, THE ISLAMIC REPUBLIC OF IRAN, MOROCCO, PAKISTAN AND FROM TUNISIA We are encouraged by recent positive developments in the global economy and international financial conditions. Strong public policy actions by a large number of advanced and developing economies have been instrumental in supporting demand, protecting the financial system from global collapse and drastic global depression. The International Monetary Fund has made unprecedented efforts to help member countries cope with the crisis, facilitating policy coordination, providing considerable financial support and injecting liquidity into the global economy. While these positive developments are cause for optimism, they should not lead to complacency, as the overall recovery is not yet firmly entrenched. It is essential to avoid a premature withdrawal of the impulse while preparing for a coordinated and timely withdrawal of exceptional support policies. Strengthening the regulation and supervision of the financial sector is also crucial for a better functioning of the system. Another important challenge is the need to accelerate efforts to help low-income countries overcome the impact of the crisis and achieve their growth and poverty reduction goals. The global crisis further underscored the crucial importance of the International Monetary Fund in the global architecture. In view of the rapid developments in the economy And the central role of the International Monetary Fund in promoting international monetary and financial stability, we agree that its supervisory role to include macro-financial stability. Continued efforts to strengthen the capacity and expertise of the International Monetary Fund in its core areas, ensure the availability of adequate permanent resources, including through the doubling of quota resources, and improve governance will strengthen the institution's relevance and legitimacy for the benefit of all member countries. Despite recent progress in improving voice and representation, much remains to be done to achieve a rebalancing of member representation. Fundamental quota reform, including through a quota formula, revised to take into account the needs of borrowing countries, is central to achieving this objective. This reform must result in a significant transfer of voting shares from advanced to developing countries, without this transfer being to the detriment of other developing countries or low-income countries. In particular, we would support a presidency in the form of a troika, with a reduced term of office of the Chairman of the Committee, in order to ensure continuity.

Title: Economic and monetary developments in 2010 and trends in the first half of 2011
text: BANK OF ALGERIA SPEECH BY MR MOHAMMED LAKSACI, GOVERNOR OF THE BANK OF ALGERIA AT THE MONETARY COMMITTEE AND INTERNATIONAL FINANCIER ON BEHALF OF AFGHANISTAN, ALGERIA, GHANA, IRAN, MOROCCO, PAKISTAN AND TUNISIA The relative improvement in the international economic and financial situation, resulting from the notable actions taken in the euro area, the improvement in economic activity in the United States and the still strong growth in emerging and developing countries (MSDS), offers a welcome respite from the heightened tensions and uncertainties of the past year. However, the recovery remains fragile and the global outlook is clouded by significant risks, including those related to a re-emergence of stress in the euro area and an abrupt rise in oil prices resulting from geopolitical tensions. Addressing these risks and putting the recovery of the global economy on a sustainable path is crucial, which requires coordinated policies and actions and the implementation of a wide range of reforms. The Consolidated Multilateral Surveillance Report and the Director-General's Action Plan provide useful guidance for achieving its objectives. We believe that adequate fiscal policy calibration in advanced economies is necessary to avoid unduly constraining short-term growth and job creation, while remaining strongly committed to medium-term fiscal consolidation and debt sustainability in order to build confidence. Reform of the tax and pension systems would provide important support for these objectives. In the current context of low inflation levels, monetary policy in these countries should remain accommodative in order to support demand, while remaining attentive to its negative effects on overall liquidity and the volatility of capital flows. It is also crucial that financial reforms continue resolutely building on the progress made to date, including by strengthening banks' capital and structuring or liquidating weak banks in the euro area, while ensuring that excessive credit contraction is avoided. Restoring the balance sheet situation of households and reviving the real estate market in the United States remains crucial. We also call for a stronger pace of completion and implementation of the comprehensive financial regulatory reform package. Although decelerating, growth in MSDS remains strong. Policies should remain oriented towards maintaining strong and sustainable growth, despite the effects of the situation in advanced economies, while working to rebuild shock absorbers and mitigate the negative impact of large and volatile capital flows. In this regard, the ongoing work to develop a comprehensive, balanced and flexible approach to the management of capital flows should not compromise the flexibility of member countries to adopt the policies and instruments they deem appropriate to their specific circumstances, taking into account the experiences of other countries. In the Middle East and North Africa region, although conditions vary between groups of countries, the main challenge is to ensure strong, sustainable and inclusive growth, despite an unfavourable external environment, including by restoring macroeconomic stability and investor confidence. The task is particularly difficult in the Arab countries undergoing political transition in view of their significant social and employment needs, which calls for the establishment of effective policies that promote investment and balanced and job-creating growth. Adequate international support, including financial and technical assistance, is crucial, with the IMF playing a key role in this regard. In particular, the commitments made under the Deauville Partnership initiative, in terms of financing and market access, must be implemented within the expected time frame. In the same vein, and in this challenging global context, enhanced international support, including from the IMF, to low-income countries is crucial to help them meet their substantial development needs and mitigate the impact of rising energy costs and potential additional increases. In this regard, member countries are called upon to contribute their shares of the 0.7 billion in profits on the sale of gold to increase the IMF's concessional financing capacity. Other actions to ensure the long-term sustainability of the financing of the Poverty Reduction and Growth Trust Fund (PRGF), including through bilateral grants and the distribution of profits on the sale of gold. We note and support the ongoing work at the IMF to strengthen the effectiveness of surveillance. We look forward to further progress towards the development of an integrated, more effective and impartial bilateral and multilateral surveillance framework. We agree on the need to ensure the timely entry into force of quota and governance reform. We also stress the importance of completing the comprehensive review of the quota formula by January 2013 and the fifteenth General Review of Quotas by January 2014, and should result in a realignment of relative shares in favour of dynamic DSDPs without this realignment at the expense of other DSMPs.

Title: Economic and monetary developments in Algeria
text: BANK OF ALGERIA 11 OCTOBER 2008 SPEECH OF MR. MOHAMMED LAKSACI GOVERNOR OF THE BANK OF ALGERIA TO THE INTERNATIONAL MONETARY COMMITTEE AND FINANCIAL FOR AFGHANISTAN, ALGERIA, GHANA, THE ISLAMIC REPUBLIC OF IRAN, MOROCCO, PAKISTAN AND THE TUNISIA Since our last meeting, the global economic situation has deteriorated considerably. Global economic growth has slowed sharply, particularly in the United States and many advanced economies, which are now on the brink of recession. The recent intensification of the financial crisis and its rapid spread to other countries, including emerging and developing countries, are further clouding the prospects for global economic growth. Against this backdrop of a shock to the global economy unprecedented since the 1930s and heightened uncertainties, despite recent actions in several major capitals, stabilizing markets and restoring confidence are our top priorities. This depends crucially on cooperation and strengthening international policy coordination, including ensuring adequate liquidity, addressing the issue of bank compromised assets and the recapitalisation of financial institutions, as well as ensuring adequate depositor collateral. At the same time, monetary and financial policies, in the context of a downward trend in inflationary pressures, must be geared towards supporting the rapid economic recovery, while preserving fiscal stability over the medium term. As a universal institution with a mandate to preserve international monetary and financial stability, the International Monetary Fund must play a proactive and leading role in promoting coordination and providing effective advice. The IMF should also stand ready to provide prompt, if necessary, the necessary assistance to member countries to contain the spillover effects of the crisis. We welcome the Managing Director's announcement of the IMF's activation of emergency procedures to respond quickly to requests for assistance, with high access to finance and mitigated conditionality. We reiterate our call for the establishment as soon as possible of a new liquidity instrument for countries with access to markets and those seeking greater integration into the global economy. When confidence is restored and the crisis is contained, the necessary lessons will have to be learned in order to ensure a sound and stable functioning of the international financial system. As the Director General points out, it is already clear that major failures in regulatory and supervisory frameworks in advanced countries, in risk management in large private financial institutions, in market discipline mechanisms, are major factors in this crisis and must be addressed in a radical way. It is also very important to point out that this crisis and its high costs to the global economy have highlighted the need for the IMF to regain lost ground for the effective fulfilment of its mandate. In particular, its central supervisory role, including systemically important economies and financial markets, needs to be significantly strengthened in order to enable early detection of stability risks and to provide timely and effective advice. In this regard, more needs to be done to ensure that candour and impartiality surveillance are one of the main weaknesses that prevented the early detection of the ongoing financial crisis. Finally, the effectiveness of IMF surveillance can only be enhanced if its recommendations and advice are taken into account by all IMF members, particularly systemically important ones. In order to ensure that the IMF's assessments and advice in its key areas of responsibility are of the highest quality and relevance, strengthening the IMF's analytical capacity and expertise in these areas, including through the recruitment and retention of high-quality staff, is crucial and should not be hampered by excessive budgetary constraints. Ensuring adequate and stable revenues for the IMF is also a priority. In this respect, it is crucial that the necessary parliamentary ratifications of the essential components of the model be obtained as soon as possible. of recently adopted revenues for the IMF, namely the extension of the IMF's investment powers and the sale of part of its gold holdings. We also reiterate our reservations about the payment of IMF technical assistance by member countries, particularly low- and middle-income countries. As the Director-General rightly pointed out, at the same time as the financial crisis is being addressed, attention must continue to be paid to the need to contain the impact of high food and energy prices on the most vulnerable member countries. In this regard, we welcome the recent amendments to the External Shocks Facility (ECF) to help these countries cope with external shocks. We encourage the IMF to continue to play a catalytic role in mobilizing greater financial assistance to countries affected by high food and energy prices, and to provide them with adequate advice and technical assistance, taking into account their socio-political circumstances and constraints. We continue to follow with interest the ongoing work on IMF governance and hope that this will help adapt the imf to the globalized economy and the new international financial environment and improve the voice and representativeness of developing countries in the IMF's decision-making process and governance structure.

Title: Statement to the International Monetary and Financial Committee on behalf of several countries
text: 12 APRIL 2008 SPEECH BY MR MOHAMMED LAKSACI GOVERNOR OF THE BANK OF ALGERIA AT THE INTERNATIONAL MONETARY AND FINANCIAL COMMITTEE FOR AFGHANISTAN, ALGERIA, GHANA, THE ISLAMIC REPUBLIC OF IRAN, MOROCCO, PAKISTAN AND TUNISIA 12 APRIL 2008 Since our last meeting, the spread of the crisis in international financial markets, linked to the deepening crisis of the us real estate market, has further clouded the global economic outlook. Economic growth slowed further in the United States and weakened in other advanced economies, reflecting continued tightening of credit conditions and weaker demand growth. Emerging and developing economies have remained resilient so far and continue to drive the global economy and play a stabilizing role. However, downside risks, linked to a deeper and longer-lasting financial crisis and a sharp slowdown in growth in advanced economies, as well as contagion effects, have increased. At the same time, inflationary pressures have become more evident in several parts of the world. Addressing these risks requires decisive action by advanced economies to counter the ongoing financial crisis and reinvigorate growth. In particular, continued and coordinated interventions to loosen liquidity contraction, greater transparency, and strengthened financial regulation and supervision are crucial to restore confidence and avoid the risk of a global credit collapse. Given its universal nature and its primary mandate to preserve the stability of the international financial system, the International Monetary Fund is well placed to, and has the responsibility to, play an important role in helping to address the ongoing crisis and contain its potential contagion effects. Of particular importance are efforts to improve the relevance and quality of IMF advice, including by strengthening bilateral, regional, and multilateral surveillance, particularly with respect to advanced economies, and by deepening the analysis of developments and risks in financial markets and the analysis of macro-financial interconnections. In the context of the IMF's medium-term strategic vision, the focus on these important aspects of the FUND's work is a step in the right direction. In view of the increase in global uncertainties and risks, it is equally crucial to intensify efforts to establish a new liquidity instrument for countries with access to financial markets and those seeking greater integration into the global economy. To be effective, the ceilings for access to the Fund's resources under this instrument must be high, with a concentration of disbursements at the beginning of the period and reduced costs. 1 We note with growing concern the recent significant increases in food and energy prices, the challenges this poses for policymakers, and the significant impact on populations in middle- and low-income countries. We call on the IMF to provide appropriate advice to help these member countries cope with this price increase without undermining their political and social stability. Where necessary, flexibility in program implementation and/or greater access to IMF resources should be considered. We remain awaiting a review of the Facility for Exogenous Shocks. The proposals for quota and voice reforms, as recently approved by the Executive Board and put to the vote of IMF Governors, include positive elements that, taken together, are an important first step towards the goal of strengthening the IMF's legitimacy and effectiveness. In this respect, we welcome the proposal to triple basic voting rights, although this is far from correcting the past erosion of their relative importance in total voting rights. We also welcome the use of GDP-PPP (Gross Domestic Product calculated on the basis of Purchasing Power Parity) in the new formula, although we believe that a higher weight of GDP-PPP in the combination used for the calculation of GDP would better reflect economic realities and improve the formula. The increase in the voting shares of the most dynamic countries, including those of several emerging countries, as well as those of low-income and other developing countries, resulting from these proposals for quota and voice reforms, are in line with the recommendations of the Singapore Resolution. The same applies to the proposal to allocate an additional Post of Junior Administrator to each of the two offices representing Sub-Saharan Africa. However, these reform proposals fall far short of the expectations of the international community, namely, a substantial change in the governance structure of the Bretton Woods institutions, including through a significant redistribution of quotas and voting shares from advanced countries to developing countries. Indeed, it would take more than the modest increase in the voting share of developing countries, as a result of the reform proposals, for this objective to be achieved. We welcome the recognition of the need to refine the formula, including in relation to the method of measuring the variables "degree of openness" and "variability", and hope that work in this area in the Executive Board will be undertaken as soon as possible. We support the call for the Executive Board to recommend additional quota adjustments in future quota reviews. Finally, we believe that the International Monetary and Financial Committee (CFP) can play a useful role in allaying the concerns and disappointment expressed both within and outside the IMF with regard to the outcome of this reform in terms of rebalancing quotas and voting power between advanced and developing countries. This could be done by indicating in the CIMF Communiqu8e that future quota adjustments should result in more voting power for emerging market and developing countries as a whole. In the same vein, we reiterate our call for efforts to address the significant under-representation of certain regions, particularly Africa and the Middle East, in IMF staff and management. We note the Executive Board's agreement on the new revenue and expenditure framework to put the IMF's finances on a sustainable path, direct its resources to its core areas of expertise, and contribute to the modernization of its structures and operations. Based on the recommendations of the Eminent Personalities Committee (EPC), the new revenue model represents a shift from loan-related revenue streams to investment-related revenue streams that are therefore more predictable and sustainable. Such as the 2 As the Managing Director stressed, it is crucial that the necessary parliamentary ratifications be obtained as soon as possible to enable the rapid implementation of key components of the model, namely the extension of the IMF's investment powers and the sale of part of its gold holdings. That said, the introduction of another component, namely the investment of part of the quotas, an important source of income recommended by the CEP, would have strengthened the sustainability of the new model. We continue to have strong reservations regarding repayments under the Poverty Reduction and Growth Facility (PRGF) to the General Resources Account (MAF). Given its importance to developing countries, we also have reservations about the proposed reduction of IMF technical assistance and the imposition of fees in this regard. Indeed, it would be a misguided signal that low-income countries, in particular, should bear the brunt of the IMF's fiscal recovery. 3

Title: Intervention before the Council of the Nation
text: 13 July 2008 ECONOMIC AND MONETARY DEVELOPMENTS IN ALGERIA Speech by the Governor of the Bank of Algeria, Dr. Mohammed Laksaci Before the Council of the Nation 1. International environment After the emergence of severe turbulence in international financial markets since mid-2007, causing global financial turmoil and significant losses for international banks, the resurgence of inflationary pressures represents a second major challenge. The risks of a slowdown in global economic growth are clearly on the rise. The growth rate of the world economy expected for 2008 would be in the order of 3.7 per cent compared to 4.6 per cent for 2007. The magnitude of the turbulence in international financial markets has been such that the health of leading banks in Europe and the United States remains a cause for concern. Indeed, after the large losses announced by international banks, it is not excluded that some of them will make significant additional impairments. In addition, the disengagement of the major banks, in particular in the form of a tightening of their lending and credit conditions, in a context of general and increasingly marked aversion to risk in the financial markets is very significant. The magnitude and persistence of funding difficulties for world-leading banks have led central banks to take exceptional measures, including: providing liquidity for longer maturities; accept a much wider range of security rights; provide facilities to a greater diversity of institutions. New facilities have also been introduced to avoid reputational problems associated with standing facilities. The readiness of central banks in industrialized countries to act together and vigorously to provide liquidity in financial markets has contributed to the worsening of the liquidity crisis. Thus, these central banks have fully played their role as providers of liquidity. In addition, as part of the strengthening of the supervisory mechanisms of the financial system, the regulatory and supervisory bodies have worked to strengthen the prudential supervision of liquidity management. With regard to strengthening surveillance mechanisms, it is worth emphasizing that at the international level: 1 the Financial Stability Forum (FSF), following a substantive review of the turbulence in financial markets, presented recommendations aimed at, in particular, to improve banks' capital adequacy and strengthen risk management, establish greater transparency (especially for off-balance-sheet entities) and improve valuation methods. the Basel Committee on Banking Supervision, at the level of the Bank of International Regulations, announced complementary initiatives for to develop the resilience of the banking system. The resurgence of inflation globally presents a second challenge, as the increase in the general price index is now close to 4.7 per cent, driven by higher oil and food prices. The global inflation rate was 3.6 per cent in 2007. These inflationary pressures have re-emerged at a time when the risks of a slowdown in global growth are evident in 2008. Emerging and developing economies are particularly affected by rising inflation, as food prices have a much greater impact on inflation in low- and middle-income countries; food occupies a larger place in household consumption expenditure. The resurgence of inflation, particularly soaring prices for basic foodstuffs, is a major shock to low-income African countries, jeopardizing poverty reduction programmes. 2. External financial position With the return to macro-financial equilibrium in the early 2000s, the sustainability of the balance of payments has emerged as a foundation in this area. Its consolidation during the years 2001 to 2007 is reinforced by the favourable external environment in terms of hydrocarbon price developments. Indeed, the average price of a barrel of crude oil rose from 65.85 in 2006 to 74.95 in 2007, an increase of 13.8%. 2.1 Balance of payments sustainability The year 2007 is characterized, from the point of view of the external position, by a strong improvement in the overall balance of payments compared to 2006, which had already recorded remarkable performances. The overall surplus (29.55 billion) far exceeded the surplus in 2006 (17.73 billion) in a context of strong growth in imports of goods and services. The year 2007 is also distinguished by a new phenomenon, namely that the overall balance of payments surplus is close to the external current account surplus, which is estimated at 30.60 billion. Hydrocarbon exports were valued at 59.61 billion in 2007, an increase of 11.2%, despite the decline in exports in volume. The share of partners in the national hydrocarbon company is down (3.90 billion) from the 2006 level of 5.29 billion. 2 This trend is linked to the windfall profit tax mechanism that was introduced in July 2006. On the other hand, non-hydrocarbon exports remained low in 2007 (0.98 billion), even down from 1.13 billion in 2006. The contribution of non-hydrocarbon exports to the sustainability of the current account balance is very small, which poses the necessary need to improve external competitiveness in the face of the increased openness of the national economy. The upward trend in imports of goods between 2003 and 2007, with a relative pause in 2006, is another phenomenon that characterizes the current account balance, particularly in 2007 when the growth rate in this area was 27.4%. The level of imports thus reached 26.35 billion, compared to 20.68 billion in 2006 and 13.32 billion in 2003. For 2007, the increase in imports is significant for semi-finished products (44 per cent), food products (30.3 per cent) and industrial and agricultural capital goods (17.2 per cent). The significant increase in food imports is largely due to soaring prices of these products on international markets. In addition, 2007 was also characterized by a very strong increase (45 per cent) in imports of non-factor services (6.93 billion in 2007 compared to 4.78 billion in 2006). This increase relates to imports of building and public works services, technical services and maritime and air transport services. This upward trend is linked, in particular, to the increase in the investment rate (investment/GDP): 35% in 2007 against 29.7% in 2006. This is correlated with the execution of the state capital budget. It is important to emphasize that the positive effect of the sharp reduction in external debt in 2005-2006 is well expressed at the level of factor services (interest payments) from 0.76 billion in 2006 to only 0.23 billion in 2007 and at the level of the capital account where repayments in principal of external debt now amount to only 1.28 billion compared to 12.87 billion in 2006. Thus, with a small deficit in 2007, the capital account is now marked by a trend towards equilibrium, especially since the foreign direct investment (net) heading is above one billion dollars in the last three years. Overall, the external financial position was particularly characterized in 2007 by an overall balance of payments balance almost double that achieved in 2006 and 2005. This performance is all the more appreciable as this overall surplus is close to the current account surplus; the latter de facto feeding the official foreign exchange reserves. The stock of official foreign exchange reserves increased from 77.781 billion at the end of 2006 to 90.960 billion at the end of June 2007 and to 110.180 billion at the end of 2007. The sustained increase in the level of official foreign exchange reserves in recent years has been combined with diversification of investment currencies to better manage foreign exchange risk between major currencies. The conduct of this diversification correlative to the pursuit of prudent management of reserves in 3 Terms of level of risk inherent in investment instruments has enabled the Bank of Algeria to cope with turbulence on international financial markets. In addition, the Bank of Algeria has further increased investments in non-risky assets, even though the yield on some of these instruments is cyclically declining. Given the acuteness of the turbulence in international financial markets and its negative effects on developing economies, the high level of official foreign exchange reserves and the stabilization of the real effective exchange rate of the dinar, in the context of the medium- and long-term sustainability of the balance of payments, constitute a double guarantee against such external shocks. 2.2 External debt sustainability After rescheduling the external debt with the Paris Club and the London Club between 1994 and 1998, to cope with the acuteness of the external debt burden, the improvement of Algeria's external financial position from 2000 onwards has made it possible to reduce external debt indicators to sustainable levels, particularly since 2004 with the implementation of external debt repayments in advance. The continuation of early repayments during 2005 and 2006 led to a sharp reduction in external public debt, reflecting the success of Algeria's external debt reduction policy and the level of external financial security. The stock of medium- and long-term external debt fell to 4.889 billion at the end of 2007, or only 3.6 per cent of gross domestic product. After a relative stabilization from 2001 to 2003 at around 22.5-23 billion, the level of outstanding external debt in the medium and long term has been on a downward trend since 2004, from 16.485 billion at the end of 2005 to 5.062 billion at the end of 2006 and 4.889 billion at the end of 2007. Following the full repayment of rescheduling loans, the structure of the stock of medium- and long-term debt by type of credit at the end of 2007 indicates a new trend where bilateral loans represent about 80%. In terms of debt servicing, 2007 was characterized by a very low ratio (2.26%). All in all, the sustained implementation of the strategic decision to reduce Algeria's external debt has allowed an economically efficient use of available financial resources, especially since the turbulence on the international financial markets since mid-2007 has led to a tightening of the credit conditions of international banks. 4 3. Recent developments in the banking system With the entry into operation of a new bank at the end of 2007, the banking system, in addition to the central bank, consists of twenty-five (25) licensed banks and financial institutions and a development bank undergoing restructuring. Public banks still predominate by the importance of their network of branches spread throughout the national territory. But the pace of setting up branches of private banks has accelerated markedly in recent years. At the end of December 2007, the network of public banks outside the Bank of Algeria included 1093 branches and branches and that of banks and private financial institutions 196 branches against 152 in 2006. The total number of counters stands at 1338, including the counters of the Bank of Algeria, i.e. one counter for 25700 inhabitants against 26200 in 2006 and 26800 in 2005. The improvement in banking services from the point of view of network development is confirmed by the ratio of the working population to bank counters, which is 7850 people of working age per counter in 2007 against 8030 in 2006. Although the level of bank intermediation is gradually improving, the related indicators remain below those achieved in Algeria's Mediterranean neighbouring countries. At the end of 2007, loans to the economy, including non-performing loans repurchased by the Treasury through the issuance of securities, represented 54.6% of gross domestic product excluding hydrocarbons. 3.1 Activities and performance As in 2006, the activity of collecting sight and term resources from banks, excluding pre-import deposits, experienced a significant development in 2007 with a growth of 27% against 19% in 2006. Pre-import deposits that are no longer included, as of 2007 (frozen deposits) in the money supply (M2), also increased sharply in 2007 (68%). In addition, as in 2006, the share of deposits in the private sector and households remains high (71.2% at the end of 2007 compared with 74.2% at the end of 2006 and 79.3% at the end of 2005), while in deposits collected from the public sector, the share of demand deposits predominates (83.9% at the end of 2007 against 76.1% at the end of 2006 and 67.9% at the end of 2005). As in previous years, 2007 was characterized by significant growth in banks' means of action (demand deposits, term deposits in dinars). The growth rates of these deposits were appreciable (31% against 20% in 2006) in a context of strong improvement in bank liquidity partly due to the evolution of deposits of hydrocarbon companies. The evolution of foreign currency deposits collected by banks fell in 2007 by 2.9 per cent compared to a growth of 3.9 per cent in 2006. As regards the allocation of resources collected by banks, the distribution of credit to the economy is increasing, but this increase has been combined with the relative increase in risky claims. 5 In the total loans distributed, the share of private banks is increasing. Although slow, this evolution, especially in 2007, is appreciable (11.5% against 9.3% in 2006). It concerns the financing of private companies and households. Total loans distributed by banks, including non-performing loans repurchased by the Treasury in 2005-2007, increased from 1994.9 billion dinars at the end of 2006 to 2298.6 billion dinars at the end of 2007, an increase of 15.2 per cent compared to 12.1 per cent in 2006. Loans to the private sector increased by 15 per cent and loans to the public sector by 15.4 per cent. The share of loans to the private sector in the total outstanding loans distributed by banks remained stable between 2006 and 2007 (52.9%). Outstanding loans distributed to the public sector, including loans repurchased by the Treasury, remain significant at 47.2 per cent of total loans to the economy, i.e. 43.4 per cent in direct loans and 3.8 per cent in purchases of bonds issued by state-owned enterprises, compared with 47.1 per cent in 2006 (42.2 per cent in direct loans and 4.9 per cent in bond purchases). From the point of view of the outstanding loans distributed by banks at the end of 2007 excluding loans repurchased by the Treasury, medium- and long-term loans represent 51.2% of outstanding loans against 48.8% for short-term loans. This is a new trend that began in 2006, due to the significant evolution of long-term loans distributed to finance investments in the energy and water sector but also the purchase of housing and other durable goods by households. As for mortgage loans, their outstanding amount increased from 94 billion dinars at the end of 2006 to 110.6 billion dinars at the end of 2007. With regard to the profitability of banks, the return on capital of private banks remains higher than that of public banks over the period 20052007. The return on equity (ROE) ratio of public banks improved significantly to 22.79% in 2007 from 17.41% in 2006 and 5.63% in 2005, while private banks recorded a decline in profitability in 2006 and an increase in 2007 to 28.01% in 2007 from 23.40% in 2006 and 25.43% in 2005. The improvement in the profitability of banks in 2007, both public and private, in a context of relative stability of their capital, is the result of the increase in their results. The rate of return on assets is also higher in private banks compared to that recorded in banks. The return on assets of public banks increased slightly in 2007 (0.84% compared to 0.75% in 2006), while the ratio of private banks improved significantly in 2007 from 2.49% in 2006 to 3.21% in 2007. 3.2 Control and Supervision To ensure the integrity and soundness of the banking system, the permanent monitoring of banks and financial institutions, including their valuation procedures, monitoring, management and control of risks, is rigorously conducted by the Bank of Algeria and the Banking Commission, on the basis of the regulations issued by the Council of Money and Credit. Thus, in addition to the control on parts carried out on the basis of declarations from banks and financial institutions sent to the Bank 6 in Algeria, on-the-spot inspection missions are dispatched to banks and financial institutions. The strategic objective is to ensure orderly development bank intermediation. For banking supervision, coin control is the first level of an alert system allowing better monitoring of the banking system. The scope of control on documents covers all 24 approved institutions, namely 18 banks and 6 financial institutions. In this context and during the years 2002 to 2007, 2558 referrals (reminders, follow-ups, requests for explanations and information) were sent to the banks and financial institutions subject to tax. They concern, in particular, delays in the transmission of reports, non-compliance with standards, errors and inconsistencies and requests for information. The audit work also covers the examination of the internal control reports of banks and financial institutions, whose regulatory framework was established in 2002. This system leads banks and financial institutions to take charge of the assessment, management and control of risks according to international standards. The ongoing improvement of banks' information systems, thanks to the modernisation of payment systems, has helped to reduce reporting delays and better monitoring of risks. However, additional efforts are expected in this area. As regards on-the-spot checks, missions are systematically planned and carried out, including 101 for the last year alone, out of a total of 409 missions for the period 2002 to 2007, including in the context of agency openings. During the same period, all banks and financial institutions were thus subject to full on-the-spot checks covering all business compartments (credit portfolios, foreign trade operations, other customer operations). While the on-site missions carried out for 2007 confirmed the existence of operational risks induced by shortcomings noted, it should be noted that the management of some of the malfunctions observed allowed a certain improvement. As regards the subsequent verification of foreign trade operations, the Sworn inspectors of the Bank of Algeria proceeded to the establishment, since 2003, 238 reports of infringement following the verification. The minutes have is transmitted to the courts concerned with the lodging of a complaint. 7 The year 2007 saw a new type of control affecting both payment systems (ARTS and ATCI). This is the first inspection of these two systems that went into production in the first half of 2006. This inspection affected, in particular, the organization and procedures, continuity and safety of operations, as well as the control of incidents and releases. Finally, as part of the strengthening of control and supervision, 2007 also saw the conduct of an on-site inspection mission to monitor the implementation of the anti-money-laundering and anti-terrorist financing system. This mission involved, in a first phase, eight banks. It was preceded by an audit based on a questionnaire from the Banking Commission sent in the second half of 2006 to all banks and financial institutions. 4. Monetary situation Macroeconomic developments over the past seven years 2000-2006 have led to the persistence of excess savings over investment as a structural feature of the national economy. This distinctive element of the macroeconomic framework is confirmed by a sound financial position, an element of sound macroeconomic management that has contributed to resilience to external shocks. As part of the conduct of sound macroeconomic management of the additional resources, the sharp reduction in external public debt inherent in the acceleration of advance repayments in 2006, for substantial amounts, was even combined with a sustained accumulation of resources from the revenue regulation fund. Thus, the completion of the sustained conduct of the external deleveraging strategy led to a more sustained accumulation of official foreign exchange reserves during 2007, a source of strong monetary expansion. Also, 2007 is part of the new trend of recovery in the pace of monetary expansion, mitigated in part by the magnitude of early repayments of external debt, after the downward cycle in this area recorded between 2001 and 2004. It was in a context of strong monetary expansion and a resumption of inflation in 2007 that the Bank of Algeria took care to absorb excess liquidity through a flexible and orderly conduct of indirect monetary policy instruments. 4.1 Monetary developments The analysis of the consolidated monetary situation during 2007 shows that the evolution of the money supply continues to be driven by that of the aggregate net foreign assets, as net foreign assets have exceeded, since the end of 2005, monetary and quasi-monetary liquidity in the national economy. Indeed, the official foreign exchange reserves held by the Bank of Algeria are the main source of money creation, especially since they largely guarantee the 8 money supply in the sense of M2. The process of monetization of foreign exchange resources repatriated and transferred, de jure with regard to hydrocarbon export earnings, to the Bank of Algeria clearly explains this causality. The aggregate net foreign assets in the consolidated monetary situation grew particularly strongly in 2007, at a rate of 34.46 per cent. This aggregate increased from 6419.44 billion dinars at the end of June 2007 to 7415.56 billion dinars at the end of December 2007, against a level of 5515.05 billion dinars at the end of December 2006. As a result of the structural expansion of the aggregate net foreign assets, 2007 was characterized by strong growth in the money supply, although the upward pace of expansion of M2 was somewhat mitigated by the magnitude of advance repayments of external debt in 2005 and 2006. Compared to this aggregate at the end of December 2006 (series of M2 made homogeneous according to the new definition), the increase amounts to 24.17% for 2007, of which 10.89% for the second half of 2007. With monetary growth above the pace of 2006 (18.6%), 2007 is therefore part of the new trend of recovery in the pace of monetary expansion after the downward cycle from 2001 to 2004. In addition, the evolution of the structure of the M2 money supply provides information on the behaviour of the main economic agents, especially in this period of recovery in the expansion of monetary and quasi-monetary liquidity. Thus, the strong expansion of bank deposits, at 27 per cent year-on-year compared to 19 per cent in 2006, is driven more by the increase in deposits from the public sector than from the private sector. In terms of deposit structure by instrument at the end of 2007, demand deposits with banks, the Treasury and CCPs represented 62.54% of total deposits compared to 55.84% at the end of December 2006, confirming the upward trend relative to the ratio of 33.89% recorded at the end of 2003. The structural upward trend in demand deposits in the banks' equity structure over the past five years is correlative to the significant increase in public sector demand deposits in the context of excess liquidity in the interbank money market. On the other hand, the evolution of the deposit structure clearly shows the sharp decline in the share of term deposits in dinars to 32.58% at the end of 2007 against 37.71% at the end of 2006 and 59.29% at the end of 2003. The analysis of the high rates of expansion of the M2 aggregate in relation to the trend of nominal gross domestic product is also useful, given the structural nature of excess liquidity. Indeed, the liquidity ratio, as an average M2/gross domestic product ratio, rose from 52.57% in 2006 to 57.63% in 2007, anchoring a new upward trend. However, excluding deposits in the hydrocarbon sector, estimated as a proxy variable, and in relation to non-hydrocarbon gross domestic product, the liquidity ratio is stable at 84.38 per cent in 2007 compared to 83.75 per cent in 2006, 83.03 per cent in 2005, 83.20 per cent in 2004 and 84.35 per cent in 2003. The latter ratio is significant for the assessment of inflation risks, in order to refine the conduct of monetary policy and establish lasting financial and monetary stability. 9 The aggregate credit to the economy, as the second counterpart of the money supply, increased by 15.22% in 2007 against 12.16% in 2006, in parallel with the resumption of the rates of expansion of the monetary aggregate M2. Even on a half-year basis, loans to the economy recorded a significant increase in 2007 (9.26% in the second half of the year) compared to 2006 (6.51% in the second half). This trend of the credit aggregate to the economy now reveals the importance of the credit "channel" in the transmission of the effects of recent monetary developments. In particular, an analysis of the structure of credits by legal sector shows that a greater share of credit continues to be allocated to the private sector. At the end of 2007, the share of loans distributed to the private sector (52.87 per cent) remained stable compared to the rate reached at the end of 2006 (52.95 per cent), reflecting a smaller increase in credit to the private sector (15.03 per cent) than in credit to the public sector (15.43 per cent). This trend is combined with a decrease in the relative share of non-performing loans, as the controls of banks' portfolios by the Bank of Algeria and the Banking Commission have intensified. In addition, the evolution of loans to the economy, from the point of view of maturity terms, testifies to the continuation of the upward trend for medium- and long-term loans intended for the financing of investments. The relative share of medium- and long-term loans increased from 49.58% at the end of December 2006 to 51.26% at the end of December 2007. This certain momentum of medium- and long-term loans is in line with the favourable nature of the bank financing conditions of the national economy, especially since the increase in investment credits comes in addition to the strong flow of financing from the budgetary sphere for disbursements made from the capital budget. This aggregate is estimated at 1420.1 billion dinars in 2007, while it had increased from 806.9 billion dinars in 2005 to 1015 billion dinars in 2006. In addition, new mixed investment projects, in particular project finance in the water and energy sectors, have increased medium- and long-term credit as a new core for the absorption of stable resources from banks. Mortgages also recorded a significant boost in 2007. Given the availability of increased loanable funds and the need for productive investment, healthy credit to the economy is expected to increase further and finance more businesses. Also, these bank financing possibilities must be conducted by banks in line with the necessary improvement in the assessment, management and control of credit risks. In addition, credit guarantee mechanisms provided by specialized bodies set up to facilitate the financing of SME investments and the acquisition of housing by households should contribute to the development of investment in non-hydrocarbon sectors. It is no longer just a question of achieving functional efficiency at the level of banks in this area, but of contributing in an orderly manner to the macroeconomic adjustment of domestic investment to national savings. 10 Overall, the quality of monetary stability that has characterized monetary and credit developments in recent years has not been affected by the recovery in the rate of monetary growth in 2006 (18.60 per cent) and 2007 (24.17 per cent), especially as core inflation has remained under control. 4.2 Money market and monetary policy conduct The gradual development of the money market during the 1990s, a period of structural adjustment and financial reform, provided a source of liquidity for banks. Indeed, refinancing with the Bank of Algeria remained the most important source of liquidity for banks until the early 2000s. With the advent of excess liquidity since 2001, the Bank of Algeria is no longer a source of liquidity supply to banks, since it has been developing, since April 2002, it has been developing instruments for reducing excess liquidity on the money market. The upward trend in the level of bank liquidity reflects the structural nature of excess liquidity on the money market; bank liquidity increased by 74.48 per cent in 2007 compared to 56.68 per cent in 2006. The outstanding bank liquidity therefore rose to 2001.18 billion dinars at the end of December 2007, after a rise from 732 billion dinars at the end of December 2005 to 1146.9 billion dinars at the end of December 2006. It is worth recalling that the formation of bank liquidity is correlated, to a large extent, with the evolution of the aggregate net foreign assets that drives monetary expansion, even though part of the monetization of foreign exchange reserves feeds into the Revenue Regulation Fund. Faced with the growing liquidity of the banking system, the interbank money market experienced a relative recovery in activity during 2007 compared to 2006, but well below the outstanding amount reached at the end of 2005 (76.4 billion dinars). To stem the excess of structural liquidity and limit its inflationary effects in 2007, the Bank of Algeria intensified its interventions on the money market through liquidity recoveries with maturities of 7 days and 3 months. This market instrument saw its role increase significantly compared to the interest-bearing deposit facility (standing facility) and the reserve requirement in the conduct of monetary policy in the second half of 2007. Careful observation of the behaviour of autonomous factors and mastery of liquidity forecasting techniques are essential for a sustained improvement in bank liquidity management, as excess liquidity in the money market has become structural. The change in the net foreign assets of the Bank of Algeria, whose growth rate was 33.59 per cent in 2007 compared to 33.12 per cent in 2006, emerges as the main explanatory variable for excess liquidity on the money market, even if part of the monetization of foreign currency assets is de facto sterilized. 11 In addition, as part of the reduction of the internal public debt, the repayment by the Treasury, in November 2007, of all the advances of the Bank of Algeria allowed an effective contraction of a source of expansion of bank liquidity. Cash circulation outside the Bank of Algeria, which emerged as a second autonomous factor in 2007, increased by 18.78% against 17.4% in 2006 and had a downward effect in bank liquidity for 203.12 billion dinars, a contraction effect greater than that of 2006 (160.39 billion dinars). Faced with the upward trend in bank liquidity, as the sum of the autonomous liquidity-providing factors is greater than that of the autonomous liquidity-taking factors, the Bank of Algeria has sharply increased liquidity recoveries from mid-June 2007, bringing them to 1100 billion dinars after a stabilization in the first half of the year to an amount of 450 billion dinars. With this decision, the Bank of Algeria strengthened the role of its interventions in the money market in order to adequately absorb excess liquidity, while leaving the banks the initiative to manage part of their cash surpluses through the 24-hour remunerated deposit facility. In adopting the quantitative growth targets for monetary and credit aggregates for 2007, as well as the revision of the target for the M2 growth rate, the Monetary and Credit Council underlined the now forward-looking stance of monetary policy in the face of the strengthening M2 expansion and the upward risks to inflation; monetary policy contributing to an environment conducive to sustainable growth. To ensure that monetary policy objectives are achieved, the Monetary and Credit Council examined, twice in 2007, the instruments for conducting monetary policy and their relevance in such a context of excess structural liquidity. Thus, the Bank of Algeria has been equipped with a monetary instrument allowing it to continue to deal with this structural phenomenon, an indication of the existence of upside risks for price stability in the medium term. In particular, at a time of increasing inflationary risks, notably from imported inflation, the management of excess liquidity in the money market is emerging as a major concern in the formulation and conduct of monetary policy, as the lender of last resort has ceased to be active since the end of 2001; the money market is de facto the almost only channel for transmitting monetary policy impulses to the economy. The improvement in 2007, with the entry into production in 2006 of the two payment systems, in the speed and completeness of bank liquidity data contributed to the conduct of monetary policy by the Bank of Algeria. In the conduct of monetary policy, and capitalizing on the sustained efforts in terms of projection of autonomous factors and forecasting of bank liquidity, the Bank of Algeria made greater use of the liquidity recovery instrument during 2007, both seven-day recoveries and forward recoveries (three months), leaving the flexible use of the facility of remunerated deposits at the initiative of the banks. 12 The context of excess structural liquidity that fully prevailed in 2007 meant that monetary policy was conducted mainly through the Liquidity Recovery Instrument, a money market instrument, as well as the deposit facility, with the aim of making the control of monetary aggregates more effective with a particular focus on the monetary base aggregate as an operational objective. Indeed, keeping monetary aggregates under control remains an objective with a relatively high priority. From the point of view of the day-to-day conduct of monetary policy, in compliance with the operational framework defined in this area, the Bank of Algeria stabilized the overall amount of recoveries at about 450 billion dinars during the first five months of 2007, then adjusted it to 1100 billion dinars from mid-June 2007, to absorb more liquidity. As a result, liquidity recoveries are emerging as the main active instrument for conducting monetary policy, with a much increased role in the second half of 2007. While the remunerated deposit facility, set up in August 2005 by the Banque d'Algerie, remained an instrument actively used by some banks during 2007 in order to sterilize part of their excess cash, its role in the day-to-day conduct of monetary policy was substantially reduced from mid-June 2007 in favour of the liquidity recovery instrument, market instrument. The relative share of the facilitated interest-bearing deposit instrument in the absorption of excess liquidity fell to 12.42 per cent at the end of June 2007, from 64.43 per cent at the end of May 2007 and from about 54.5 per cent at the first quarter of 2007. The minimum reserve instrument, whose operational framework was redefined in 2004, was another active instrument throughout 2007, representing between 17% and 20% of bank liquidity with the Bank of Algeria and thus helping to mitigate excess liquidity in 2007. Thus, the orderly combination of liquidity recovery instruments, interest-bearing deposit facilities and minimum reserves in the conduct of monetary policy by the Bank of Algeria shows the priority given to improving the regulation of bank liquidity, taking into account the characteristics of the moment and the evolution of the interbank money market. The Bank of Algeria applies interest rates on its three active monetary policy instruments with the aim of reducing excess liquidity. Also, by setting up a "range" of interest rates, the Bank of Algeria is de facto paying increasing attention to the short-term interest rate at the operational level. The orderly conduct of monetary policy during 2007, characterized by the continued resumption of monetary expansion and increasing inflationary risks, enabled the inflation target strategy to be successful. The inflation rate of 3.5 per cent, on an annual average, for 2007 is in line with the ultimate objective of monetary policy, expressed in terms of medium-term price stability around an inflation rate of 3 per cent. Indeed, imported inflation induced by the strong growth in the prices of food products, especially those of cereals and dairy products, combined with inflation 13 due to endogenous causes, constitutes an external shock to price stability in the medium term, the ultimate objective of monetary policy, especially since 2007 confirms the significant resumption of monetary expansion. Finally, the combination of the inflation target with the quantitative monetary objectives leads the Bank of Algeria to increasingly refine monetary programming, particularly infra-annual, and to use flexibly the appropriate instruments for conducting monetary policy: liquidity recovery, minimum reserves and the facility for remunerated deposits. 5. Key Recent Monetary and Financial Trends With regard to 2008, the indicators for the first quarter point to favourable financial developments likely to further strengthen algeria's macro-financial indicators and external financial position. Indeed, given the favourable developments in hydrocarbon prices on international markets, exports of goods and services in the 1st quarter of 2008 grew sharply to 20.83 billion, compared with 13.77 billion in the 1st quarter of 2007. On the other hand, imports of goods and services recorded a significant increase (34.1% overall) from 7.71 billion in Q1 2007 to 10.34 billion in Q1 2008. This significant increase concerns, in particular, imports of food products (68%) and capital goods (47%). Indeed, the overall balance of payments balance of payments for the 1st quarter of 2008 reached an amount of 9.96 billion compared to 5.35 billion in the first quarter of 2007. The stock of official foreign exchange reserves at the end of March 2008, including the valuation effect of the Euro and the Pound Sterling, amounted to 123.46 billion, an increase of 13.38 billion in the first quarter. This trend continues, with official reserves reaching 125.95 billion at the end of April 2008. It is worth pointing out that the positive effect of the favourable hydrocarbon price environment on the balance of payments, a 32.5 per cent increase in prices in the first quarter of 2008, is partly offset by the important price effect of imports of goods and services in a context of rising global inflation. In addition, the sustained sustainability of the balance of payments in the 1st quarter of 2008 is reflected in the net foreign assets of the Bank of Algeria at the end of March 2008. These assets increased from 7382.9 billion dinars at the end of December 2007 to 8086.8 billion dinars at the end of March 2008. Loans to the economy increased by 4.1% in the first quarter of 2008 compared to 1% in the first quarter of 2007. Given the importance of medium- and long-term credit to the energy sector, the flow of credit distributed is greater to the public sector than to the private sector and households. The money supply increased by 4.7% in the first quarter of 2008; the hydrocarbon company's deposits remain relatively stable, indicating the likely acceleration of its investments. 14 With the resurgence of global inflation, imported inflation is taking an increased share in the evolution of the consumer price index at the domestic level. Thus, and despite the sustained effort of the Bank of Algeria in terms of recovering excess bank liquidity, inflation by costs is on the rise. Inflationary pressures are largely due to rising prices of imported food products. Indeed, the annual average increase in the consumer price index rose from 3.5% in 2007 to 4.47% at the end of April 2008. On a year-on-year basis, however, the inflation rate stood at 5.63% in March and 6.44% in April 2008. To help stem this new type of inflation, the Bank of Algeria is pursuing the stabilization of the effective exchange rate while rigorously conducting monetary policy actions. In such a context of external shocks, fiscal measures are likely to strengthen the macroeconomic financial stability necessary for an orderly implementation of economic and social development. 15
