Title: Acceleration of inflation in 2012: the need to contain inflationary phenomenon in 2013
text: BANK OF ALGERIA Algiers, 18 February 2013 ACCELERATION OF INFLATION IN 2012 IN THE CONTEXT OF MONETARY DECELERATION: THE NEED TO STEM THE INFLATIONARY PHENOMENON IN 2013 Introduction After the adjustment period, Algeria experienced a long period of moderate inflation, i.e. more than ten years of inflation rates contained at less than 5%. However, the inflation rate exceeded this threshold in 2009 (5.74 per cent on average per year), in the context of soaring commodity prices on the international market and strong increase in fresh produce prices on the domestic market. Imported inflation has thus been combined with the phenomenon of endogenous inflation. While the average annual inflation rate fell to 3.91% in 2010, 2011 was marked by a shock to domestic prices of some commodities at the beginning of the year, leading to a new upward trend in consumer prices in the second half of the year. On an annual average, the inflation rate rose from 3.49% in June 2011 to 4.20% in October and 4.52% in December 2011. 1. An inflationary surge of an endogenous nature The rise in consumer prices that began in the second half of 2011 continued acutely in 2012 from the beginning of this year. An examination of the monthly evolution of the overall consumer price index shows a sharp and sudden increase in January 2012 (2.31%), i.e. 5.5 times the average monthly increase in this index for 2011 (equivalent to a half-year of average inflation). As a result, the inflation acquis (the jump in the level of the price index), on an annual average, in January 2012 is 4.4%, half of the average annual inflation observed in 2012 (8.89%). This means that if consumer prices had remained stable over the next eleven (11) months (February to December), the average annual inflation for the whole of 2012 would have been 4.4%. In fact, the average annual inflation rate reached 5.91% in March, 7.29% in June and 7.95% in September, reflecting the acceleration in this area. In December 2012, the consumer price index of Greater Algiers, base 100 in 2001, stood at 158.48 points, corresponding to an annual inflation rate of 8.89%. This pace is almost double that recorded in 2011 (4.52%). It is important to note that it is also the historically highest inflation rate over the last fifteen years. Excluding food, inflation is estimated at 6.09% on an annual average in 2012, up 1.3 points compared to the previous year. As a result, 2012 was characterised by a very strong acceleration in the inflation of food prices (12.22%) and particularly of fresh agricultural products (21.37%); the latter category comprising eight products. The annual average inflation of fresh food products in the first quarter of 2012 was 20.5%, almost all (96%) of the average annual inflation for this category of goods recorded in 2012 (21.37%). This means that if fresh produce prices had remained stable over the next nine (09) months of 2012 (April to December), their average annual inflation for the whole of 2012 would have been 20.5%. With regard to sheepmeat, whose weight in this category of goods is 33.8%, the inflation acquis in the first quarter of 2012 is 24.12%, or 79.7% of the average annual inflation of this property recorded in 2012 (30.28%). In addition, while inflation in the "miscellaneous" group (13.42 per cent) is well above average inflation, the price increase for all other product groups ranges from 2.88 per cent (education - culture) to 5.77 per cent (clothing - footwear). An analysis of the contributions of the different product groups to the rise in prices shows that this drift in food prices contributes 62.80% to the inflationary "peak" recorded in 2012, while the increase in prices of the "miscellaneous" group contributes 14.93%. The high inflation in 2012 is mainly generated by the price effect of these two groups whose respective contributions are much higher than their respective weights in the price index (43.09% and 8.64%). Under food, it is important to note that soaring sheepmeat prices (30.28%) contributed more than half (50.7%) to fresh food inflation, more than a quarter (25.8%) contributed to fresh food inflation, while its weight within the food group is 13.3% (5.72% in the overall index). What further distinguishes the inflationary effect of 2012 is that 4.9 points of the 12.22 points of food inflation and 2.22 points of the 8.89 points of headline inflation are attributable to sheepmeat alone. Finally, year-on-year, sheepmeat price inflation for all months of 2012 ranged from 21.84% to 40.83% compared to 0.55% to 7.73% for the months of 2011. All in all, the inflationary phenomenon emerged with particular acuteness in 2012, especially since it is essentially endogenous inflation anchored on a very limited number of fresh products. This raises the issue from the point of view of the need to limit the erosion of household purchasing power, given the soaring prices of fresh food products, or even that of preserving macroeconomic stability in the long term. 2. Determinants of the sharp rise in inflation in 2012 The "peak" of inflation in 2012 was combined with a deceleration in the pace of monetary expansion. The M2 monetary aggregate grew by only 11.47% compared to 19.9% in 2011, the slowest pace in the last seven years with the exception of 2009, the year of the large external shock. As for fiat money, despite a decline of nearly 8 percentage points, its growth rate nevertheless remains high in 2012 (14.81% against 22.53% in 2011). In addition, the upward trend in the fiat currency/M2 ratio continued during 2012; Strongly correlated with household spending, this would indicate a substantial increase in consumer demand generated by the strong income increases in 2011 and 2012 and which probably could not be balanced by that of supply, especially for fresh produce, which weighed on retail prices. Nevertheless, in past years, larger increases in the money supply and fiat money have not been accompanied by inflation of the same magnitude as in 2012. The monetary deceleration recorded during the year under review and that, in a very marked way, in 2009 were combined with a surge in the prices of fresh products, or even a very limited number of these products. As a result, the pace of monetary expansion cannot explain this inflationary surge in 2012, especially since the year under review is marked by a strong increase in term deposits (19.46%) and a contraction in fiat money in November and December. Nor can imported inflation be invoked as a determinant of the acceleration of inflation in 2012; the International Monetary Fund estimates that raw material prices (excluding fuels) fell by 9.8% in 2012. Indeed, on the world free market, the prices of commodities imported by Algeria all fell in 2012. On an annual average and by product, they fell from 5.6% to 16.25% and, moreover, the national currency remained relatively stable against the two main currencies in which the country's imports are denominated, which should have helped to steer domestic prices downwards rather downward. Moreover, the numerous exemptions and tax breaks (VAT, customs duties) on imported agricultural products should also have acted in the same direction of price stability. It is therefore necessary to examine the other causes, which are more of an organizational and behavioural nature. The first of these, the large wage increases granted and the so-called "resonance" effect of propagation to all economic actors, encourage sellers to "confiscate" the improvement in the purchasing power of employees. These large wage increases de facto fuel inflation in fresh produce prices, while the high and persistent level of fresh produce prices plays an important role in the formation of inflationary expectations. Secondly, and probably the most decisive, lies in the organization of wholesale and retail trade: few organized wholesale markets for agricultural products, opaque price formation, lack of price advertising and invoicing, weak control in terms of compliance with the laws and regulations in force. All these factors facilitate and encourage abusive price increases, while dominant positions reinforce these practices. The payment of cash transactions and the rejection of the use of modern means of payment (cheque and payment card) make the latter even less transparent, judging by the increased scale of informal transactions. Finally, inflation is also related to the psychology of economic agents and the formation of their expectations that feed and reinforce inflationary behavior. 3. Monetary policy measures As soon as the acceleration of inflation in the first quarter of 2012, which reached 5.91% in March 2012, the Bank of Algeria has: increased the amount of liquidity recoveries by 250 billion dinars, increasing liquidity recoveries from 1100 billion dinars to 1350 billion dinars as of April 30, 2012; increased the minimum reserve requirement rate by two percentage points (from 9% to 11%) from 15 May 2012 (start of the minimum reserve maintenance period). These monetary policy measures have helped to better manage excess liquidity in the money market, thereby mitigating its inflationary effect, in a situation of moderate growth in the M2 money supply (11.47%). Moreover, this pace is in line with the quantitative objective set by the Currency and Credit Council for 2012. Given the high level of inflation recorded over the past year, the Bank of Algeria introduced a new monetary policy instrument as of 15 January 2013, namely the six-month liquidity recovery at a rate of return of 1.50%. This extension of the maturity of liquidity recoveries is intended to absorb more stable liquidity from banks. The expected correlative objective is to encourage banks to increase the remuneration of term deposits, which would lead to a greater increase in household term deposits at longer maturities. The result would be a partial substitution of financial savings for household consumption, especially since 2012 saw a strong expansion in term deposits. Also, in parallel with the financial inclusion measures for the benefit of households (opening accounts, improving banking services, etc.) initiated at the beginning of January 2013, banks are called upon to stimulate more, through better remuneration, households' financial savings, particularly for reasons of access to housing. 4. Structural measures to stem endogenous inflation Given the multidimensional nature of inflation (monetary, increased incomes, etc.), it is important to stress that the monetary policy measures undertaken by the Bank of Algeria must necessarily be accompanied, particularly in 2013, by economic policy measures relating to: incomes, which should evolve periodically in the future, in line with productivity and inflation, to avoid demand shocks such as those of 2011 and 2012; their large and sudden increases maintaining the income-inflation spiral; the expansion of the supply of goods which would contribute to reducing equilibrium prices on the markets even if recent developments do not show fundamental imbalances between supply and demand. In particular, increasing the supply of housing would satisfy strong household demand and stimulate additional savings, thereby reducing demand for current consumption. Proactive action by the public authorities in the field of promotional housing programmes, based on a broad information campaign, would ensure the success of this approach; the organisation of wholesale markets, the number of which is expected to increase significantly, the transparency of transactions (through price advertising, invoicing, the use of non-cash means of payment,...), the monitoring of the application of the laws and regulations in force in commercial matters and the elimination of dominant positions on certain markets leading to speculative behaviour by economic operators and their expectations. These measures aim to ensure the necessary traceability of price formation and thus to stem the inflationary effect inherent in situation rents that hinder the expected effect of the strong subsidies and exemptions decided by the State; improving the regulation of the markets for fresh produce, mainly sheepmeat. For the record, the conditions that currently prevail in the markets constitute a fertile ground for the occurrence of episodes of inflationary surge feeding on the slightest opportunity such as sharp increases in income disconnected from productivity progress. Indeed, twice, in early 2011 and 2012, for different product ranges including fresh products, sudden and wide price increases were observed; those of January 2012 appearing to be totally endogenous and therefore more worrying than those of January 2011 where imported inflation could be partially invoked. The persistence in January 2013 of the significant impact of the rise in sheepmeat prices on headline inflation is demonstrative in this area. Within the food group, it should be noted that higher sheepmeat prices contributed the most to inflation in this group, in monthly variation, in January 2013. Indeed, the monthly increase in sheepmeat prices (4.91%) contributes more than 38% to headline inflation and almost 80% to inflation in the food group (1.18%). In addition, this monthly inflation rate for the sheepmeat subgroup is the second highest rate in the last two years, after that recorded in January 2012 (13.06%). At the same time, the analysis of the contribution of the different product groups shows that inflation in January 2013 (1.17% in monthly variation), is mainly generated by the 4.6% increase in the prices of the "transport-communication" group to 62.29% (its weight in the overall index is 15.85%), followed by the "food" group which contributed 47.92% (its weight in the overall index is 43.09%); the contribution of the "education, culture and leisure" group was negative (-20.2%). At the end of January 2013, consumer price index inflation, on an annual average, reached a new record high of 8.91%, although it was relatively stagnant compared to the level reached in December 2012 (8.89%). However, it should be recalled that inflation, on an annual average, increased each month, on average, during the year 2012 by 0.36 percentage points compared to an increase of only 0.02 percentage points in January 2013. All in all, the rigorous monitoring of consumer price developments and the detection of the resurgence of persistent price effects for some fresh products require a detailed diagnosis and the taking of adequate and timely measures. Any corrective measures taken by the public authorities should therefore be both structural and long-term and should be directed mainly, in the current economic situation, towards the markets for fresh products, particularly sheepmeat.

Title: Intervention at the regional conference on globalization and the challenges and opportunities faced by the Maghrebian financial institutions
text: 18 MARCH 2008 SPEECH BY MR. MOHAMMED LAKSACI GOVERNOR OF THE BANK OF ALGERIA AT THE REGIONAL CONFERENCE ON THE GLOBALIZATION AND THE CHALLENGES AND OPPORTUNITIES FACED BY MAGHREB FINANCIAL INSTITUTIONS. JOINTLY ORGANIZED BY THE INTERNATIONAL INSTITUTE OF FINANCE AND THE BANK OF ALGERIA Ladies and Gentlemen, Our conference is being held opportunely in a global context marked by the effects of the international financial crisis linked to the subprime market crisis in the United States. This crisis and the spread of its effects, the full extent of which is not yet known, is a reminder that globalization certainly brings considerable benefits, particularly in terms of the development and growth of integrated economies, but that at the same time, the strong integration and the increasing complexity of integration instruments, including financial instruments, involve major risks, the main characteristic of which is their high degree of transmissibility. It is therefore necessary, for economies still at a moderate stage of integration into the world economy, such as the economies of our region, to draw the essential lesson, namely to work continuously for the establishment and development of economic and financial systems capable of limiting the perverse effects inherent in the integration process. In particular, and with regard to financial systems, their continuous strengthening, in line with the best standards, practices and operating rules, is crucial to ensure their stability, improve their performance and competitiveness and increase their resilience. These are prerequisites for sound and strong integration into the international financial system. To this end, Algeria has been working for several years to implement the necessary reforms and structural adjustments to ensure an orderly opening and a lasting solidity of the system. The implementation of these financial reforms is taking place in a situation of continuous strengthening of macroeconomic stability, a context that has favoured growth. 1 strong and sustained economic activity, particularly in the non-hydrocarbon sector, and a sharp reduction in unemployment. In this regard, allow me to recall here some key indicators of this stability, including the control of inflation, the strengthening of the fiscal and external situations and the stabilization of the real effective exchange rate at its equilibrium level. 1- The pursuit of prudent fiscal and monetary policies, in a context of increasing liquidity inherent, mainly, in the increase in hydrocarbon export earnings, has made it possible to contain inflation to a level below 3% on average over the last five years, below the 3% target set for the medium term. The rate of 3.5 per cent recorded in 2007 mainly reflects the sharp rise in food import prices. Fiscal prudence has manifested itself, in particular, through the large accumulation of fiscal savings in the revenue regulation fund, despite the increase in public capital expenditure inherent in the implementation of the important public investment programme and anticipated external deleveraging. Monetary policy has been based mainly and flexibly on indirect instruments for absorbing excess liquidity (including liquidity recovery and reserve requirements). As excess liquidity has become structural since 2002, the Bank of Algeria has therefore no longer intervened as lender of last resort since that date. 2- The strengthening of the budgetary position, a corollary of prudent management of public spending in the context of a substantial increase in oil and ordinary tax revenues, has reinforced the preponderance of budgetary savings in domestic savings, although the savings of companies and households have also increased. Thus, the excess of savings over investment gradually increased to a ratio of nearly 25 per cent in 2006 (22 per cent in 2007) compared with 13 per cent in 2004. This excess of savings over investment thanks to the evolution of hydrocarbon prices on international markets has resulted in a significant and gradual increase in official foreign exchange reserves at the level of the Bank of Algeria. At the same time and from 2004, Algeria undertook the early repayment of a large part of the external debt. This twofold development, namely the increase in official foreign exchange reserves and the sharp reduction in external debt, has resulted in a considerable improvement in Algeria's net external financial position. 3- The continuous improvement of financial intermediation, an essential support for strong and sustainable economic growth, is based on a comprehensive structural reform programme that concerns all segments of the financial system at rates and sequences that take into account priorities and developments in other sectors of the economy. With regard to banking reforms, it should be noted in particular: 2 the implementation of banking regulations to international standards in various areas of banking activity and covering more particularly the Basel principles; the strengthening, with the promulgation of the new Banking Law of 2003, of the conditions for the authorisation of banks. At the end of 2007, the Algerian banking sector consisted of 26 institutions including six public banks, thirteen private banks, six (6) financial institutions and a development bank under restructuring. The network of banks and financial institutions includes 1290 branches, including 1045 for public banks and 190 for private banks; strengthening the role of the private sector in the banking sector by launching the process of privatization and/or opening up the capital of public banks; the consolidation of public banks to increase their competitive capacity; improving their governance, in particular through the establishment of performance contracts binding the directors of public banks as well as the members of the boards of directors of these banks to the shareholder; the continuous strengthening of banking supervision both from the point of view of control on the basis of documents and from the point of view of on-the-spot control. The strengthening of coin control focuses on intensifying the use of early warning and stress test techniques in order to better understand banking developments. The strengthening of on-the-spot supervision is done under the dual aspect of strengthening supervisory teams and gradually improving their assessment capacities, in particular the risk management and management activities of banks and financial institutions; the modernisation of credit risk information centres in order to improve their management; the modernisation and development of payment systems with the ultimate objective of meeting the requirements of a modern economy, reducing settlement times, streamlining and improving payment collection procedures and mechanisms, enhancing the efficiency and security of exchanges, ensuring the traceability of transactions and promoting the development of electronic payment instruments. Since 2006, these modernization efforts have resulted in the establishment of a system of real-time gross settlements of large amounts and urgent payments and a system of remote clearing of mass payments. As a result of the modernization of payment systems, banks have had to improve their internal information and telecommunications systems, allowing, in particular, the substantial improvement of the assessment, management and control of banking risks as well as the strengthening of the quality of internal control and the supports of banking supervision. 3 Finally, banks are actively preparing to implement the new international accounting standards for which the legal framework is promulgated; the implementation of these standards is an essential prerequisite for the transition to Basel II standards. In 2008, the Bank of Algeria attached particular importance to preparing the introduction of these standards. In addition, several actions have been taken by the authorities to improve the environment for the distribution of credit, particularly investment credit to small and medium-sized enterprises. Credit guarantee funds have been set up to cover investment loans to SMEs and mortgages. In order to diversify the scope of banking activity, a law on risk capital has defined the conditions for the exercise of private equity companies as well as the procedures for the creation of these companies and their operation. In addition, the law on the creation and operation of savings and credit cooperatives has defined the modalities of constitution, organization and management of these new institutions called upon to develop the micro credit segment. To improve credit risk management, legislation has been developed to enable banks to accelerate the implementation of mortgage guarantees and the distribution of leases. In the same vein, and in order to improve the control of mortgage risks, a law on the securitization of mortgages has been promulgated. 4. In terms of overall financial performance, it is worth noting that: - the structure of financial savings with banks shows a rapid increase in the savings of the hydrocarbon sector but also in the savings of private companies and households. Indeed, the financial savings collected by banks are increasing appreciably. The ratio of bank deposits to gross domestic product increased from 39% in 2005 to 46% in 2007; - the ratio of distribution of credits to the State and the economy to gross domestic product was 37.5% in 2005, 36.8% in 2006 and 35% in 2007. The level of resources collected by banks thus remains higher than the level of distribution of credit to the economy and participation in state financing, reflecting an excess capacity of pre-stable bank funds. On the other hand, significant efforts have been made in terms of the distribution of credit to the private sector. The share of loans to this sector in total credit to the economy has gradually increased, from 43% at the end of 2004 to 53% at the end of 2007. By maturity, more credits were distributed in the medium and long term; the share of these appropriations in total appropriations increasing from 44% at the end of 2004 to 52% at the end of 2007. The banks' project financing activity increased significantly during 2007, particularly in terms of project financing in the energy and water sectors. Finally, it should be noted that the bond compartment of the financial market has developed appreciably in recent years. Indeed, companies resort to 4 more to this mode of financing, which promotes increased competition that can stimulate better banking performance. 5. Despite significant progress, much remains to be done to complete the modernisation and development of the Algerian financial system in general and the banking system in particular, to strengthen its soundness and resilience and to enable it to take advantage of globalisation. With this in mind, the authorities remain committed to continuing their efforts to continuously improve the framework for financial intermediation and to ensure that the soundness, stability and integrity of the financial system are preserved. This consistency in approach as well as the increased macroeconomic stability and increased investment opportunities, in the context of the implementation of the public investment programme, the encouragement of private investment and the increased openness of the economy (particularly in the context of the implementation of the Association Agreement with the European Union and the forthcoming accession to the WTO), offer banks a most favourable environment for further modernisation and of development. 5

Title: Statement to the International Monetary and Financial Committee on behalf of several countries
text: Financial stability and developments in the banking sector in Algeria: lessons to be learned from the international financial crisis 1. Macro-financial stability Algeria's economic performance during the 20012007 period confirmed the marked soundness of the macroeconomic framework, following the return to macroeconomic stability in 2000. Despite an unfavourable external environment, economic and financial developments during 2008 are part of this trend, judging by:  sustained growth in non-hydrocarbon gross domestic product (GDP), estimated at 6% in 2008 (roughly the same rate, 6.3%, recorded in 2007), driven mainly by public investment programmes, the first of which was launched in the second half of 2001. These programmes now include major infrastructure projects, contributing in particular to improving the business investment climate;  inflation under control at an annual average of 4.3% in November 2008 (compared to 3.5% in 2007) while inflationary pressures have increased since mid-2007 in emerging and developing countries, reaching, in some cases, double-digit rates in 20072008;  an effective absorption by the Bank of Algeria of the very high excess liquidity on the money market, through new monetary policy instruments (liquidity recovery, deposit facility, etc.), thus helping to stem the inflationary effect of excess liquidity;  a comfortable net external financial position, anchored on a level of foreign exchange reserves which reached US138.345 billion at the end November 2008, while the medium- and long-term external debt is more, at that date, than about US4 billion. The important early repayments of external debt mainly in 2006, in fact, contributed significantly to the low external debt as an important element of resilience to Medium term the Shock external;  nominal and real effective exchange rates that are relatively stable and close to equilibrium levels. Over the first eleven months of 2008, on average, the real effective exchange rate and the nominal exchange rate appreciated by 1% and 2% respectively, despite the extreme volatility of the 1 rate of change some country partners;  a solid public finance position with an overall budget surplus estimated at 9% of GDP in 2008 compared to 4.9% of GDP in 2007. In addition, the significant accumulation of resources in the revenue regulation fund, i.e. 4192.5 billion dinars at the end of November 2008 (nearly 40% of GDP estimated for 2008) reinforces the budgetary capacity to finance the public investment program, especially since the internal public debt is decreasing. Thus, the enhanced stability of the macroeconomic framework, the high level of foreign exchange reserves and the resources accumulated in the revenue regulation fund allow the Algerian economy to calmly cope with the effects of the international financial crisis and the marked deterioration of the world economic situation. In addition, the risk of pure financial contagion affecting the banking sector is very limited, due in part to the low or even no exposure of the sector to international financial markets. 2. Recent developments in the banking sector In any economy, the banking and financial system plays a decisive role in supporting economic activity. In many emerging and developing countries, including Algeria, the role of banks in financing productive investments is all the more increased because of the low level of development of financial markets. It is therefore vital for the economy, and this is one of the lessons to be learned from the ongoing international financial crisis, that the soundness of the banking and financial system be strengthened and preserved. Strengthening the regulation and supervision of the system, in relation to the stages of financial development achieved and the objectives of economic development, thus emerges as a first priority in the tasks of regulatory and supervisory bodies, in particular central banks. 2.1 In Algeria, the development of the banking sector has been marked by a series of reforms undertaken since the promulgation of the 1990 Banking Law. These include, among other things, the establishment of banking and prudential regulations in accordance with international standards, the consolidation of public banks and their functional development, the establishment of banking supervision bodies and their permanent strengthening and the opening of the sector to domestic and foreign private capital. 2 The first financial reforms initiated in the 1990s were accompanied by the failures of small private banks, or even the bankruptcy of some of them, leading to withdrawals of licences between mid-2003 and early 2006 and the compensation of depositors from the resources of the Deposit Guarantee Fund. It is in such a context of consolidation of the banking sector and in application of the provisions of the new banking law (ordinance of 26 August 2003), that additional reforms have been undertaken. These reforms, undertaken in a favourable macroeconomic situation and aimed at the stability and integrity of the banking system, have focused in particular on:  strengthening the conditions for entry into the sector and raising the minimum capital of banks and financial institutions;  strengthening the supervision of banks and financial institutions and setting up early warning indicators;  the modernisation and development of payment systems, namely the RTGS put into production in February 2006 and the tele-compensation system in May 2006. Also, the improvement of banks' information systems and the establishment of a safe, reliable and secure telecommunications network of private subscribers between the Bank of Algeria and the banks have led to a significant improvement in basic banking services;  the development of different segments of the credit market (mortgage credit, loans to SMEs, real estate leasing,...) and the improvement of the functioning of the central risks and non-payments. In addition, a project for the integrated modernisation of power plants, including the Retail Credit Centre, as a new compartment of integrated power plants, is being implemented and aims to improve risk management by banks and financial institutions. In addition to these major reforms, actions have been taken by the State owner of public banks to improve their governance (performance contract with the presidents of public banks, State/administrator agreements,..) and ensure the upgrading of their own funds, in addition to the consolidation of their portfolios. 2.2 In terms of the results achieved, the deepening of banking reforms, mainly between 2003 and 2008, has led to the strengthening of the stability of the banking sector. In particular, its resilience to "shocks" has been relatively consolidated, in the context of a gradual improvement in bank intermediation and an increase in the functional efficiency of public banks. Thus, the challenge for the Algerian banking sector lies in its development rather than in its stability. As this is a predominantly public banking sector in terms of assets and deposits, the support provided by the State to 3 Public banks over the past fifteen years have played an important role in this area. This financial support from the State is estimated at 2.6% of the gross domestic product on average per year for the period 1991-2002 and 1.7% for the years 2005-2006. The main characteristic of the financial sector in Algeria is that it remains banking-oriented, even if the bond compartment of the financial market has developed rapidly since 2004 to reach, at the end of 2007, a capitalization of 3.1% of NON-hydrocarbon GDP. The banking sector therefore remains the main channel of financing for companies and households, in a macroeconomic context of excess savings over investment. At the end of November 2008, the Algerian banking sector comprised six public banks, fourteen private banks with foreign capital (compared to twelve at the end of 2007), one bank specializing in the distribution of credit to agriculture and five financial institutions (compared to six at the end of 2007). The latter, in accordance with the legislation in force, do not collect deposits from the public. The branch network of public and private banks is gradually increasing, i.e. in 2007 one bank counter for every 25700 inhabitants (7870 people of working age). The rate of banking in terms of network development is still low compared to the level reached in countries whose development is close to that of Algeria. From the point of view of the solvency of banks, and at the end of 2007, the ratio of equity to risks incurred averaged 12.85% against 15.15% at the end of 2006; banks that provisioned more in 2007. The risk coverage ratio is between 11.3% and 20% for countries on the southern shore of the Mediterranean, with the regulatory ratio being 12% in some of these countries. In addition, the ratio of core capital to total assets net of provisions constituted was 6.39% at the end of October 2008 for banks operating in Algeria, a relatively low level compared to the average rate of the countries of the region. This weakness in the core capital of banks operating in Algeria is confirmed by the level of the ratio of core capital to total liabilities, which is estimated at 6.43% at the end of October 2008. In terms of the size of the banking sector, in the light of the ratios used at the international level, the first indicator represented by the ratio of money supply M2 to gross domestic product shows a gradual expansion of the banking sector in Algeria: 53.8% in 2005, 56.7% in 2006 and 64.4% in 2007. This ratio is estimated at 62.1% at the end of 2008, due to a sharp decline in the growth rate of M2 to 14% against 24.2% in 2007. The level of this ratio does not fully reflect the development of the banking sector in Algeria, as part of the savings 4 budget is accumulated in the Revenue Regulation Fund, i.e. the central currency that is not part of the M2 money supply (broad money). By integrating this type of central currency into M2, to make the ratio comparable to those of the countries of the region, the indicator reaches 99% in 2007 against 93% in 2006 and 78.2% in 2005. For the year 2008, it is estimated at 100.2%. At the end of 2007, the M2/GDP ratio was 65.4% for Tunisia and 104.8% for Morocco. The second indicator of the development of the banking sector, represented by the ratio of total bank assets to gross domestic product, stands at 69.2 per cent for banks in Algeria in 2007, compared with 60.7 per cent in 2006 and 54.7 per cent in 2005. It is estimated at 67% in 2008. This ratio is higher, taking the total non-deposit assets of the hydrocarbon sector that are ultimately with the Bank of Algeria, and relative to non-hydrocarbon GDP, i.e. 99.3% in 2007 against 95.8% in 2006 and 86.4% in 2005. This ratio, which better reflects the effort of bank financing of the national economy, is estimated at 100.8% for the year 2008. With the development and modernization of payment systems in 2006, the RTGS processing an average daily amount of 2363 billion dinars in 2008 and tele clearing an average daily number of compensated transactions of 38357, the quality of banking services has gradually improved judging by:  the reduction of recovery times for payment instruments;  the management and regular monitoring of customer accounts;  and progress in risk analysis, monitoring and control Bank. Correspondingly, the management of public banks is experiencing an improvement driven by the State shareholder. As the third indicator of the size of the banking sector, resource collection increased relative to gross domestic product: 39.1 per cent in 2005, 41.3 per cent in 2006, 48.5 per cent in 2007 and 46.8 per cent estimated at the end of 2008. This adjusted ratio, i.e. "non-hydrocarbon deposits/non-hydrocarbon GDP", increased from 58.5 per cent in 2005 to 60.1 per cent in 2006 and from 62.4 per cent in 2007 to an estimated 63.9 per cent in 2008. Such an adjusted ratio better expresses the effort to collect financial savings by banks in Algeria. For the countries on the southern shore of the Mediterranean and at the end of 2007, this indicator is between 45.4% for Syria and 119.1% for Jordan. 5 The fourth indicator on bank intermediation, seen from the point of view of the ratio of loans to the economy (including loans repurchased by the State by bonds issued and not repaid) / GDP excluding hydrocarbons (the hydrocarbon sector is self-financing), increases from 54.2% in 2005 to 53.8% in 2006 and 52.9% in 2007. For 2008, this ratio is estimated at 52.5%, reflecting the good recovery of loans to the economy allocated in particular to investment financing, despite the early repayment of part of the credits repurchased by the Treasury. For the countries of the southern shore of the Mediterranean and at the end of 2007, this indicator varies between 36.3% for Syria and 106% for Jordan. Some countries in the region have developed more credit to households. Outstanding loans to the private sector as a proportion of total loans distributed increased significantly, from 44% in 2004 to 53% in 2007 and 55% in October 2008; in 2008, with 14% growth in loans to the economy. As a result, the ratio of private sector credit to non-hydrocarbon GDP increased from 17.6 per cent in 2004 to 21.3 per cent in 2005 and 23.3 per cent in 2007. Its level is estimated at 23.3% in 2008, a stabilization. The level of credit to private enterprises and households is on an upward trend, judging by the level reached by the level of credit stock to the private sector, which exceeds that of credit to the public sector. At the end of 2007, total loans were distributed to 47% to the public sector and 53% to the private sector, while the private sector share reached up to 55% at the end of October 2008. It is worth recalling that from 2006 onwards, banks are conducting financial arrangements for major investment projects, so that medium- and long-term loans reach 54.2% of the total loans distributed at the end of October 2008, compared with 51.3% at the end of 2007 and 48.1% at the end of 2005. The expansion of bank investment credit in recent years is combined, however, with compromised loans under concentrated old loans which are the subject of significant provisioning. With the ongoing measures to upgrade public and private companies, the level of compromised receivables is set to decrease. In terms of the soundness of the banking sector, the profitability rate of banks (fifth indicator) is increasing. Also, the ROAA (return on average assets) ratio improved from 0.89% in 2006 to 1.06% in 2007. The return on bank assets in Algeria is in line with the average of the countries in the region. In addition, the return on equity continues to improve from 6 18.83% in 2006 to 24.59% in 2007. This level places banks operating in Algeria in the upper bracket of banks in the region. While liquid assets relative to total assets remain high, rising from 40% in 2005 to 46% in 2007 and affecting the profitability of banks, especially state-owned banks, it is important to note that the liquidity ratio (liquid assets to current liabilities) is close to one (0.989 in 2007 compared to 0.992 in 2005). The level of the latter ratio shows a certain adequacy between short-term supply and use, in a context of ample bank liquidity. The review of these indicators of development of the banking sector in Algeria makes it possible to assess the degree of resilience of the banking system, in the current context of serious international financial crisis. 3. Impact of the financial crisis 3.1 The global financial system has been in crisis for more than fifteen months, with an intensification from September 2008. To contain the effects of this severe financial crisis, developed countries are implementing important packages of measures where central banks have from the outset placed themselves at the forefront by injecting significant liquidity. The international financial crisis first manifested itself as a liquidity crisis as early as August 2007, when severe disturbances appeared in money markets in developed countries. The abnormal high level of spreads on the money and interbank markets, the shortening of maturities and the narrowing or even disappearance of certain segments of the money market bear witness to this. While, more than a year later, these tensions are still present on the money markets in developed countries, affecting the financing of the economy through the credit crunch, it should be stressed that the contagion effect of the financial, monetary and exchange rate markets in emerging countries emerges acutely in the fourth quarter of 2008. This crisis also appeared as a securitization crisis, because securitization was used in very unstable financial structures, financing in the short term complex and structured products, very illiquid and with very high value. 7 uncertain, while a favourable rating and an insurance guarantee made it possible to artificially improve their quality. The appearance and rise of non-performing loans, first of all defaults on subprime loans, have fuelled the financial crisis that continues to this day despite the first protective measures. As a result, the liquidity provided by central banks quickly dried up, while the succession of asset write-downs and losses incurred eroded the solvency of leading financial institutions, including large investment banks that had sheltered a concentration of securitised credit risks. Indeed, the accumulation of depreciations and losses destroys their capital to the point of leading them to bankruptcy, like Lehman Brothers. The magnitude of the crisis is such that, in addition to substantial liquidity inflows by central banks, which have also adjusted their operational frameworks, public interventions (Treasuries) now support banks' financing and capital. As part of bailouts of their financial systems, the Governments of several developed countries guarantee the refinancing of banks, so that they themselves can properly finance the economy, while supporting them through recapitalization. States are therefore intervening to support the solvency and soundness of banks, at this stage of intensification of the financial crisis where liquidity problems remain crucial. In total, the asset impairments and losses reported by a number of major international banks are estimated by the Bank for International Settlements at 650 billion. The International Monetary Fund, for its part, estimates asset write-downs and losses suffered by major international banks, linked to the US financial market, at more than 1400 billion. In addition, the Bank of England estimates that the market to market losses inherent in the "market to market" for a range of securities and credit market instruments in the United States, the Eurozone and the United Kingdom are 2800 billion (at current prices). The rapid spread of the effects of the financial crisis, with its intensification from September 2008, to emerging economies has largely affected three categories of countries. Countries with external current account deficits that are finding it increasingly difficult to mobilize the required external financing, given the sharp contraction in external financing and the sharp tightening of their conditions. Countries with significant short-term external debt (banks' short-term liabilities) and facing significant short-term external debt service payments for high levels of corporate debt denominated in foreign currencies. In several cases, a strong expansion of bank credit has been financed by borrowing from the international banking market. Finally, it is worth noting the case of commodity- and commodity-producing countries that have spent rather than spared the additional resources inherent in the high prices of these commodities. 8 The acuteness of the rapid contagion of emerging markets quickly led to the emergence of the external financing problems of certain emerging countries that are experiencing an external balance of payments crisis and even had to resort, as early as October 2008, to exceptional financing from the International Monetary Fund. To meet financing demands and the current financial crisis, on October 29, 2008, the IMF created the "Short-Term Liquidity Facility," which allows for rapid disbursement of up to 500 percent of quota, for the benefit of member countries with strong economic policies but facing liquidity challenges in global capital markets. In addition, to help improve liquidity conditions in global financial markets and the raising of foreign currency financing by certain countries, the United States Federal Reserve, the Central Bank of Brazil, the Bank of Mexico, the Bank of Korea and the Monetary Authorities of Singapore announced on 29 October 2008, the establishment of temporary currency swaps (reciprocal credit agreements). In addition, in order to allow certain foreign banks to obtain liquidity in Swiss francs, the Swiss National Bank and the European Central Bank have entered into a swap agreement. From the perspective of the supervision and supervision of the financial systems of developed countries, the crisis has highlighted the need to rethink the foundations of banking and financial regulation, to strengthen risk management and to review the organization of financial markets. In particular, attention will be paid to the supervisory architecture, with a stronger interaction between supervision and the Central Bank's role as lender of last resort. It is also important to integrate into supervision the stability objectives not only of the institutions, but of the financial system as a whole, by developing a so-called macroprudential policy. 3.2 The review of financial stability indicators shows that the purely financial risks of contagion are very limited for Algeria, which in recent years has:  conducted prudent management of foreign exchange reserves (no investment in risky assets), ensuring the strategic objective of immunizing asset portfolios (official foreign exchange reserves) against any loss of capital. Indeed, the sharp fall in oil prices significantly reduces the country's export earnings and, consequently, the capacity for fiscal savings. A sustained weakness in oil prices would therefore result in a sharp decline in accumulated savings, as well as a corresponding decline in foreign exchange reserves; reduce the return on the investment of foreign exchange reserves, as a result of low interest rates on international markets. 11

text: Algiers, 20 April 2009 ALGERIA'S PARTICIPATION IN THE IMF'S GENERAL DATA DISSEMINATION SYSTEM Algeria began today its participation in the General System of Dissemination of IMF data (GDDS), taking an important step in the development of its statistical system. Detailed information on the statistics produced and broadcast by Algeria are now available in English on the Bulletin Board some Standards of Data (TOOTH) ( /). Metadata in French are also available on the websites of the various Algerian producer organizations of statistical data, i.e. the Bank of Algeria ( ), the Ministry of Finance ( ) and the National Statistics Office ( ). The Governor of the Bank of Algeria, Hon. Mohammed Laksaci, said: "With its effective participation in the GDDS, Algeria is determined to strengthen its national statistical system in order to meet the requirements of international best practices. The GDDS provides an excellent framework for the development of statistical systems and our participation is proof of the commitment of the relevant statistical institutions to implement, in the short and medium term, the improvement plans aimed at strengthening our statistical system. I am convinced that Algeria's participation in the GDDS will lead to the production of more reliable and available statistics in a shorter time." Ms. Aldelheid Burgi-Schmelz, Director of the IMF's Statistics Department, welcomed Algeria's participation in the GDDS and noted that "Algeria's participation in the GDDS is an important step in Algeria's statistical development. I am confident that Algeria will benefit from the framework provided by the SGDD to continue the development of its statistical system. Algeria's participation should also encourage other countries in the region to follow the same path." The GDDS was established by the IMF in 1997. It provides an appropriate framework to assist countries to develop a statistical system that generates complete and accurate statistics to better document analysis and decisions. Algeria is the 95th country to participate in the GDDS.

Title: Improvement in fiduciary circulation in 2012 and 2013
text: BANK OF ALGERIA Improving cash circulation in 2012 and 2013 Communication from the Governor on the occasion of the annual meeting of directors of branches and branches of the Bank of Algeria Algiers, 21 March 2013 1 1. In accordance with the provisions of Article 2 of Ordinance No. 03-11 of 26 August 2003 on currency and credit as amended and supplemented, the privilege of issuing in the national territory fiat money (banknotes and metallic coins) is delegated by the State on an exclusive basis to the Bank of Algeria. For the Issuing Institute, this is a public service. The Bank of Algeria produces banknotes and metal coins and supplies banks and Algeria Post at their request. Historically, Algeria is the first country to produce its banknotes on the African continent. Before the 2000s, net outflows of banknotes were relatively low, because the marked increase in exits in the run-up to religious holidays, at the beginning of summer or at the beginning of the school year was absorbed in the following months by the effect of additional inflows of banknotes at the branches of the Bank of Algeria. On the other hand, since 2006, the cycle of banknote outflows has completely changed, as monthly cash outflows have rarely been lower than fiat money inflows through the branches of the Bank of Algeria. During the period 2006-2011 the net flow of fiat money was negative only for three (3) months. This new phenomenon has generated the increase in the share of fiat money (fiat money issues by the Bank of Algeria minus bank cash) in the M2 money supply. This share increased from 22.1% at the end of 2008 to 25.3% at the end of 2010, then to 25.9% at the end of 2011 and finally to 26.7% at the end of 2012. This evolution reflects the increased role of the budgetary sphere in the expansion of liquidity, judging in particular by the surge in deposits to the CCP and the Treasury whose outstanding deposits have increased, for the first from 265.6 billion dinars at the end of 2008 to 590.3 billion dinars at the end of 2012 and for the second from 194.2 billion dinars at the end of 2008 to 783.3 billion dinars at the end of 2012. In addition to these developments, the demand for household cash increased from 2008 and particularly between 2011 and 2012. For example, the average monthly outflow of fiat currency increased between 2006 and 2011, from an average monthly flow of 13.486 billion dinars in 2006 to 21.701 billion dinars in 2008 and then to 23.523 billion dinars in 2010 and reaching 39.857 billion dinars in 2011. In 2012, the net outflow of fiat money continued during the first ten months of the year, while during the last two months, the net outflow of fiat money was negative to the tune of 18.926 billion dinars in November and 33.888 billion dinars in December 2012, resulting in a decrease in the average monthly flow of fiat money (32.228 billion dinars) compared to 2011 ( 39.857 billion dinars). Indeed, during the period 2006-2012, the main characteristics of net issues of fiat money by the Bank of Algeria are: 2  a bullish monthly trend of fiat money outflows (only five months during which inflows were higher than outflows including two months for the year 2012 alone) between 2006-2011 with a high trend in 2012 despite its decrease compared to 2011;  an evolution disconnected from periods of traditional high outputs of fiat currency (end of month, holidays, summer, school entrance,...);  an increasing preference of households and probably private companies for fiat money, while the system of mass payments (telecompensation), with international standards, safe and reliable, operates without technical problems to date and this, since May 2006. This secure system ensures the traceability of payments and should normally encourage the preferential use of scriptural money. 2. In order to meet the bullish demand for fiat money, the Bank of Algeria increased the production of the 1000 DA and 500 DA denominations and issued the new 2000 DA denomination in April 2011. The production of the latter accelerated in 2012. At the end of 2012, the 2000 DA denomination represented 26.86% of the total amount of banknotes in circulation, the 1000 DA denomination reached a relative share of 68.11%, while the 500 DA denomination represented only 3.03%. The shares of the other denominations are minimal. At the end of 2012, the 200 DA denomination (1983 series) represented only 1.34% of the outstanding fiat currency in circulation (in value) excluding the Bank of Algeria. The process of withdrawing the 200 DA notes (1983 series) continues as payments (reflux) to the Bank of Algeria are made. It should be noted that gross annual outflows of fiat money are rising sharply. For example, cash outflows were 1479.6 billion dinars in 2009, of which a share of 82.27% allocated to Algerie Poste, 1633.4 billion dinars in 2010 of which 87.52% to The benefit of Algerie Poste, 1977.8 billion dinars in 2011 including 92.43% to Algeria Post and 2475.0 billion dinars including a share of 92.02% allocated to Algeria Post. The average monthly ticket outflow to Algeria Post was 101.4 billion dinars in 2009, 119.1 billion dinars in 2010, 152.3 billion dinars in 2011 and 189.8 billion dinars in 2012. Indeed, despite the fire at the Hotel des Monnaies on August 19, 2012, the Bank of Algeria was able to continue to respond favorably to the demand for banknotes and metal coins from banks, the Treasury and Algeria Post. Thus, Algeria Post holds significant cash holdings, i.e. more than 60 billion dinars on average per day during the third quarter of 2012, more than 43 billion dinars during the fourth quarter of 2012 and more than 50 billion dinars for the months of January and February of 2013. These cash balances and the daily deliveries of fiat currency by the Bank of Algeria allow Algerie Poste to respond to any request for withdrawal from its customers, especially households. 3 In addition, cash cash available at the bank of Algeria branches and branches across the national territory reached 188 billion dinars at the end of February 2013. The large cash available at all branches and branches of the Bank of Algeria, as of March 19, 2013 (196.9 billion dinars), makes it possible to cover on average the equivalent of 36 working days of demand at the national level. The Bank of Algeria is working to consolidate this performance at the national level and by wilaya, while these cash balances in fiat currency are widely disseminated throughout the national territory. The Caisse Generale (Bank of Algeria) also has an appreciable cash balance, i.e. more than 60 billion dinars as of March 19, 2013, to fully and permanently carry out its missions relating to the issuance of fiat money. This is in line with the prerogatives of the Issuing Institute under Article 35 of the Law on Money and Credit which stipulates that the Bank of Algeria "... is responsible for regulating the circulation of money, ... . Despite the appreciable effort in terms of the availability of fiat money and refreshment in this area, the Bank of Algeria has strengthened its production capacity for banknotes and metal coins at the Hotel des Monnaies. Today, in addition to the 2000 DA and 1000 DA denominations, the 500 DA cut-off is also in production. The 500 DA denomination is expected to take an increased share in cash circulation. This monetary aggregate is expected to grow by almost 10% in 2013. In conclusion, the quantitative and qualitative improvement of cash circulation in 2012 and the first quarter of 2013 should not obscure the opportunity and the need to further develop non-cash payment instruments (cheques, cards, etc.). In this respect, the focus should be on wholesale and semi-wholesale commercial transactions and real estate transactions, especially since the appropriate payment system (tele clearing) has been operational since mid-2006 and remains in use at only 10 % of its capacity. While payment security is an important element of financial stability, the necessary development of non-cash payment instruments is part of the strategic objective of developing financial inclusion, particularly for the benefit of households whose deposits at bank level are growing strongly (13.1% in 2012). The exercise of the right to an account and the facilitation of account opening at the level of banks are part of this objective. The Bank of Algeria completed the regulatory framework in December 2012, while its branches and branches across the national territory are fully committed to the development of financial inclusion. 4 Title: Presentation of the 2010 annual report
text: Speech by Mr. Mohammed Laksaci Governor of the Bank of Algeria To the International Monetary and Financial Committee On behalf of the Islamic Republic of Afghanistan, Algeria, Ghana, the Islamic Republic of Iran, Morocco, Pakistan and Tunisia Washington DC, September 24, 2011 Since our last meeting, overall growth has weakened, financial stress has intensified, and adverse risks have increased significantly, severely affecting the overall outlook. As highlighted in the IMF Managing Director's Consolidated Report on Multilateral Surveillance, this reflects a weak commitment to collective action on the issue of sovereign debt and banking stress in the euro area and concerns about growth and public debt sustainability in the United States and Japan. Given their systemic importance, decisive and coordinated action to address the considerable vulnerabilities in these countries is urgently needed if another crisis is to be avoided and if the prospects for degrowth and employment are to be revived. The challenges are well identified and include supporting growth and employment in the short term, adopting medium-term fiscal consolidation plans, particularly in the United States and Japan, addressing the sovereign debt crisis decisively in the euro area and strengthening banks' capital and restructuring or liquidation of weak ones as well as redressing balance sheet situations of households and the revival of the real estate market in the United States. The performance of emerging market and developing economies continues to be strong despite the recent slowdown in growth. The challenges they face include maintaining strong and balanced growth while rebuilding fiscal buffers and adopting appropriate policies to limit risks related to volatile capital flows and inflation. In the Middle East and North Africa, the policy agenda is important. Pressures on fiscal and current accounts have increased in the wake of recent events in some countries. At the regional level, ongoing political and social reforms should provide an enabling environment for strong and inclusive growth. This should be supported by appropriate macroeconomic policies, structural reforms and, where necessary, external assistance. Low-income countries have made substantial progress in recent years and have weathered the crisis relatively well. However, the deterioration of the overall economic and financial situation, high commodity prices and declining external assistance jeopardize hard-won gains in growth and poverty reduction. We support the Director-General's action plan to strengthen the effectiveness of the Fund in carrying out its missions towards member countries in this difficult phase and, in general, to improve the overall architecture. The focus on enhancing the effectiveness and impartiality of oversight is crucial in this regard. The importance of adapting policy advice to the particular circumstances of member countries, strengthening the analysis of cross-country impacts, macro-financial issues and stability, especially in systemically important countries, should be stressed. The envisaged review of conditionalities and of the CFL and LCP facilities should contribute to strengthening the Fund's crisis prevention and resolution instruments. Additional avenues for strengthening the Fund's lending capacity should be explored to enable the institution to be in a better position to provide assistance to its members as and when needed. Improving the Fund's capacity to assist low-income countries should be among the priorities of the action plan. The mobilization of concessional assistance, including bilateral contributions and the use of revenues related to the sale of gold, is crucial. Technical assistance remains essential to help member countries formulate and implement sound policies. In this regard, the resources allocated to these activities must be preserved and the fresh application to the beneficiary countries avoided. Together with the forthcoming entry into force of the 2010 quota reform, a comprehensive review of the quota formula as of January 2013, as requested by the Governing Council, should strengthen the legitimacy of the decision-making process by reflecting not only the weight of member countries but also their vulnerabilities. In this regard, it is important that any further realignment of quotas to dynamic emerging and developing countries (developing countries) should not be at the expense of other developing countries. The Fund must also continue to warn against protectionism and promote the benefits for overall growth and employment of an early conclusion of the Doha Round of trade negotiations.
