Title: Communication on monetary and financial trends in the third quarter of 2013
text: MONETARY AND FINANCIAL TRENDS IN THE FIRST NINE MONTHS OF 2013 Algiers, 26 December 2013 Introduction The purpose of this note is to analyse the main financial and monetary trends of the first nine months of the current year, with a particular focus on the third quarter of 2013 marked by financial volatility that particularly affects emerging economies. The national economy, while sheltered from the volatility of capital flows that is severely affecting some emerging economies, is affected by other risks to the short-term outlook of the world economy, notably through the price of oil. 1 - Balance of payments developments The evolution of the current account balance in the first three quarters of the current year confirms the vulnerability of the external balance of payments to any underperformance of hydrocarbon exports, especially since the upward trend in imports of goods persists in 2013. This comes after the large-scale external shock of 2009, followed by a strengthened sustainability of the external balance of payments in 2011 and 2012, driven by the strengthening of oil prices, the average annual level of which was 112.94/barrel and 111.05/barrel respectively. This average price had increased from 62.3/barrel in 2009 to 80.15/barrel in 2010. The average monthly oil price fluctuated between 101.45 and 115.79/barrel in the first nine months of 2013, an average of 109.19 compared to 111.27/barrel for the same period last year. The improvement in prices in the third quarter of 2013 means that the average price over the period under review is better than the half-yearly one (108.55/barrel). Indeed, after an increase in the first quarter of 2013 (112.51/barrel) compared to the last quarter of 2012 (110.24/barrel), the average quarterly price of crude oil fell in the second quarter of 2013 to 104.40/barrel, a decrease of 7.21%, in a situation of sharp decline in the quantities of hydrocarbons exported (-10.97%) for the first half of 2013. This rate of contraction, which increased in the second quarter (-13.31%), stood at 8.97% for the first nine months of the current year. As a result, according to provisional external balance of payments data, hydrocarbon exports in value terms contracted by 12.25% during the period under review compared to the same period of 2012, corresponding to a lower underperformance compared to that in half-year (13.95%), i.e. the first half of 2013 compared to the same half of 2012. They stood at 47.08 billion for the first nine months of 2013, down 12.25% from the same period last year (53.67 billion). The quarterly profile of hydrocarbon exports indicates a contraction in the second quarter of 2013, followed by a stabilization in the third quarter of 2013 at 14.81 billion. This negatively affected the trade balance, especially in the second quarter, while imports of goods 1 continued their upward trend in the context of structural weakness in non-hydrocarbon exports (0.808 billion for the first nine months of 2013 compared to 0.769 billion for the same period in 2012). Imports of fob goods increased by 10.25% in the period under review compared to the first nine months of the previous year, reaching 40.66 billion from 36.88 billion. Quarterly data indicate an upward trend through the second quarter of 2013, while the third quarter of the current year saw a decline in FOB imports to 12.11 billion (14.70 billion in the second quarter) on lower imports of petroleum products, food, semi-finished products and industrial equipment. Analysis of the structure of imports indicates that imports of "industrial capital goods", which rank first with a share of 36.1%, increased by around 20% compared to the first nine months of 2012. In addition, despite their relative decrease in the third quarter of 2013, this group contributed 46.47% to the increase in total imports during the period under review. As for the contribution of "semi-finished products", which reached 19.90% of total imports in September 2013, thus occupying the second place, it is estimated at 10.12%. Imports under this group increased 7% in the first nine months of 2013 compared with the same period last year. On the other hand, with a share of 17.65%, imports of "food goods" which occupy the third place increased by 11.78% and contributed by 14.36% to the increase in total imports. As for imports of "non-food consumer goods", which rank fourth with a share of 14.52%, their contribution to the increase in total imports is estimated at 16.27%, equivalent to their growth rate (16.98%) during the period under review compared to the same period in 2012. In addition, imports under the "energy & lubricants" group, which ranks fifth in the structure of total imports (7.80%), increased by 23.20% to 3.246 billion in September 2013 (2.635 billion in September 2012). As a reminder, imports of petroleum oils and bituminous products had increased from 569.78 million at the end of 2010 to 1.57 billion at the end of 2011, reaching 2.26 billion in the first nine months of 2012. This is a new phenomenon that characterizes the last three years and is correlated with the strong increase in imports of vehicles (tourist, commercial and other). After a surplus of 4.02 billion in the first quarter of 2013, a better performance than that recorded in the third and fourth quarters of 2012, the trade balance deteriorated in the second quarter of 2013 (0.20 billion) mainly due to the contraction of hydrocarbon exports. Subsequently, lower imports of goods in the third quarter led to the rebuilding of the trade surplus (2.52 billion) in the third quarter of the current year, reflecting a favourable trend supported by the stabilization of hydrocarbon exports. In total, in the first nine months of 2013, the trade surplus is estimated at 6.73 billion compared to 17.55 billion for the same period last year, based on provisional balance of payments data for the period under review. This reflects the vulnerability of the trade balance to the profile of hydrocarbon exports, which are contracting in volume terms, in a situation of persistently strong growth in imports of goods. As for imports of services excluding factor income, after stabilizing in the first half of 2013 compared to the same period last year, they increased slightly during the period under review compared to the first nine months of last year, mainly due to the increase in those for maritime transport, insurance and other services, 2 offset by a contraction in imports of services under "building and public works". On a quarterly basis in 2013, services imports stabilized at 2.8 billion, while services exports rose in the second quarter to stabilize in the third quarter. This favourable trend contributed to a slight decline in the deficit in services excluding factor income, a deficit of 4.93 billion at September 2013 (-5.17 billion at September 2012). Reflecting a widening of the "factor income" deficit and a decrease in net transfers, combined with a contraction in the trade surplus, the current account of the external balance of payments recorded a deficit of 0.94 billion in the first nine months of 2013. This underperformance contrasts with the surplus of 10.995 billion achieved for the same period of 2012, even though the deficit was in the second quarter of 2013 only. Given the stabilization of oil prices, this raises the profile in terms of hydrocarbon export capacity in volume terms, as efforts to promote non-hydrocarbon exports do not seem to be producing the expected full effects and achievements in terms of import substitution fall far short of expectations. As a result, and despite a relative stabilization of foreign (net) direct investment and the improvement in the capital account, whose deficit narrowed to 0.75 billion in the first nine months of the current year from 1.46 billion in the same period of 2012, the overall balance of external payments recorded a deficit of 1.70 billion in the period under review, as can be seen from the compilation of the relevant provisional data. Despite this deficit, the stock of foreign exchange reserves (excluding gold) is estimated at 191.866 billion at the end of September 2013 compared to 189.750 billion at the end of June 2013 and 190.661 billion at the end of December 2012. In addition, while reserve growth has slowed in the first three quarters of the current year, Algeria's net external financial position is solid, in a historically low level of external debt (3.478 billion at the end of September 2013 against 3.676 billion at the end of December 2012). Indeed, the level of accumulated reserves exceeds the usual adequacy thresholds for emerging countries, which allows Algeria to cope with possible external shocks and preserve external stability. In 2013, the Bank of Algeria continued the prudent management of official foreign exchange reserves by increasingly emphasizing rigorous monitoring and risk management, including through appropriate prudent measures to protect investment capital from any loss, while achieving an acceptable level of return given the persistence of the environment of low global interest rates. At the end of September 2013, 10-year government bonds in the United States had a yield of 2.61% compared to 1.78% for German government securities of the same maturity. In addition, the prudent management of official foreign exchange reserves by the Bank of Algeria contributes to external financial stability over the medium term, in the context of conducting the dinar's effective exchange rate policy close to its fundamental equilibrium level. To this end, the intervention of the Bank of Algeria in the interbank foreign exchange market has made it possible to mitigate the impact of the increased volatility on the international foreign exchange markets from May 2013 on the national economy, while it has resulted in risks to financial stability in several emerging countries, including the depreciation of their currencies. It is in such a context of volatility of the exchange rates of the main currencies from May 2013, that the average price of the first nine months of the dinar against the US dollar has depreciated by 2.66% compared to the same period of 2012, from 77.0781 USD/DZD in 2012 to 79.1291 USD/DZD in 2013, after an assessment in 2012. At the same time, the average exchange rate for the first nine months of 3 the year 2013 of the dinar against the euro depreciated by 2.09% compared to the same period of the previous year, from 102.082 EUR/DZD in 2012 to 104.2136 EUR/DZD in 2013. This is a slight depreciation compared to those of the currencies of some emerging countries against both the dollar and the euro. For example, the average rate of the dollar over the first nine months of 2013 recorded appreciations against the Brazilian real and the Indian rupee of the order of 10.38% and 8.09% respectively. As for the euro, its average price in the first nine months of 2013 compared to the same period of 2012 appreciated by 13.58% against the Brazilian real, 11.19% against the Indian rupee and 4.68% against the Russian ruble. In total, and under the effect of the narrowing of the inflation differential between Algeria and its 15 main trading partner countries, i.e. to 3.35% in September 2013 against 6.23% in December 2012, and the increase in relative prices, the real effective exchange rate of the dinar depreciated by only 1.72% on average during the first three quarters of 2013 compared to the same period of 2012. Despite the balance of payments deficit situation that marked the period under review, the real effective exchange rate of the dinar remains appreciated by about 5% in September 2013 compared to its equilibrium level determined according to fundamentals. 2 - Monetary developments The deceleration in the pace of monetary expansion that characterized 2012, with an increase in the monetary aggregate M2 of only 10.92% against 19.91% in 2011, is confirmed during the first three quarters of the current year when the growth rate of M2 is estimated at only 6.78%, with a contraction in the second quarter, compared to 10.23% for the first nine months of 2012. The deceleration in the pace of monetary expansion also concerns the monetary aggregate M2 (excluding deposits in the hydrocarbon sector), i.e. 9.01% in September 2013 against 14.83% in September 2012 (16.57% in 2012). The money supply in the sense of M2 reached 11760.39 billion dinars at the end of September 2013 against 10944.62 billion dinars at the end of September 2012 (11013.39 billion dinars at the end of 2012 and 11259.31 billion dinars at the end of June 2013), under the effect of the significant growth in loans to the economy in the context of moderate increase in net foreign assets in the aggregate monetary situation. Despite the deceleration of their growth rate to 5.13% in September 2013, mainly in the first half of the year, against 7.57% for the same period last year, net foreign assets, which reached 15706.19 billion dinars at the end of September 2013, continue to play a role in the money creation process, especially since this aggregate occupies a very significant place in the consolidated monetary situation and has greatly fuelled the excess liquidity on the money market between 2004 and 2008. Nevertheless, the sustained accumulation of resources in the Revenue Regulation Fund by the Treasury is a form of sterilization that has helped to contain, to some extent, this excess liquidity. Moreover, after a quasi-stabilization of the State's net financial position in the monetary situation between the end of 2011 and the end of March 2013, the second quarter of 2013 recorded an improvement, i.e. about 8% for the first half of 2013 against a decrease of nearly 2% in 2012. This improvement in the State's net financial position was reversed in the third quarter so that at the end of September 2013 it stood at 1.04% against 0.20% in September 2012. This trend was combined with the deceleration in the growth rate of CCP and Treasury deposits to 9.03% in September 2013, with a stabilization in the third quarter, compared to 29.54% in September last year (30.46% in 2012). Thus, the financial position of the State as a net creditor vis-88-vis the banking system remains appreciable despite the significant increase in the aggregate credits to the economy. However, the outstanding financial savings of the Treasury, namely the savings on its accounts opened at the Bank of Algeria, increased slightly to 5754.72 billion dinars at the end of September 2013 against 5713.46 billion dinars at the end of December 2012 (5743.05 billion dinars at the end of September 2012), 4 in the context of the relative stabilization of the overall stock of Treasury securities issues, by way of auction on the money market. This outstanding amount increased from 600.85 billion dinars at the end of December 2012 to 592.2 billion dinars at the end of March 2013, to close at 577.14 billion dinars at the end of September 2013. As a result, the strong pace of growth in credit to the economy (22.56% as at September 2013) emerges as the main determinant of monetary expansion in the first nine months of the current year, almost double the pace of growth recorded in September 2012 (12.30%). The dynamism of bank loans to the economy, supported by the facilitation and support measures taken by the public authorities at the beginning of the year, is more significant in real terms in 2013. At the end of September 2013, bank loans to the economy reached 5268.06 billion dinars against 4184.88 billion dinars at the end of September 2012 (4298.45 billion dinars at the end of December 2012 and 4903.65 billion dinars at the end of June 2013). Indeed, the dynamism of bank loans was more sustained in the second and third quarters of the current year. At the end of the period under review, loans to private companies reached 2290.22 billion dinars (2161.78 billion dinars at the end of June 2013) against 1940.32 billion dinars at the end of 2012, so that loans to the private sector (including households) (2630.84 billion dinars) equal the outstanding loans to the public sector (2636.87 billion dinars). In addition, the period under review is marked by an increase in both private and public sector loans, although at a higher rate for the public sector (28.6%), which absorbed more medium- and long-term financing. In parallel with the very strong growth in loans to the economy during the first nine months of 2013, the analysis of the structure of loans to the economy by maturity confirms the increase in the relative share of medium- and long-term loans to 71.36% at the end of September 2013 (71.12% at the end of June 2013, 68.31% at the end of 2012 and 63.41% at the end of 2011). The dynamism of bank loans to the economy, judging by medium- and long-term loans, which increased by 28% in September 2013 compared to December 2012, reflects the improvement in the structure and conditions of financing (extension of maturity and reduction of cost), correlative to the facilitation measures taken at the beginning of 2013 which made the State's support system more effective in the context of credit development. healthy for SMEs to stimulate economic growth. Loans to households are also on the rise in the context of financial inclusion, mainly for mortgage loans (8.10% at September 2013) which should be driven by the development of the real estate market. After this broad review of the counterparties of the M2 money supply and particularly the increased role of the credit aggregate in 2013, the analysis of the structure of M2 provides information on the financial saving behaviour of economic agents and its impact on the banks' means of action. Excluding hydrocarbon deposits, which suffered a very sharp contraction in the second quarter of 2013, as a result of the external balance of payments shock, the M2 growth rate stood at 9.01% at the end of September 2013 (14.83% at the end of September 2012). As a result, the ratio of loans to the economy to M2 (excluding hydrocarbon deposits) increased to 46.58% at the end of September 2013, after stabilizing in 2012 at 41% compared to the end of 2011. This clearly indicates an impetus in bank intermediation from the point of view of credit allocation, while the mobilization of resources is less and less based on those of the hydrocarbon sector in a situation of still significant potential with regard to the banking of private companies and households. Dinar deposits collected by banks increased by 5.69% during the period under review against 7.49% year-on-year in September 2013, growth thwarted by the effect of the contraction in the second quarter, which mainly concerned demand deposits in the hydrocarbon sector. Indeed, after weak growth in the first quarter (4.9%), deposits in the hydrocarbon sector contracted sharply 5 in the second quarter, recording a decrease of 29.5% in September 2013 compared to December 2012 (-29.6% in September 2012). This reveals the continued decline in the self-financing capacity of the hydrocarbon sector in the face of the sectoral investment programme. In addition, imports of petroleum products contribute to this trend. As for demand and term deposits in dinars of public companies (excluding the hydrocarbon sector), they increased by 13.9% in the first nine months of 2013, mainly in the first quarter. In contrast to the situation of the hydrocarbon public sector, this increased flow contributed to the development of the banks' means of action during the period under review. Over the same period, cash and term deposits in dinars by private companies and households increased by 5.5%, after a significant expansion recorded in 2012 (14.7%). The breakdown of these deposits shows that the demand and term deposits in dinars of private companies with banks increased by 7.4%, well below the growth rate of bank loans to this type of economic agent (18%) who allocated part of this financing to their import operations. Households' dinar-term and demand deposits with banks, with a relative share of 35.11%, increased by 4.6% during the period under review compared to 13.8% in 2012, in relation to the household income effect. Their deposits to CCPs and the Consolidated Revenue Fund, which represent the bulk of this category of deposits, continued to increase in the first nine months of 2013 (9%), but in a slower pace compared to the same period last year (29.5%) and stabilization in the third quarter of 2013. In addition, foreign currency deposits increased by 13.8% (7.2% in 2012), reaching 66.7% of the stock of foreign currency deposits mobilized by banks at the end of September 2013. As a result of the evolution of foreign currency deposits and term deposits in dinars, the quasi-currency aggregate grew at a higher rate (8.8%) than that of the M2 money supply (6.8%), but very close to that of M2 (excluding hydrocarbon deposits) (9%). This pace in the first nine months of the current year represents a sharp deceleration in the expansion of quasi-money compared to the same period last year (17.3%), due to a slight increase in term deposits in a situation of excess investment on savings. In addition, banks' resource base is now less vulnerable to an external shock affecting the hydrocarbon sector. Finally, the stabilization of cash circulation relative to the monetary aggregate M2 at the end of September 2013 compared to the end of December 2012 indicates a stability in household demand for financial savings and cash, in the context of a deceleration in consumer price inflation. The monetary deceleration also affected cash circulation, which increased by only 1.18% in the first half of 2013 (1.45% in the first quarter), reaching a rate of 6.7% for the period under review, compared to 14.7% in the first nine months of the previous year. Indeed, after cash outflows through the Algeria Post network in January and February 2013, then a more moderate increase in this area in March and April 2013, fiat money recorded a contraction during the months of May and June 2013. On the other hand, the third quarter was rather marked by an expansion in demand for fiat money, but which is much lower than the issuing capacity of the Bank of Algeria. In view of the high level of inflation recorded over the past year, the Bank of Algeria introduced in mid-January 2013 a new monetary policy instrument, namely the recovery of liquidity at a six-month rate of return of 1.50%. This strengthening of monetary policy instruments came after the measures taken in April 2012 d0 increasing the amount of liquidity recoveries by 250 billion dinars to 1350 billion dinars d0 and May 2012, namely the increase of two percentage points (from 9% to 11%) in the rate of constitution of minimum reserves. The latter was raised again to 12% in May 2013, for 6 consolidate the effectiveness of monetary policy in effectively absorbing excess liquidity in the money market. Thus, the extension of the maturity of liquidity recoveries from January 2013 aims to absorb more stable liquidity from banks and thereby better manage excess liquidity on the money market. Bank liquidity, which remained stable in the first quarter of 2013, contracted in the second quarter to 2542.49 billion dinars at the end of June 2013 against 2865.94 billion dinars at the end of March 2013 and 2876.26 billion dinars at the end of December 2012. It improved slightly in the third quarter of 2013, to 2604.31 billion dinars at the end of September 2013. The excess liquidity was effectively absorbed by liquidity recovery instruments (1350 billion dinars), in a situation of lower use by banks of the 24-hour deposit facility (263.90 billion dinars at the end of September 2013 against 838.08 billion dinars at the end of December 2012). The banks have also, within the framework of the minimum reserves, increased their holdings in accounts with the Bank of Algeria. In addition, while the interbank money market remained almost inactive in the first quarter of 2013, due to the spread of excess liquidity, interbank lending and borrowing resumed from May 2013 with interest rates formed on the interbank market close to 2%. Finally, the preservation of macroeconomic stability remains a primary objective. Monetary policy, underpinned by the flexible conduct of exchange rate policy, plays an active role, especially since the Bank of Algeria consolidated its instruments for reducing excess liquidity at the beginning of the year, with the aim of stemming the inflationary phenomenon. While the role of monetary policy in the fight against inflation is ensured by the Bank of Algeria, the endogenous nature of the inflationary phenomenon in Algeria since 2009 calls for other economic policy measures, particularly structural ones. 3 - Trend towards deceleration in inflation After a long period of moderate inflation following structural adjustment, inflationary emerged particularly acutely in 2012, following the domestic price shock of some commodities in early 2011 and the acceleration of inflation in the second half of the same year. In 2012, the inflationary phenomenon was essentially endogenous in nature, anchored on a very limited number of fresh products whose prices soared in the first quarter of 2012. Indeed, as early as January 2012, the overall consumer price index of Greater Algiers showed a sudden and sudden increase (2.31%), equivalent to 5.5 times the average monthly increase in this index for 2011. The surge in the prices of a very limited number of fresh products in the first quarter of 2012 explains 96% of the inflation, on an annual average, of this product category for the whole of 2012 (21.37%). On the other hand, consumer price inflation (excluding food) was only 6.09% in 2012, when the inflation rate reached the historic "peak" of 8.89%. After 19 months of uninterrupted upward trend (from July 2011 to January 2013), inflation, on an annual average, began to decline in February 2013. Indeed, the annual average inflation rate was 8.07% in March 2013 and 6.59% in June 2013 compared to 8.89%, 8.91% and 8.56% respectively in December 2012, January and February 2013. The deceleration in the pace of inflation continued in the third quarter of 2013, reducing the annual average rate to 5.32% in September 2013, lower than in September 2012 (7.95%). Year-on-year to September 2013, the increase was more moderate (2.18%), while the average index for the first nine months of 2013 increased by 4.15% compared to the same period of the previous year. In addition, at the end of the first nine months of 2013, the general price level in the capital is almost stable at its January 2013 value, while it fell by 0.9 points at the national level. However, despite the evident disinflation in the first nine months of 2013, food price growth has remained high even though it is on a downward trend. 7 On an annual average as at September 2013, the inflation of the "food" (6.69%), "clothing" (7.37%) and "transport and communication" groups (5.76%) are the only ones that exceed the headline inflation (5.32%). This confirms the high impact of food prices; a situation similar to that of the previous year when the average annual increase in September 2012 was 9.9%. In addition, their contribution in September 2013 (56.86%), up 1.7 points in one year, far exceeds their weighting (43.1%) in the consumer price index. With regard to the impact of imported inflation, it should be noted that the domestic prices of imported agricultural products do not sufficiently reflect the downward trend in their world prices, especially since they benefit from implicit subsidies such as exemptions from taxes and customs duties. As a result, domestic price levels are almost always well above those of world prices, although they are expected to move in tandem with both upwards and downwards. In addition, the trend among Algeria's main economic partners is towards disinflation, with the year-on-year pace being less than two percent in June 2013, i.e. 1.8% for the United States and 1.6% for the euro zone. Within the food group, fresh agricultural products experienced double-digit inflation but declined from 15.9% in September 2012 to 10.8% in September 2013. These products, which represent only 16.9% of the index, generated almost half of inflation in September 2013 (45.2%) compared to 41.5% a year earlier, while the increase in industrial food prices was relatively moderate. Their inflation is estimated at only 2.9% in September 2013 against 4.9% a year earlier and, moreover, their contribution fell by 2 points to 13.4%, for a weighting of 26.2%. Judging by their contribution to the sharp rise in prices of the food group, the subgroup - meat and sheep offal - which represents 5% of the index, generated 54.1% of the inflation of this group in September 2013. In addition, this contribution has increased by 16.7 percentage points since September 2012. Manufacturing price inflation is relatively moderate, at 3.26% as of September 2013, down 3.8 percentage points, while their contribution fell by 10.5 points to 22.3%. In addition, services price inflation accelerated from 4.7% in September 2012 to 6% in September 2013, with a contribution to inflation (19.2%) up 8.8 points since September 2012. In terms of structural or core inflation, the disinflation trend that began in August 2012 (5.93%) continued steadily to reach 3.9% in September 2013. Forecasts made in September indicate that inflation in 2013, on an annual average, would be within the medium-term objective set by the Monetary and Credit Council and should be less than 4%. Monetary policy has played an active role in this context of monetary deceleration, while the moderation of disbursements from the State budget and the continuation of regulatory and market organization actions have contributed to this disinflation. As a result, the trend towards disinflation was confirmed in the first nine months of 2013 both on an annual average and on a year-on-year basis. However, the still high level of prices makes it necessary to maintain the effort to control liquidity and the expansion of demand and to ensure that supply increases. In addition, it is expected that sustained action to mobilize household financial savings by banks can contribute to the fight against inflationary and further consolidate macroeconomic stability. 8 The achievements on external financial stability, in particular the strength of the position of foreign exchange reserves and the real effective exchange rate close to equilibrium, and monetary stability argue in favour of the gradual realisation of the real potential for economic growth from 2014 onwards, when productive investment is expected to make an effective contribution. Also, the necessary development of productive investment will be based on the national saving capacity, which is appreciable, judging by the financial savings accumulated over the last twelve years. The aim is to establish a new financing scheme that permanently eliminates any recourse to external debt. Finally, the dynamics of credit to the economy in 2013, which is part of the development of healthy loans to the economy, aimed at stimulating domestic production, shows that the bank credit channel remains potentially important in terms of financing both productive investment, SMEs and promotional housing (mortgage loans). In support of this important objective of allocating resources to inclusive growth, the gradual absorption of excess liquidity in the money market must be accompanied by sustained efforts by commercial banks to mobilize the forward financial savings of companies and households, driven by adequate remuneration in real terms. 9

Si le rle de la politique montaire dans la lutte contre linflation est assur par la Banque dAlgrie, le caractre endogne du phnomne inflationniste en Algrie depuis 2009 appelle dautres mesures de politique conomique dordre notamment structurel. 3 - Tendance  la dclration de linflation Aprs une longue priode dinflation modre qui a suivi lajustement structurel, le phnomne inflationniste a merg avec une acuit particulire en 2012, conscutif au choc des prix intrieurs de certains produits de base dbut 2011 et  lacclration de linflation au second semestre de la mme anne. En 2012, le phnomne inflationniste a t essentiellement de nature endogne, ancr sur un nombre trs limit de produits frais dont les prix ont connu une envole au premier trimestre 2012. En effet, ds janvier 2012, lindice global des prix  la consommation du Grand Alger faisait ressortir une hausse brutale et subite (2,31 %), quivalente  5,5 fois la hausse mensuelle moyenne de cet indice au titre de lanne 2011. Lenvole au premier trimestre 2012 des prix dun nombre trs limit de produits frais explique 96 % de linflation, en moyenne annuelle, de cette catgorie de produits pour toute lanne 2012 (21,37 %). Par ailleurs, linflation des prix  la consommation (hors produits alimentaires) na t que de 6,09 % en 2012, anne o le taux dinflation a atteint le  pic  historique de 8,89 %. Aprs 19 mois de tendance haussire ininterrompue (de juillet 2011  janvier 2013), linflation, en moyenne annuelle, a entam un mouvement de baisse en fvrier 2013. En effet, le taux dinflation en moyenne annuelle sest tabli  8,07 %  mars 2013 puis  6,59 %  juin 2013 contre, respectivement, 8,89 %, 8,91 % et 8,56 %,  dcembre 2012, janvier et fvrier 2013. La dclration du rythme dinflation sest poursuivie au troisime trimestre 2013, faisant reculer le taux en moyenne annuelle jusqu 5,32 %  septembre 2013, soit  un niveau infrieur  celui de septembre 2012 (7,95 %). En glissement annuel  septembre 2013, la hausse est plus modre (2,18 %), pendant que lindice moyen des neuf premiers mois de 2013 a augment de 4,15 % par rapport  celui de la mme priode de lanne prcdente. En outre, au terme des neuf premiers mois de 2013, le niveau gnral des prix dans la capitale est quasiment stable  sa valeur de janvier 2013, pendant quil flchissait de 0,9 point au niveau national. Cependant, en dpit du phnomne de dsinflation manifeste au cours des neuf premiers mois de 2013, la hausse des prix des produits alimentaires est reste leve mme si elle est en tendance dcroissante. 7 En moyenne annuelle  septembre 2013, linflation des groupes  alimentation  (6,69 %),  habillement  (7,37 %), et celle du groupe  transport et communication  (5,76%) sont les seules qui dpassent linflation globale (5,32 %). Cela confirme la forte incidence des prix de lalimentation ; une situation analogue  celle de lanne prcdente o la hausse annuelle moyenne  septembre 2012 tait de 9,9 %. De plus, leur contribution en septembre 2013 (56,86 %), en progression de 1,7 point en un an, dpasse largement leur pondration (43,1 %) dans lindice des prix  la consommation. Pour ce qui est de limpact de linflation importe, il convient de relever que les prix intrieurs des produits agricoles imports ne refltent pas suffisamment la tendance baissire de leur cours mondiaux, dautant quils bnficient de subventions implicites que sont les exonrations de taxes et de droits de douanes. Les niveaux des prix intrieurs sont ainsi quasiment toujours bien suprieurs  ceux des prix mondiaux, alors quils devraient voluer paralllement  la hausse comme  la baisse. Par ailleurs, la tendance chez les principaux partenaires conomiques de lAlgrie est  la dsinflation, le rythme annuel en glissement tant infrieur  deux pourcent  juin 2013, soit 1,8 % pour les Etats-Unis et 1,6 % pour la zone euro. Au sein du groupe alimentation, les produits agricoles frais ont subi une inflation  deux chiffres mais en recul, passant de 15,9 % en septembre 2012  10,8 % en septembre 2013. Ces produits qui ne reprsentent que 16,9 % de lindice, ont gnr prs de la moiti de linflation en septembre 2013 (45,2 %) contre 41,5 % un an auparavant, pendant que la progression des prix des produits alimentaires industriels a t relativement modre. Leur inflation est estime  seulement 2,9 % en septembre 2013 contre 4,9 % un an auparavant et, de surcrot, leur contribution a baiss de 2 points  13,4 %, pour une pondration de 26,2 %. A en juger par leur contribution  la forte hausse des prix du groupe de produits alimentaires, le sous-groupes - viandes et abats de mouton- qui reprsente 5 % de lindice, gnrent 54,1 % de linflation de ce groupe en septembre 2013. En outre, cette contribution a progress de 16,7 points de pourcentage depuis septembre 2012. Linflation des prix des produits manufacturs est relativement modre, avec un taux de 3,26 %  septembre 2013, en recul de 3,8 points de pourcentage, pendant que leur contribution a flchi de 10,5 points  22,3 %. Par ailleurs, linflation des prix des services sest acclre, passant de 4,7 % en septembre 2012  6 % en septembre 2013, avec une contribution  linflation (19,2 %) en progression de 8,8 points depuis septembre 2012. En termes dinflation structurelle ou fondamentale, la tendance de la dsinflation amorce en aot 2012 (5,93 %) sest poursuivie rgulirement pour atteindre 3,9 %  septembre 2013. Les prvisions effectues en septembre indiquent que linflation de 2013, en moyenne annuelle, serait dans les limites de lobjectif  moyen terme arrt par le Conseil de la Monnaie et du Crdit et devrait se situer  moins de 4 %. La politique montaire y a jou un rle actif, en contexte de dclration montaire, pendant que la modration des dcaissements au titre du budget de lEtat et la poursuite des actions de rgulation et dorganisation des marchs ont contribu  cette dsinflation. En consquence, la tendance  la dsinflation sest confirme au cours des neuf premiers mois de 2013 tant en moyenne annuelle quen glissement. Cependant, le niveau encore lev des prix commande de maintenir leffort de matrise de la liquidit et de lexpansion de la demande et de veiller  laccroissement de loffre. En outre, il est attendu quune action soutenue de mobilisation de lpargne financire des mnages par les banques puisse contribuer  la lutte contre le phnomne inflationniste et  consolider davantage la stabilit macroconomique. 8 Les acquis en matire de stabilit financire extrieure, notamment la solidit de la position des rserves de change et le taux de change effectif rel  proximit de lquilibre, et la stabilit montaire militent en faveur de la ralisation progressive du vritable potentiel de croissance conomique  partir de lanne 2014 o linvestissement productif devrait apporter une contribution effective. Aussi, le ncessaire dveloppement de linvestissement productif reposera sur la capacit dpargne nationale qui est apprciable,  en juger par les pargnes financires accumules au cours des douze dernires annes. Il sagit dasseoir un nouveau schma de financement qui vacue durablement tout recours  lendettement extrieur. Enfin, la dynamique des crdits  lconomie en 2013 qui sinscrit dans le cadre du dveloppement de crdits sains  lconomie, visant  stimuler la production intrieure, montre que le canal crdits bancaires reste potentiellement important en matire de financement  la fois de linvestissement productif, des PME et du logement promotionnel (crdits hypothcaires). En appui  la ralisation de cet important objectif dallocation des ressources  la croissance inclusive, labsorption progressive des excs de liquidits sur le march montaire doit tre accompagne par des efforts soutenus des banques commerciales en matire de mobilisation des pargnes financires  terme des entreprises et des mnages, impulse par une rmunration adquate en termes rels. 9

Title: Strengthening control and supervision of foreign trade operations
text: Strengthening the control and supervision of foreign trade operations in the context of current convertibility Introductory speech by the Governor of the Bank of Algeria at the working meeting with bank officials Algiers, 15 August 2013 1/9 The purpose of our meeting today is to take stock of the conduct of exchange control operations, in compliance with the framework of the current convertibility of the dinar. Before doing so, it is useful to analyse in broad strokes the recent evolution of imports, the level and upward trend of which represent a vulnerability for the balance of payments. 1. Evolution of imports The economic note for the first quarter of 2013, presented by the Bank of Algeria on 16 June 2013, highlighted a relative shock to Algeria's trade balance over this period. Indeed, hydrocarbon exports contracted, in value terms, by 8.6% in the first half of 2013 compared to the same half of 2012, while imports of goods continued their upward trend in the first half of the current year to the tune of 17.6%. In addition to the negative impact of the increase in overall imports on the balance of payments in the context of high dependence on hydrocarbon exports and the structural weakness of non-hydrocarbon exports, the evolution of the structure of these imports is an additional cause for concern. Indeed, after their slight increase between 2009 and 2010, respectively to 37.40 billion and 38.89 billion, imports of F.O.B goods increased by 20.67% in 2011 and by 9.89% in 2012 to reach 46.93 billion and 51.57 billion respectively. This upward trend continued in the first half of 2013, when imports of goods reached 27.8 billion. It is important to remember that prior to 2007, Algeria's annual import bill for goods never exceeded 21 billion. The breakdown of imports of goods, by product group, shows that their runaway over the last two years 2/9 years and the first half of 2013 is due, to a large extent, to the surge in imports of non-food consumer goods. While total imports increased by 20.67% and 9.89% respectively in 2011 and 2012 and by 17.6% in the first half of 2013 compared to the same period in 2012, imports of non-food consumer goods increased by 22.4%, 39.8% and 15.03% respectively over the same periods. It is important to note that these imports of non-food consumer goods contributed 59.1% to the increase in total imports in 2012 and 16.5% in the first half of 2013. Imports of industrial capital goods, down 16.8% in 2012, rose 18.56% in the first half of 2013. These developments, which are harmful to the national economy, led to a significant change in the structure of Algeria's imports between 2009 and 2012, followed by a relative reversal in the first half of 2013, as shown in the table below:  The share of non-food consumer goods in overall imports, from 15.9% in 2009, rose to 20.34% in 2012 to 19.28% in the first half of 2013.  And, that of capital goods fell from 38.9% in 2009 to 27.2% in 2012, and then rose to 29.59% in the first half of 2013. For the first half of 2013, imports of passenger vehicles and accessories reached nearly 2.46 billion, in C.I.F. 4/9 It should be noted that the last regulation on banking conditions of June 2013, aimed at greater diversification of bank intermediation, regulates the tariffs for banking services related to import and transfer operations. At the end of this analysis of the evolution and structure of imports, what about the monitoring and control of operations with the outside world? 2. Stability of the exchange rate regime and strengthening of control mechanisms As part of the liberalization of the exchange rate regime in the context of structural adjustments in 1994-1998, the process of convertibility of the dinar for international current transactions was completed in September 1997 when Algeria adopted the provisions of Article VIII of the Articles of Agreement of the International Monetary Fund. As a reminder, the mechanism defined by Regulation No. 95-07 of 23 December 1995 (amending and replacing Regulation No. 92-04 of 22 March 1992) on exchange rate control had already made decisive progress in terms of the current convertibility of the dinar, following the commercial convertibility introduced in 1991. Indeed, the current convertibility of the dinar relates to current transactions in the balance of payments, namely goods and services, factor income and transfers. Article 3 of Regulation No. 07-01 of 3 February 2007 on the rules applicable to current transactions with foreign countries stipulates: "Payments and transfers relating to current international transactions shall be free. They shall be carried out by approved intermediaries'. The application of foreign exchange regulations being delegated by the Council of Money and Credit to banks, authorized intermediaries, by the Ordinance on Money and Credit, 5/9 modified and supplemented, they play a preponderant role in controlling foreign exchange transactions and those resulting from foreign trade. This control must be carried out by the approved intermediaries, both a priori and a posteriori, that is to say from the domiciliation to the clearance of the files and this, in accordance with the regulatory texts in force. In this area, the new internal control regulation issued in 2011 requires banks to put in place internal control procedures enabling banks to ensure the compliance of their operations, including foreign trade. For foreign direct investment, transfers of income, profits and dividends are covered by current convertibility (Regulation No. 07-01 of 3 February 2007), providing that the transfer of the proceeds of disposal or liquidation of the investment is carried out without delay through intermediaries authorized under Regulation No. 05-03 of 6 June 2005 on foreign investments, pursuant to Article 31 of Ordinance No. 01-03 of 20 August 2001, as amended and supplemented, on the development of investment. As part of the strengthening of the traceability system for payments with the outside world for bona fide transactions, the supplementary finance law for 2009 introduced new measures, contributing to the traceability of financial flows and the fight against the informal. This makes banks operating in Algeria more responsible, which have, by virtue of their authorization, a responsibility for first-level control of operations with the rest of the world. Algeria also enshrines the stability of its exchange rate regime, in line with its commitments under Article VIII of the Articles of Agreement of the International Monetary Fund and those under the Association Agreement with the European Union, particularly in the field of current payments and capital movement. 6/9 In addition, the amendment in August 2010 of Ordinance 96-22 on the punishment of infringements of foreign exchange laws and regulations and the movement of capital to and from abroad further strengthened the system for combating foreign exchange offences. It is worth recalling that this legislative amendment has made substantial changes aimed at ensuring a better effectiveness of the system in place, through the relaxation and simplification of the procedures for prosecuting infringements found and the aggravation of sanctions against offenders, whether economic operators or banks, authorised intermediaries. The obligation of the prior complaint for the initiation of public proceedings has thus been abolished, which allows the territorially competent public prosecutor to initiate proceedings on the basis of the minutes sent to him by the agents authorized to establish the offences including the sworn inspectors of the Bank of Algeria. New offences have also been incorporated into the law, as it is prescribed the confiscation of the body of the offence as well as of all means used for fraud, whereas previously only means of transport were concerned. In addition, a national register of offenders has been established to identify the perpetrators of foreign exchange offences to whom administrative sanctions may be applied (precautionary measures). In addition, the conditions for the use of the transaction in this area have been tightened. It is within such a legal and regulatory framework that the Bank of Algeria continued during the period 2010-2013 its sustained effort to control a posteriori current transactions with abroad, because the operations of the capital account are subject to prior authorization by the Council of Currency and Credit and are subject to a priori control. 7/9 If the exercise of exchange control is delegated to banks, authorized intermediaries, by law, the exercise by the Bank of Algeria of its powers in terms of a posteriori control is carried out by means of documentary control and on-the-spot control. The control on documents is carried out on the basis of the declarations sent monthly by the banks, authorized intermediaries, to the Bank of Algeria -declaration of opening of domiciliation files, declaration of cleared files and declaration relating to unpurified files-, while the on-the-spot control is carried out unexpectedly at the counters of the banks, authorized intermediaries, by sworn inspectors. The system of control on documents was strengthened between 2007 and 2011 and led to precautionary measures prohibiting bank domiciliation and transfer of funds abroad taken by the Bank of Algeria, like 143 operators banned in 2013 at the end of the process of clearing their foreign trade files. This type of control may also lead to foreign exchange offence reports drawn up by sworn inspectors of the Bank of Algeria, in application of the provisions of Ordinance No. 96-22, as amended and co-appointed. As part of on-the-spot exchange control, at bank counters, the years 2010 to August 2013 recorded an intensification of control missions: thematic missionsforeign trade, full control missions and specific investigations. At the end of these missions, the sworn inspectors of the Bank of Algeria drew up 208 foreign exchange offence reports, some of which followed checks on documents, in application of the provisions of Ordinance No. 96-22 as amended and supplemented. It is worth pointing out that a significant number of these reports have been drawn up against economic operators. In total, the control system for balance of payments transactions with the outside world has been strengthened in recent years under 8/9 the angle of control and traceability of payments (transfers) at the level of banks, authorized intermediaries, both goods and services. Although the exercise of exchange control is delegated by law to banks, authorized intermediaries, the intensification of post-clearance audits, on the basis of documents and on the spot, by the Bank of Algeria has continued and the results achieved are demonstrative in this area. Finally, and as far as goods are concerned, the so-called control of transactions is the responsibility of customs. Coordination between the Bank of Algeria, in charge of the post-clearance control of regulations, and the customs administration in terms of compiling trade balance data and combating exchange rate offences is effective on the ground. However, the control of customs values will require more effort. Before giving the floor to the heads of the banks, authorized intermediaries, I would like to ask the Director-General of Foreign Exchange and the Director of External Inspection to give a brief update on the control and supervision operations concerning foreign trade and transfer operations. 9/9

Stabilit du rgime des changes et renforcement des dispositifs de contrle Dans le cadre de la libralisation du rgime des changes en contexte d'ajustements structurels en 1994-1998, le processus de convertibilit du dinar pour les transactions internationales courantes a t complt en septembre 1997 lorsque l'Algrie a adopt les dispositions de l'article VIII des statuts du Fonds Montaire International. Pour mmoire, le dispositif dfini par le rglement n 95-07 du 23 dcembre 1995 (modifiant e t remplaant le rglement n 92-04 du 22 mars 1992) relatif au c ontrle des changes avait dj permis une avance dcisive en matire de convertibilit courante du dinar, suite  la convertibilit commerciale mise en place en 1991. En effet, la convertibilit courante du dinar porte sur les transactions courantes de la balance des paiements,  savoir les biens et services, les revenus des facteurs et les transferts. Le rglement n 07-01 du 03 fvrier 2007 relatif aux rgles appl icables aux transactions courantes avec l'tranger stipule, dans son article 3 :  les paiements et transferts affrents aux transactions internationales courantes sont libres. Ils s'effectuent par les intermdiaires agres. Lapplication de la rglementation des changes tant dlgue par le Conseil de la Monnaie et du Crdit aux banques, intermdiaires agrs, de par lordonnance relative  la monnaie et au crdit, 5/9 modifie et complte, celles-ci jouent un rle prpondrant en matire de contrle sur les oprations de change et celles issues du commerce extrieur. Ce contrle doit tre assur par les intermdiaires agrs, aussi bien a priori qua posteriori, c'est--dire de la domiciliation jusqu lapurement des dossiers et ce, en conformit avec les textes rglementaires en vigueur. Dans ce domaine, le nouveau rglement relatif au contrle interne dict en 2011 impose aux banques la mise en place de procdures de contrle interne permettant aux banques de sassurer de la conformit de leurs oprations, y compris de commerce extrieur. Pour les investissements directs trangers, les transferts de revenus, bnfices et dividendes sont couverts par la convertibilit courante (rglement n 07-01 du 03 fvrier 2007), p endant que le transfert du produit de cession ou de liquidation de l'investissement s'effectue sans dlai par le biais des intermdiaires agrs en vertu du rglement n05-03 du 06 juin 2005 relatif aux in vestissements trangers, pris en application de l'article 31 de l'Ordonnance n01-03 du 20 aot 2001 modifie et complte, relative au dveloppement de l'investissement. Title: Statement to the International Monetary and Financial Committee (CMFI) during the meeting held on April 16, 2020
text: Statement to the IMFC by Mr. AIMENE BENABDERRAHMANE, Governor of the Bank of Algeria Speaking on behalf of Afghanistan, Algeria, Ghana, Iran, Libya, Morocco, Pakistan and Tunisia. On behalf of the authorities of the countries in our constituency, I would like to express My deepest sympathy for the loss of life and human suffering in countries affected by the COVID-19 outbreak. This Crisis is unlike any other and no country is immune. We Let us face a common enemy that can only be defeated by our joint efforts. Since our last virtual meeting in the framework of the Monetary Council and Financial, the pandemic has continued to wreak havoc around the world whole and on several fronts. Economic Outlook Report April 2020 (WEO) significantly reduced the projections of this year's economic growth. The Great Recession of 2020 should be deeper and broader than the global financial crisis of 2008-2009, and the outlook is surrounded by extreme uncertainties and significant downside risks. Expectations are for a fast and almost symmetrical recovery. While this is what we hope, we need to be prepared for a longer and less symmetrical recovery and be aware of scars of the crisis on the world economy, trade and supply chains. -- The immediate priority, however, is to save lives and eradicate pandemic in the world. The loss of life is permanent, while economic and financial benefits can be addressed through a proportionate and appropriate policy response and cooperation strengthened global. We welcome the first steps taken by major economies that are expected to have positive spillovers Important; Increased coordination and synchronization would also amplify their global impact. The authorities of the countries in our constituency spare no Efforts to contain the spread of the virus and cope with the crisis resulting acute health care. Our authorities have also launched stimulus plans to mitigate the immediate impact of the crisis on economic activity and employment, protecting the vulnerable population and Paving the way for a sustainable and inclusive recovery. Countries oil exporters in our constituency are also affected by the collapse of international oil prices. The strong fluctuations in oil prices create uncertainty and do not benefit exporters or importers of oil in the long term. The impact of the crisis on low-income countries (LICs)  many of them are already burdened by high debt and poverty - has been deep. Those countries will need, more urgently and on a larger scale than before, concessional financing, grants and debt relief to help them through the crisis and beyond. The plight of fragile and conflict-affected states, some without recourse to IMF resources, is particularly disastrous. We urge the international community to intensify its humanitarian support and to assist to cover the costs of refugees and internally displaced persons their country. The IMF is at the heart of the global effort to combat the crisis. The fund has acted quickly to streamline internal processes and doubled limits on access to its emergency funding during the crisis, sending thus a strong signal of its willingness to help members through the crisis. A number of our constituency members have already accessed the urgency applied by the IMF, will also have access to financing from the IMF in the coming weeks. Under extraordinary conditions, the IMF Emergency Financing Should Be Available to All Members impartially and without exception. In an environment of extreme uncertainty, the resource envelope of the IMF should be large enough to deal effectively with This crisis continues. We welcome the improvements contributed to the Disaster Containment and Relief Fund for Relieving debt-servicing pressures on low-income countries (LIF) and call on the IMF to intensify discussions on a short-term liquidity line. The recent doubling of new Arrangements to borrow and the new round of bilateral borrowing arrangements, have were important milestones. A temporary increase in limits of access to other IMF facilities would be appropriate, taking into account the significant funding needs of members. We ask also a substantial allocation of SDRs to increase liquidity by supplementing members' foreign reserves, as was done during the last crisis. IMF quotas are the main source of IMF resources. We strongly support the review, at an early date for the adequacy of IMF quotas and the continuation of the IMF governance reform process under the 16th General review of quotas. We endorse the Director-General's focused global policy, which appropriately addresses the theme "exceptional times-actions" exceptional" - calling for immediate action to slow down the Spread of the virus, strengthening the resilience of health systems and mitigate the economic fallout of the pandemic. We strongly support the Director-General's call for a more Greater global cooperation to restore growth and trade and members to avoid trade restrictions on medical supplies and other life-saving essentials valuable during this truly global threat. It is important that the humanitarian dimension of this crisis be kept in plain sight, then that we focus on the common good. Finally, our authorities express their deep gratitude to the management and staff for their swift action and dedicated efforts, and tirelessly to help members through this crisis.

Title: Speech by Governor Salah Eddine TALEB on the occasion of the 47th session of the Council of Arab Governors
text: word H.E. Salehuddin Talib Governor of Algeria Bank President of the forty-seventh session At the opening meeting of the forty-seventh session Council of Governors of Central Banks and Monetary Institutions Arabic Algeria. People's Democratic Republic of Algeria 71 September (September) 3202 Your Excellency Mr. Ayman Ben Abderrahmane, Prime Minister, Your Excellency Dr. Abdul Rahman bin Abdul Allah Al-Hamidy, Director General and Chairman of the Board of Directors of the Arab Monetary Fund, Your Excellencies Governors of Central Banks and Arabic Monetary Institutions, Dear Ladies and Sisters, At the outset of my statement on the occasion of the forty-seventh session of the Council of Governors of Central Banks and Monetary Institutions Arabic, I am pleased to welcome you to your second country, the People's Democratic Republic of Algeria. I would also like to extend my sincere thanks and appreciation for honoring me and Algeria Bank with chairing this session. I would also like to thank His Excellency the Governor of the Central Bank of Tunisia for presiding over the previous session. It is also extended to His Excellency Dr. Abdulrahman bin Abdullah Al-Humaidi, Director General and Chairman of the Board of Directors of the International Monetary Fund, and to all the sisters and brothers working in the Fund for their distinguished efforts in order to make the work and activities of the Board and its committees a success, as well as their constructive contribution to the organization and preparation of this meeting. We are grateful to the IMF for the many important topics and issues addressed at our meeting this year, which reflect the priorities of central banks and Arabic monetary institutions. Excellencies, Sisters and Brothers, The global economy and the economies of the Arabic region face many challenges as a reflection of the current international and regional developments, as the rise in commodity prices and the tightening of monetary policy by raising interest rates to alleviate the global inflationary wave, the high indebtedness of some countries, and the impact of a number of countries The task of these other repercussions of climate change, portrayal of challenges. These exceptional circumstances prompted international and regional institutions to reassess the economic conditions, by reconsidering their forecasts for economic growth, as the International Monetary Fund expects global economic growth to slow in 2023 and 2024 to reach about 3.0 percent, compared to about 3.5 percent estimated in 2022. In a related context, the Arab Monetary Fund expects the economic growth rate of Arabic countries to be about 3.5 percent in 2023 and about 4.0 percent in 2024, compared to about 5.6 percent estimated in 2022, with a decline in global economic activity. With regard to inflation, influenced by IMF estimates, according to the level of the global rate of inflation, it is expected to witness a decline of 6.8 percent in 2023 and 5.2 percent by about 2024, compared to the estimated 8.7 percent in 2022. Central banks play a pivotal role in consolidating opportunities for economic, financial and monetary stability, coordinating policies to address current challenges and enhancing the health of the financial and banking sector. In light of these circumstances, the importance of maintaining macroeconomic and financial stability as a condition for facing economic challenges in the medium and long term is highlighted, and I cannot but commend the efforts of the Arab Monetary Fund in issuing the annual report on financial stability in Arabic countries, and the important analyses it contains in this regard. Excellencies, Sisters and Brothers, A good occasion to discuss developments The meeting of our Council Duma represents economic, financial and monetary, and the challenges they pose to central banks. We are pleased with the issues and topics on our agenda today. The meeting will discuss the effectiveness of monetary policy in confronting inflation arising from supply imbalances, and the balance between promoting digitization Financial services and maintaining financial stability. Discussions will also address independence and enhancing transparency, accountability and governance in the work of central banks. Discussions of the meeting also include the priorities of the Financial Action Task Force (FATF) and the challenges of implementing the FATF standards in the Arabic region. In this regard, we would like to thank all the speakers for their participation in making presentations on the topics raised. I also thank the Arab Monetary Fund and the International Monetary Fund for their cooperation in organizing the workshop tomorrow, Monday, on "Current Challenges Facing Central Banks: The Interplay of Monetary and Fiscal Policies", as you are aware of the increasing importance of this topic due to the challenges it poses to the financial and banking sector. In this context, we also appreciate the great efforts made by the Arab Monetary Fund and the speed of its response to the needs of Arabic countries, whether through the speed of providing loans, or at the level of holding High-level meetings and meetings, meetings of committees and working groups emanating from the Council, or through the issuance of a number of important guidelines and guidelines that have a role in providing advice and technical assistance to assist Arabic countries in adopting appropriate policies. In this context, we are grateful for the great efforts made by the Arab Monetary Fund within the framework of the work of the Modern Financial Technology Group, in terms of addressing various axes of digital financial transformation topics, as well as at the level of the regional initiative to enhance inclusion, to commend the financial in the region Arabic. Perhaps it is also a good occasion here with the activities and great efforts made by central banks and Arabic monetary institutions in cooperation with banking institutions, during the Arab Day for Financial Inclusion, corresponding to April 27 of each year, and we look forward to preparing for the activities of the next year 2024, which contributes to raising awareness of financial inclusion issues. I also thank the Arab Monetary Fund for its initiative to establish Green and Sustainable Finance Network in Arabic countries, which reflects the growing interest shown by Arab countries in this regard. Excellencies, Sisters and Brothers, I would like to take this opportunity to commend Buna, which was established by your esteemed Council, for its innovative and distinguished services and international acceptance as a model for enhancing the efficiency and safety of cross-border payment and transfer transactions. There is no doubt that the support of central banks Arabic the platform in contributing to the achievement of strategic dimensions is crucial for the platform in enhancing opportunities for regional financial integration and linking with the global economy, contributing to the development of the compliance system in payment and settlement operations, expanding the use of Arabic currencies in transfers and financial, investment and inter-commercial transactions and settling these transfers in a timely and immediate manner efficiently. and competitive cost. We need to complete efforts to include currencies Arabic and connect the rest of the banks, and urge banks to activate transfers through them and come up with initiatives that enhance access to their services. At Algeria Bank, we have directed all banks operating in the local market to intensify their transactions through Buna's payment platform in all listed currencies. Excellencies, Sisters and Brothers, At the level of the Arab world, the impact of recent geopolitical changes has not been the same for all countries, which requires more solidarity and action on our part, especially in defining economic policies to counter cyclical fluctuations by forming anti-shock savings structures. In this context, the Algeria Revenue Control Fund has absorbed a significant part of the oil price fluctuations since 2014. The Special Refinancing Programme, launched in 2021 to support the post-COVID-19 economic recovery, was a balanced response to its consequences. Today, Algeria is witnessing remarkable developments in macroeconomic and financial indicators despite various recent global crises, as it continues to diversify and modernize its economy and move towards innovation, and in this regard, within the framework of the banking and financial field, a new monetary and banking law was issued this year, which aims to keep pace with global banking developments, develop modern financial technologies, and approve frameworks for Islamic banking and green finance, while ensuring the strengthening of the powers of the Monetary and Banking Council as well as the powers of Banking Commission to achieve a monetary policy objective and financial stability. In these circumstances, Algeria has come to support the brotherly countries of the Arabic facing various difficulties, and calls for joint Arab action within the framework of international institutions to provide them with the prompt and necessary support.
