Title: Communication on monetary and financial trends in the fourth quarter of 2013
text: MONETARY AND FINANCIAL TRENDS IN THE FOURTH QUARTER OF 2013 The purpose of this note is to analyse the main financial and monetary trends during 2013, with a particular focus on the second half of the year marked by financial volatility, which particularly affected emerging economies. The global economy entered an important phase of change in 2013, a transition in which recovery in advanced economies was combined with a slowdown in emerging and developing economies. Correlative to the strong increase in international trade, the recovery of advanced economies was more sustained in the second half of the year, driven by the acceleration of growth in the US economy in the fourth quarter of 2013 and the exit of the euro area from recession in the same quarter. Favourable banking and financial conditions have contributed to the strengthening of the recovery in advanced economies in the context of very moderate inflation. In the face of such a strengthening of the pace of growth in developed countries, the recovery has been moderate in emerging and developing countries, some of which have experienced macro-financial imbalances in a situation of sluggish domestic demand, while facing a tightening of overall financial conditions and capital outflows linked to the acuteness of financial volatility in the second half of 2013. As a result, the currencies of several emerging markets have come under severe pressure that has led central banks to intervene in foreign exchange markets to mitigate exchange rate adjustments, drawing on their official reserves. In addition, risks to a reversal of capital flows are on the rise for emerging markets, ahead of the normalization of US monetary policy. The national economy, while among the emerging economies that are resilient today  low external financial exposure, high foreign exchange reserves and exchange rate flexibility  is affected by other risks to the short-term outlook of the global economy, notably through the price of oil. 1. EVOLUTION OF THE BALANCE OF PAYMENTS The evolution of the current account balance during 2013 confirms the vulnerability of the external balance of payments to any underperformance of hydrocarbon exports, judging by the evolution recorded in the second and third quarters, in the context of the persistence of the upward trend in imports of goods in 2013. After the large external shock of 2009 (62.3/barrel), followed by a strengthened sustainability of the external balance of payments in 2011 (112.94/barrel) and 2012 (111.05/barrel), 2013 recorded a slight current account surplus with an average price per barrel of 109.55/barrel. The average monthly oil price fluctuated between 101.45 and 115.79/barrel during 2013. After an increase in the first quarter of 2013 (112.51/barrel) compared to the last quarter of 2012 (110.24/barrel), the average quarterly price of crude oil fell in the second quarter of 2013 to 104.40/barrel (-7.21%), resulting in a half-year average of 108.55. On the other hand, an improvement in prices was observed in the third and fourth quarters of 2013 at 110.59/barrel and 110.63/barrel respectively. As a result, and under the effect of a sharp decline in the quantities of hydrocarbons exported (-7.37%), hydrocarbon exports in value terms contracted by 10.27% during the period under review compared to 2012. They amounted to 63.33 billion in 2013 (70.58 billion in 2012), with a half-yearly amount down from 32.3 billion to 31.1 billion. The quarterly profile of hydrocarbon exports indicates a contraction in the second quarter of 2013 (14.61 billion compared to 17.66 billion in the first), followed by a stabilization in the third quarter of 2013 at 14.60 billion. Subsequently, they rose to 16.46 billion in the fourth quarter of 2013. As for non-hydrocarbon exports, they stabilized at 1.1 billion in 2013 compared to their level in 2012 and 2011, confirming their structural weakness in the context of an upward trend in goods imports on an annual basis. Imports of FOB goods increased 6.9% in the period under review compared to 2012, reaching 55.13 billion from 51.57 billion. This level of imports reached in 2013 is unsustainable, given the profile of exports in both volume and value. Quarterly data indicate an upward trend in the first half of 2013, while the third quarter recorded a decline in FOB imports to 12.46 billion ( 15.14 billion in the second quarter against 14.13 billion dinars in the first). They then stood at 13.41 billion for the fourth quarter of 2013, confirming the decline in imports of goods in the second half of the year due to the contraction of those of petroleum products, food goods, raw materials, semi-finished products and capital goods. Analysis of the structure of imports indicates that imports of "industrial capital goods", which rank first with a share of 27.6%, increased by 18.9% compared to 2012. In addition, despite their decrease in the third quarter of 2013 and their stabilization in the fourth, this group contributed 68% to the increase in total imports during the period under review. As for the contribution of "semi-finished products", which reached 19.2% of total imports in 2013, thus ranking second, it is estimated at 15.9%. Imports under this group increased 5.7% in 2013 compared with the previous year. As for imports of "non-food consumer goods", which rank third with a share of 19.1 per cent, their contribution to the increase in total imports is estimated at 31.7 per cent, with a growth rate of 12 per cent. On the other hand, with a share of 16.4%, imports of "food goods", which rank fourth, increased by 6.3% and contributed 14.9% to the increase in total imports. In contrast, imports under the "energy & lubricants" group, which ranks fifth in the structure of total imports (7.4%), fell 12.1% to 4.097 billion in 2013 from 4.658 billion in 2012. After a surplus of 3.86 billion in the first quarter of 2013, a better performance than that recorded in the third and fourth quarters of 2012, the trade balance recorded a deficit in the second quarter of 2013 (-0.23 billion) mainly due to the contraction of hydrocarbon exports, while remaining in surplus for the first half of 2013. Subsequently, lower imports of goods in the third quarter led to the rebuilding of the trade surplus (2.32 billion) in this quarter, reflecting a favourable trend supported by the stabilization of hydrocarbon exports. The trade surplus improved in the fourth quarter of 2013 (3.35 billion) to 9.29 billion for the full year under review from 3.62 billion in the first half. This reflects the vulnerability of the trade balance to the profile of hydrocarbon exports, which are contracting in volume terms, in a situation of persistent increase in imports of goods at an annual rate even if the second half of 2013 recorded a decrease in this area. This is a favourable trend since their level is even lower than in the second half of 2012. Imports of services excluding factor income, which stabilized at around a half-yearly amount of 5 billion in 2013, declined slightly compared to 2012. This favourable trend contributed to a slight decline in the deficit in services excluding factor income, a deficit of 6.73 billion in 2013 compared to 7.13 billion in 2012. Reflecting a decrease in net transfers to 2.44 billion from 3.12 billion in 2012 and a relative stabilization of the "factor income" deficit (-4.16 billion), the external balance of payments current account closed 2013 with a surplus of 0.85 billion, after recording a deficit of 0.99 billion in the first nine months of the year under review. The performance in this area in the fourth quarter is all the more appreciable, as the surplus recorded (1.84 billion) more than offset the deficit of the first nine months, which mainly concerned the second quarter (-1.63 billion). Overall, the current account surplus in the external balance of payments is very small compared to 2012 (12.30 billion) and 2011 (17.77 billion). Given the stabilization of oil prices and the decrease in imports in the second half of 2013, this sharp decline in the external current account surplus is of concern from the point of view of hydrocarbon export capacity in volume. In addition, efforts to promote non-hydrocarbon exports do not seem to be producing the expected full effects, despite the measures taken in 2011 by the Council of Money and Credit and the Bank of Algeria, and that achievements in terms of import substitution are well below expectations. Despite a relative improvement in the foreign (net) direct investment item to 1.87 billion in deficit of the item "net official capital", the capital account and financial operations recorded an estimated deficit of 0.72 billion for the year 2013. As a result, the overall balance of external payments closed with a surplus of only 0.13 billion, a near equilibrium after the large surpluses of 2012 (12.06 billion) and 2011 (20.14 billion). In total, the stock of foreign exchange reserves (excluding gold) is estimated at 194.012 billion at the end of December 2013 compared to 190.661 billion at the end of December 2012, in a situation of low reserve flows combined with the valuation effect. Their level had declined to 189.750 billion at the end of June 2013, driven by the current account deficit in the second quarter, before rising to 191.866 billion at the end of September 2013. Moreover, while the increase in reserves was weak compared to 2012 and 2011, Algeria's net external financial position remains solid, supported by a historically low level of external debt (3.396 billion at the end of December 2013 compared to 3.676 billion at the end of December 2012). The level of reserves thus accumulated exceeds the usual adequacy thresholds for emerging countries, which allows Algeria to cope with possible external shocks and preserve external stability. In 2013, the Bank of Algeria continued the prudent management of official foreign exchange reserves by increasingly emphasizing rigorous monitoring and risk management, including through appropriate prudent measures to protect investment capital from loss, while achieving an acceptable level of return given the persistence of the environment of low global interest rates. At the end of December 2013, 10-year government bonds in the United States had a yield of 3.03% compared to 1.92% for German government securities of the same maturity. In addition, the prudent management of official foreign exchange reserves by the Bank of Algeria contributes to external financial stability over the medium term, in the context of flexible conduct of the dinar's effective exchange rate policy, close to its fundamental equilibrium level. To this end, the intervention of the Bank of Algeria in the interbank foreign exchange market has made it possible to mitigate the impact on the national economy of volatility on international foreign exchange markets from May 2013, while this has resulted in sharp depreciations of the currencies of several emerging countries and even risks to their financial stability that have led some central banks to intervene in foreign exchange markets and tighten their monetary policy. It is in such a context of volatility in the exchange rates of the main currencies from May 2013, that the average annual rate of the dinar against the US dollar has depreciated by 2.36%. The average annual exchange rate of the Algerian dinar against the US dollar was USD 79.3809/DZD in 2013 compared to USD 77.5519/DZD in 2012. On the other hand, the average monthly exchange rate of the dinar against the US dollar depreciated by only 0.6% between December 2012 (USD 78.1868/DZD) and December 2013 (USD 78.6569/DZD). The monthly end-of-period exchange rate of the Algerian dinar against the US dollar reached a high of USD 81.4128/DZD at the end of September 2013 against a high of USD 81.9104/DZD at the end of July 2012. In terms of quarterly year-end change, the fourth quarter of 2013 saw an appreciation of the dinar against the US dollar of 4% compared to the third quarter of the same year, when the end-of-period price increased from USD 81.4128/DZD at the end of September to USD 78.1524/DZD at the end of December 2013. Nevertheless, from the perspective of the quarterly average price, the appreciation of the dinar against the US dollar is 0.34% between the third quarter and the fourth quarter of 2013, i.e. respectively a rate of 80.3915 USD/DZD and 80.1209 USD/DZD. This favourable development should be seen in relation to the current account surplus in the last quarter of the year under review, after the deficit recorded in the first nine months. At the same time, the average annual exchange rate of the dinar against the euro depreciated by 3.21% in 2013 compared to 2012, from 102.1627 EUR/DZD in 2012 to 105.4374 EUR/DZD in 2013, while the latter appreciated by 3.37% against the US dollar in 2013 (1.3281 /USD in 2013 against 1.2848 /USD in 2012). The average quarterly rate of the dinar against the euro recorded a depreciation of 2.39% between the third and fourth quarters of the year under review. On the other hand, in terms of quarterly variation at the end of the period, the exchange rate of the dinar against the euro appreciated by 2.75% in the fourth quarter of 2013 compared to the third quarter of the same year, when the price rose from 109.9155 EUR/DZD in the third quarter to 106.8930 EUR/DZD in the fourth quarter of 2013. This is a slight depreciation compared to those of the currencies of some emerging countries against both the dollar and the euro. For example, the average dollar in 2013 recorded appreciations against the Brazilian real and the Indian rupee of around 10.44% and 9.68% respectively. As for the euro, its average annual rate for 2013 compared to 2012 appreciated by 14.23% against the Brazilian real, by 13.47% against the Indian rupee and by 12.28% against the Russian ruble. In total, and under the effect of the narrowing of the inflation differential between Algeria and its 15 main trading partner countries, i.e. to 1.71% in December 2013 against 6.23% in December 2012, and the increase in relative prices, the real effective exchange rate of the dinar depreciated by 2.34% on average in 2013 compared to the same period of 2012. However, the real effective exchange rate of the dinar remains appreciated by about 4% in December 2013 compared to its equilibrium level determined according to fundamentals. 2. MONETARY DEVELOPMENTS The M2 money supply is estimated at 11945.82 billion dinars at the end of December 2013 against 11015.14 billion dinars at the end of 2012 and (11261.44 billion dinars at the end of June 2013), an annual growth rate of 8.45% including 6.08% in the second half. This confirms the deceleration in the pace of monetary expansion that characterized 2012 (10.94% against 19.91% in 2011). The deceleration in the pace of monetary expansion also concerns the monetary aggregate M2 (excluding deposits in the hydrocarbon sector), whose rate fell to 10.21% in 2013 from 16.59% in 2012. However, the M2 money supply (excluding deposits in the hydrocarbon sector) grew faster, and at almost the same half-year pace, than M2 in the broad sense in 2013, confirming the diminishing role of hydrocarbon sector resources in banks' means of action. The single-digit deceleration in the pace of monetary expansion in 2013 was combined with significant growth in credit to the economy in the context of moderate growth in net foreign assets in the aggregate monetary situation. Net foreign assets, with an outstanding amount of 15218.17 billion dinars at the end of December 2013 against 14939.97 billion dinars at the end of December 2012, increased slightly in 2013 (1.86%) compared to the previous year (7.31%), in line with the evolution of the external position. Even with a small role in the money creation process in 2013, this aggregate occupies a very significant place in the consolidated monetary situation. In particular, the ratio of net foreign assets to M2 reached 1.274 at the end of 2013, after a rise from 0.834 at the end of 2004 to 1.473 at the end of 2008. This confirms the importance of the position of external assets as a guarantee of monetary signs in the national economy. Moreover, after several years of sustained accumulation of resources in the Revenue Regulation Fund by the Treasury, 2013 recorded a relative stabilization of the State's net financial position in the monetary situation, even if the second quarter recorded an improvement in this area. As a component of the aggregate net claims on the State, deposits in the CCP and the Treasury grew by 10.1% in 2013, mainly in the first half of the year (9.1%). Thus, the financial position of the State as a net creditor vis-a-vis the banking system remains appreciable, despite the significant increase in the aggregate credits to the economy in 2013 in a situation of deceleration in the pace of monetary expansion. However, the outstanding financial savings of the Treasury, namely the savings on its accounts opened at the Bank of Algeria, increased to 5994.93 billion dinars at the end of June 2013 against 5712.24 billion dinars at the end of December 2012, to fall to 5646.65 billion dinars at the end of December 2013, in context of relative stabilization of the overall outstanding amount of issues of Treasury securities, by way of auction on the money market. This outstanding amount increased from 600.85 billion dinars at the end of December 2012 to 592.2 billion dinars at the end of March 2013, then 577.14 billion dinars at the end of September 2013, to close at 590.37 billion dinars at the end of December 2013. As a result, the strong pace of growth in credit to the economy (20.21%) is emerging as the main determinant of monetary expansion in 2013. This rate of growth, which is equally important in half-year terms, is much higher than that recorded the previous year (15.1%). The dynamism of bank loans to the economy, supported by the facilitation and support measures taken by the public authorities at the beginning of the year, is more significant in real terms in 2013 compared to 2012. Indeed, the year 2013 recorded a record growth in loans to the economy in real terms, anchored on the domestic means of action of banks and not dependent on financial savings in the hydrocarbon sector. Also, the ratio of loans to the economy to M2 (excluding deposits in the hydrocarbon sector) rose to 45.1% at the end of December 2013 against 41.3% at the end of December 2012 (41.9% at the end of 2011). This clearly indicates a clear impetus in bank intermediation from the point of view of credit allocation, while the mobilization of resources is less and less based on those of the hydrocarbon sector in a situation of still significant potential with regard to the banking of private companies and households. Bank loans to the economy reached 5154.24 billion dinars at the end of December 2013 (4742.67 billion dinars at the end of June 2013) against 4287.64 billion dinars at the end of December 2012 and 3726.51 billion dinars at the end of December 2011. On a quarterly basis, the dynamism of bank loans was more sustained in the second and third quarters of the year under review. At the end of December 2013, loans to private companies reached 2366.69 billion dinars (2164.53 billion dinars at the end of June 2013) against 1940.24 billion dinars at the end of 2012, so that loans to the private sector, including households, (2721.57 billion dinars) exceeded the outstanding loans to the public sector (2432.32 billion dinars). In addition, the period under review was marked by an increase in both loans to the private sector (21.12 per cent) and to the public sector (19.22 per cent), although the latter absorbed more long-term financing. The substantial growth of loans to the economy in 2013 is driven by the dynamism of medium- and long-term loans, whose relative share reached 72.43% at the end of December 2013 (70.07% at the end of June 2013) against 68.24% at the end of 2012 and 63.42% at the end of 2011), while that of short-term loans fell to 27.57% at the end of 2013 (31.76% at the end of 2012). Indeed, with an outstanding amount of 3732.98 billion dinars at the end of 2013, medium- and long-term loans increased by 27.58% in 2013 against 23.80% in 2012. This reflects the improvement of the financing structure and conditions (extension of maturity and reduction of cost), in line with the facilitation measures taken at the beginning of 2013 which made the State support system more effective in the context of the development of healthy loans to SMEs to stimulate economic growth. For the record, this system was initiated in the fourth quarter of 2011, then boosted during 2013. Loans to households are also up (16.03%) in the context of financial inclusion, mainly for mortgage loans (18.74% at December 2013) driven by the development of the real estate market. In particular, the flow of mortgage loans increased by 60.52% in 2013. After this analysis of the increased role of the credit aggregate in 2013, as one of the counterparties of the M2 money supply, the evolution of the structure of M2 provides information in particular on the financial saving behaviour of economic agents and its impact on the means of action of banks. In a situation of low growth in assets net external and a sharp contraction in hydrocarbon deposits (-20.15%), the growth rate of M2 (excluding hydrocarbon deposits) stood at 10.21% in 2013 (4.76% in the first half of the year) compared with 8.45% for the broad M2 aggregate. Despite the sharp contraction in deposits in the hydrocarbon sector, dinar deposits collected by banks increased by 7.90% in 2013 (0.91% in the second half) against 6.02% in 2012. It is worth noting that the effect of the contraction in the second quarter mainly concerned demand deposits in the hydrocarbon sector (-73.53% for the first half of the year), which led to a 4.88% decrease in demand deposits collected by banks in the first half of 2013. However, the latter increased by 10.85% in the second half of 2013, to close the year with a growth rate of 5.44%. Indeed, after a sharp contraction in the first half of the year, deposits in the hydrocarbon sector increased by 30.57% in the second half of 2013, to reach an outstanding amount of 509.61 billion dinars at the end of the period. This amount represents 79.85% of the level at the end of 2012 and only half (49.53%) of the outstanding amount at the end of 2011, reflecting the decrease in the self-financing capacity of the hydrocarbon sector in the face of the sectoral investment programme. In addition, imports of petroleum products contribute to this downward trend. As for the demand and term deposits in dinars of public companies (excluding the hydrocarbon sector), they increased by 11.07% in 2013, mainly in the second half of the year. This contributed to the development of banks' means of action during the period under review, while the situation in the hydrocarbon sector had a contraction effect. Over the same period, demand and term deposits in dinars of private companies and households increased by 9.47%, after a significant expansion recorded in 2012 (14.7%). The breakdown of these deposits shows that the demand and term deposits in dinars of private companies with banks increased by 16.54%, well below the growth rate of bank loans to this type of economic agent (21.98%) who allocated part of this financing to their import operations. As for households' dinar-denominated demand and term deposits with banks, with a relative share of 30.8%, they increased by 6.16% in 2013 against 13.8% in 2012, in relation to the household income effect. In addition, their deposits to CCPs and the Treasury, which represent the bulk of this category of deposits, continued to increase during 2013 (10.07%), but in a slower pace compared to the same period of the previous year (30.46%). As for foreign currency deposits, they increased by 12.45% (7.2% in 2012), reaching 68.40% of the outstanding foreign currency deposits mobilized by banks at the end of December 2013. The quasi-money aggregate grew at a higher rate (10.78 per cent) than that of the M2 money supply (8.45 per cent), reflecting changes in foreign currency deposits and term deposits in dinars. This represents a sharp deceleration in the expansion of quasi-money compared to 2012 (19.59%), due to a slight increase in term deposits in a situation of sharp reduction in the excess of savings on investment. In addition, banks' resource base is now less vulnerable to an external shock affecting the hydrocarbon sector. Finally, the monetary deceleration also affected cash circulation, which increased in 2013 at the same rate (8.52%) as the monetary aggregate M2, with more sustained growth in the second half (7.25%) compared to the first half of 2013 (1.18%). As a result, the cash circulation/M2 ratio remained stable at the end of 2013 (26.8%) compared to the end of 2012, indicating a stability in demand. of household financial savings and cash, in a situation of decreasing inflationary pressures. In addition, in view of the surge in the inflation rate recorded during 2012 (8.89%), the Bank of Algeria introduced in mid-January 2013 a new monetary policy instrument, namely the recovery of liquidity at six months at a rate of return of 1.50%. In addition to extending the maturity of liquidity recoveries from January 2013 to absorb more stable liquidity from banks, the minimum reserve requirement ratio was raised in May 2013 to 12%, twelve months after it was raised by two percentage points (from 9% to 11%). This strengthening of monetary policy instruments is intended to consolidate the effectiveness of monetary policy in effectively absorbing excess liquidity in the money market. Bank liquidity, which remained stable in the first quarter of 2013, contracted in the second quarter to 2542.49 billion dinars at the end of June 2013 against 2865.94 billion dinars at the end of March 2013 and 2876.26 billion dinars at the end of December 2012. It improved slightly in the third and fourth quarters of 2013, to 2692.99 billion dinars at the end of December 2013. Indeed, the excess liquidity was effectively absorbed by liquidity recovery instruments (1350 billion dinars), in a situation of lower use by banks of the 24-hour deposit facility (479.90 billion dinars at the end of December 2013 against 838.08 billion dinars at the end of December 2012). The banks have also, within the framework of the minimum reserves, increased their holdings in accounts with the Bank of Algeria. In addition, while the interbank money market remained almost inactive in the first quarter of 2013, due to the spread of excess liquidity, interbank lending and borrowing resumed from May 2013 with interest rates formed on the interbank market close to 2%. Finally, in the context of preserving macroeconomic stability as a primary objective, monetary policy, underpinned by the flexible conduct of exchange rate policy, plays an active role. To do this, the Bank of Algeria effectively absorbs excess liquidity and helps to stem the inflationary phenomenon. 3. DECELERATION OF INFLATION The inflationary phenomenon emerged particularly acutely in 2012, after a long period of moderate inflation following structural adjustment. This is a phenomenon essentially of an endogenous nature and anchored on a very limited number of fresh products whose prices soared in the first quarter of 2012. Indeed, as early as January 2012, the overall consumer price index of Greater Algiers showed a sudden and sudden increase (2.31%), equivalent to 5.5 times the average monthly increase in this index for 2011. The surge in the prices of a very limited number of fresh products in the first quarter of 2012 explains 96% of the inflation, on an annual average, of this product category for the whole of 2012 (21.37%). On the other hand, consumer price inflation (excluding food) was only 6.09% in 2012, when the inflation rate reached the "peak" of 8.89%. After 19 months of uninterrupted upward trend, between July 2011 and January 2013, inflation, on an annual average, began to decline in February 2013. Indeed, the annual average inflation rate was 8.07% in March 2013 and 6.59% in June 2013 against 8.89% in December 2012. Inflation continued to decelerate, to stand at 5.32% in September 2013 and 3.26% in December 2013, its lowest level since July 2007. This corresponds to a decrease of 5.63 percentage points compared to December 2012, but which is less than the deceleration in the rate of inflation for the food and non-alcoholic beverages group (9.04 percentage points), which is heavily weighted in the consumer price index. Year-on-year to December 2013, the increase is more moderate (1.15%), while the average index for the year increased by 3.26% compared to the previous year. In addition, at the end of the twelve months of 2013, the general price level in the capital is almost stable at its January 2013 value, while the national index rose by 0.9 percentage points. The disinflation observed during 2013 affected more the "food" and "miscellaneous" groups with inflation rates averaging 3.18% and 0.75% respectively, i.e. levels lower than headline inflation (3.26%). Indeed, by product group, the annual average inflation of three of the eight groups is higher than that of headline inflation (3.26%). These are the groups "clothing and footwear" (7.75%), "transport and communication" (5.61%) and "health and personal hygiene" (4.14%). By product category and still on an annual average, compared to 2012, inflation for "food and beverages including alcoholic beverages" saw the largest decline of 9.04 percentage points, followed by inflation for "manufactured goods" by 4.63 percentage points, while "services" edged up 1.2 percentage points. Average annual food inflation, down since February 2013, reached 3.18% in December 2013, the lowest level since September 2011. Within this category, inflation for "fresh agricultural products" reached 4.02%, a decrease of 17.35 percentage points compared to a decrease of only 2.30 percentage points for "industrial food products". In terms of the contribution to headline inflation on an annual average in 2013, the cumulative contribution for food and services is 78.15%, well above their cumulative weight of 60.19%. Food goods, with a relative weight of 43.13% in the index, contributed 45.96%, down 16.84 percentage points from December 2012. On the other hand, up 22.33 percentage points from 2012, the contribution of services is estimated at 32.19%, almost twice its relative weight (1.90 times). The contribution of fresh agricultural products estimated at 28.42%, down 21.23 percentage points compared to 2012 and representing 1.68 times its weight, explains the decline in that of food goods. On the other hand, the contribution of industrial food prices to food price inflation increased by 17.23 percentage points in 2013 compared to 2012, reaching 38.17%. The trend towards disinflation was confirmed and amplified in 2013, both in the advanced economies, 1.5% for the United States and 1.4% for the euro area, and in emerging economies. The expansion of international trade and the convergence of the relative prices they induce has led to the spread of the disinflationary process, which consequently makes it possible to maintain or slightly improve real incomes in a context of moderate nominal growth and low inflation. In line with disinflation among the main economic partners and for the first time since 2000, the prices of imported goods led to a decline in the level of the price index with a high import content (-3.5%) on an annual average and year-on-year basis in December 2013. However, with regard to the impact of imported inflation, it should be noted that the domestic prices of imported agricultural products do not sufficiently reflect the downward trend in their world prices, especially since they benefit from implicit subsidies such as exemptions from taxes and customs duties. La ventilation de ces dpts montre que les dpts  vue et  terme en dinars des entreprises prives auprs des banques ont progress de 16,54 %, soit un rythme bien en de du taux de croissance des crdits bancaires  ce type dagents conomiques (21,98 %) qui ont allou une partie de ces financements  leurs oprations dimportations. Pour ce qui est des dpts  vue et  terme en dinars des mnages auprs des banques, avec une part relative de 30,8 %, ils ont progress de 6,16 % en 2013 contre 13,8 % en 2012, en relation avec leffet-revenu des mnages. Par ailleurs, leurs dpts aux CCP et au Trsor, qui reprsentent lessentiel de cette catgorie de dpts, ont poursuivi leur progression au cours de lanne 2013 (10,07 %), mais en situation de ralentissement de leur rythme comparativement  la mme priode de lanne prcdente (30,46 %). Quant aux dpts en devises, ils se sont accrus de 12,45 % (7,2 % en 2012), pour atteindre 68,40 % de lencours des dpts en devises mobiliss par les banques  fin dcembre 2013. Lagrgat quasi-monnaie sest accru  un rythme plus lev (10,78 %) que celui de la masse montaire M2 (8,45 %), sous leffet de lvolution des dpts en devises et des dpts  terme en dinars. Cela reprsente une nette dclration de lexpansion de la quasi monnaie par rapport  2012 (19,59 %), sous leffet dune faible progression des dpts  terme en situation de net amenuisement de lexcs de lpargne sur linvestissement. Par ailleurs, la base de ressources des banques est aujourdhui moins vulnrable  un choc externe affectant le secteur des hydrocarbures. Enfin, la dclration montaire a concern galement la circulation fiduciaire qui sest accrue en 2013 au mme rythme (8,52 %) que lagrgat montaire M2, avec une croissance plus soutenue au second semestre (7,25 %) par rapport au premier semestre 2013 (1,18 %). En consquence, le ratio circulation fiduciaire/M2 est rest stable  fin 2013 (26,8 %) comparativement  fin 2012, indiquant une stabilit de la demande dpargne financire et dencaisses des mnages, en situation de diminution des tensions inflationnistes. Par ailleurs, eu gard  lenvole du taux dinflation enregistre au cours de lanne 2012 (8,89 %), la Banque dAlgrie a introduit ds mi-janvier 2013 un nouvel instrument de politique montaire,  savoir la reprise de liquidit  six mois  un taux de rmunration de 1,50 %. En plus de lallongement de la maturit des reprises de liquidit  partir de janvier 2013 pour absorber plus de liquidits stables des banques, le taux de constitution des rserves minimales obligatoires a t relev en mai 2013  12 %, douze mois aprs son relvement de deux points de pourcentage (de 9 %  11 %). Ce renforcement des instruments de politique montaire vise  consolider lefficacit de la politique montaire dans la rsorption effective de lexcs de liquidit sur le march montaire. La liquidit bancaire, reste stable au premier trimestre 2013, sest contracte au second trimestre  2542,49 milliards de dinars  fin juin 2013 contre 2865,94 milliards de dinars  fin mars 2013 et 2876,26 milliards de dinars  fin dcembre 2012. Elle sest lgrement amliore au troisime et quatrime trimestre 2013, pour stablir  2692,99 milliards de dinars  fin dcembre 2013. En effet, lexcs de liquidits a t rsorb de manire effective par les instruments de reprise de liquidit (1350 milliards de dinars), en situation de moindre recours des banques  la facilit de dpts  24 heures (479,90 milliards de dinars  fin dcembre 2013 contre 838,08 milliards de dinars  fin dcembre 2012). Les banques ont, par ailleurs et dans le cadre des rserves obligatoires, augment leurs avoirs en comptes auprs de la Banque dAlgrie. En outre, si le march montaire interbancaire est rest quasi inactif au premier trimestre 2013, vu la dissmination de lexcs de liquidit, les prts et emprunts interbancaires ont repris  partir de mai 2013 avec des taux dintrt forms sur le march interbancaire proches de 2 %. Enfin, dans le cadre de la prservation de la stabilit macroconomique en tant quobjectif primordial, la politique montaire, taye par la conduite flexible de la politique de taux de change, y joue un rle actif. Pour ce faire, la Banque dAlgrie rsorbe de manire effective lexcs de liquidit et contribue  endiguer le phnomne inflationniste. 3. DE LA DECELERATION DE LINFLATION Le phnomne inflationniste a merg avec une acuit particulire en 2012, aprs une longue priode dinflation modre qui a suivi lajustement structurel. Il sagit dun phnomne essentiellement de nature endogne et ancr sur un nombre trs limit de produits frais dont les prix ont connu une envole au premier trimestre 2012. En effet, ds janvier 2012, lindice global des prix  la consommation du Grand Alger faisait ressortir une hausse brutale et subite (2,31 %), quivalente  5,5 fois la hausse mensuelle moyenne de cet indice au titre de lanne 2011. Lenvole au premier trimestre 2012 des prix dun nombre trs limit de produits frais explique 96 % de linflation, en moyenne annuelle, de cette catgorie de produits pour toute lanne 2012 (21,37 %). Par ailleurs, linflation des prix  la consommation (hors produits alimentaires) na t que de 6,09 % en 2012, anne o le taux dinflation a atteint le  pic  de 8,89 %. Aprs 19 mois de tendance haussire ininterrompue, soit entre juillet 2011 et janvier 2013, linflation, en moyenne annuelle, a entam un mouvement de baisse en fvrier 2013. En effet, le taux dinflation en moyenne annuelle sest tabli  8,07 %  mars 2013 puis  6,59 %  juin 2013 contre 8,89 % en dcembre 2012. Linflation a continu  dclrer, pour se situer  5,32 %  septembre 2013 et  3,26 % en dcembre 2013, son plus bas niveau depuis juillet 2007. Cela correspond  une baisse de 5,63 points de pourcentage par rapport  dcembre 2012, mais qui est infrieur  la dclration du rythme dinflation au titre du groupe  alimentation et boissons non alcoolises  (9,04 points de pourcentage) dont la pondration est importante dans lindice des prix  la consommation. En glissement annuel  dcembre 2013, la hausse est plus modre (1,15 %), pendant que lindice moyen de lanne augmentait de 3,26 % par rapport  lanne prcdente. En outre, au terme des douze mois de 2013, le niveau gnral des prix dans la capitale est quasiment stable  sa valeur de janvier 2013, pendant que lindice national progressait de 0,9 point de pourcentage. La dsinflation observe au cours de lanne 2013, a touch plus les groupes  alimentaire  et "divers" avec des taux dinflation en moyenne annuelle de 3,18 % et 0,75 % respectivement, soit des niveaux infrieurs  linflation globale (3,26 %). En effet, par groupe de produits, linflation en moyenne annuelle de trois des huit groupes est suprieure  celle de linflation globale (3,26 %). Il sagit des groupes  habillements et chaussures  (7,75 %),  transport et communication  (5,61 %) et  sant-hygine corporelle  (4,14 %). Par catgorie de produits et toujours en moyenne annuelle, par rapport  2012, cest linflation des  biens alimentaires y compris les boissons alcoolises  qui a connu la plus forte baisse de 9,04 points de pourcentage suivie par celle des  biens manufacturs  de 4,63 points de pourcentage, alors que les services  ont connu une lgre hausse de 1,2 point. Linflation en moyenne annuelle des biens alimentaires en baisse depuis fvrier 2013 a atteint 3,18 % en dcembre 2013, soit le niveau le plus bas depuis le mois de septembre 2011. Au sein de cette catgorie, linflation des  produits agricoles frais  a atteint 4,02 %, soit une baisse de 17,35 points de pourcentage contre une baisse de seulement 2,30 points des  produits alimentaires industriels . Sous langle de la contribution  linflation globale en moyenne annuelle en 2013, celle cumule au titre des biens alimentaires et services est de 78,15 %, bien suprieure  leur poids cumuls qui est de 60,19 %. Les biens alimentaires, avec un poids relatif de 43,13 % dans lindice, ont contribu  hauteur de 45,96 %, en baisse de 16,84 points de pourcentage par rapport  dcembre 2012. Par contre, en hausse de 22,33 points de pourcentage par rapport  2012, la contribution des services est estime  32,19 %, soit presque deux fois son poids relatif (1,90 fois). La contribution des produits agricoles frais estime  28,42 %, en baisse de 21,23 points de pourcentage par rapport  2012 et reprsentant 1,68 fois son poids, explique la baisse de celle des biens alimentaires. Par ailleurs, la contribution des prix des produits alimentaires industriels  linflation des prix des biens alimentaires a augment de 17,23 points de pourcentage en 2013 par rapport  2012, en atteignant 38,17 %. La tendance  la dsinflation sest confirme et amplifie en 2013, aussi bien dans les conomies avances, soit 1,5 % pour les Etats-Unis et 1,4 % pour la zone euro, qumergentes. Lexpansion des changes internationaux et la convergence des prix relatifs quils induisent, a conduit  la diffusion du processus dsinflationniste permettant en consquence de maintenir ou damliorer lgrement les revenus rels en contexte de progression nominale modre et de faible inflation. En cohrence avec la dsinflation chez les principaux partenaires conomiques et pour la premire fois depuis 2000, les prix des biens imports ont gnr la baisse du niveau de lindice des prix  fort contenu dimport (- 3,5 %) en moyenne annuelle et en glissement annuel  dcembre 2013. Cependant, pour ce qui est de limpact de linflation importe, il convient de relever que les prix intrieurs des produits agricoles imports ne refltent pas suffisamment la tendance baissire de leur cours mondiaux, dautant quils bnficient de subventions implicites que sont les exonrations de taxes et de droits de douanes. Les niveaux des prix intrieurs sont ainsi quasiment toujours bien suprieurs  ceux des prix mondiaux, alors quils devraient voluer paralllement  la hausse comme  la baisse. Linflation sous jacente, en moyenne annuelle, mesure hors produits alimentaires a atteint en dcembre 2013, un taux de 3,32 %, soit une baisse de 2,77 points de pourcentage par rapport  2012. De mme, linflation fondamentale mesure hors produits agricoles frais reste aussi modre avec un taux de 3,03 %  fin 2013 contre 5,64 % en fin 2012. En conclusion, la tendance  la dsinflation sest confirme en 2013 tant en moyenne annuelle quen glissement, ancre sur une nette dclration montaire. Cette stabilit montaire, tout comme les acquis en matire de stabilit financire extrieure, notamment la solidit de la position des rserves de change et le taux de change effectif rel  proximit de lquilibre, militent en faveur de la ralisation progressive du vritable potentiel de croissance conomique  partir de lanne 2014. Aprs les importants efforts en matire dinvestissements publics et leur contribution effective  la croissance hors hydrocarbures, linvestissement productif dans les secteurs hors hydrocarbures devrait apporter une contribution accrue au potentiel de croissance. Ce dernier devrait tre port aussi,  court terme, par une dynamique plus soutenue en matire de ralisation des investissements dans le secteur des hydrocarbures o lautofinancement restera de vigueur. La capacit dpargne nationale qui est apprciable,  en juger par les pargnes financires accumules au cours des douze dernires annes, permettra dasseoir un nouveau schma de financement de linvestissement productif  partir de 2014, tout en vacuant durablement tout recours  lendettement extrieur. Enfin, la dynamique des crdits  lconomie en 2013 montre que le canal crdits bancaires reste potentiellement important en matire de financement  la fois de linvestissement productif et des PME. Le ncessaire dveloppement de lintermdiation bancaire devra sinscrire dans le cadre du dveloppement de crdits sains  lconomie, visant une amlioration durable de lallocation des ressources  la croissance inclusive. Aussi, dans le cadre de la promotion de linclusion financire, des efforts soutenus des banques commerciales en matire de mobilisation des pargnes financires  terme des entreprises et des mnages, impulse par une rmunration adquate en termes rels, sont escompts  partir de 2014.

Title: Communication on monetary and financial trends in the first half of 2013
text: Algiers, 25 September 2013 Monetary and financial trends in the first half of 2013 Introduction Indicators for the first half of 2013 show signs of a gradual improvement in the outlook for the global economy, supported by measures taken at the level of advanced economies and the strong performance of emerging market and developing economies. The continued recovery of the US economy in the context of an improving labour market, the exit from recession in the euro area in the second quarter and the sustained growth of some emerging economies in Asia and Latin America testify to this improvement, even if the growth of the Chinese economy, based on the first half of 2013, is slightly below its performance of the previous year. This improvement was combined with the emergence of financial market volatility from June 2013, in a situation of uncertainty linked to the very high levels of public debt-to-GDP ratios in developed countries, while the central banks of these countries maintain or even further ease their very accommodative monetary policy; the inflation rate is low in both the United States and the euro area. It is important to note that financial volatility particularly affects emerging economies. This has resulted in risks to financial stability in emerging markets, judging by volatility in foreign exchange markets where the currencies of several emerging markets have depreciated, reflecting their vulnerability following a long period of low interest rates and large-scale capital inflows. The reverse flow of capital outflows that began in May-June 2013 and which concerned certain emerging countries, which have experienced a long period of massive capital inflows, seems to be part of the more global phenomenon of portfolio restructuring through a reallocation, particularly between emerging countries, taking into account country-specific factors. As for the national economy, while it is immune to the volatility of capital flows that is severely affecting some emerging economies, it is affected by other risks to the short-term outlook for the world economy, notably through the 1 oil prices. Its external financial position remained strong in the first half of 2013, despite a balance of payments deficit in the second quarter and the negative impact of very low global interest rates. 1. Balance of payments developments After the external shock of 2009, a strengthened sustainability of the external balance of payments characterized the years 2011 and 2012, driven by the strengthening of the price of oil, whose average annual level was 112.94/barrel and 111.05/barrel respectively, compared to 80.15/barrel in 2010. The average monthly oil price fluctuated between 101.45 and 115.72/barrel in the first half of 2013, a half-year average of 108.65/barrel compared to 113.37/barrel in the same period of the previous year. After an increase in the first quarter of 2013 (112.51/barrel) compared to the last quarter of 2012 (110.24/barrel), the average quarterly price fell in the second quarter of 2013 to 104.60/barrel, a decrease of 7.03%, in a situation of sharp decline in the quantities of hydrocarbons exported (-10.61%) during the semester under review; a rate of contraction that increased in the second quarter (-12.55%). In terms of value, hydrocarbon exports contracted by 14.31% in the first half of 2013 compared to the same half of 2012, down 37.50 billion to 32.14 billion. This negatively affected the trade balance, especially in the second quarter, while imports of goods continued their upward trend in the context of structural weakness in non-hydrocarbon exports (0.682 billion in the first half of 2013 compared to 0.473 billion in the first half of 2012). Imports of fob goods (28.379 billion) increased by 20.04% in the first half of 2013 compared to the same half of the previous year (23.641 billion), mainly due to the continued expansion of imports of non-food consumer goods (8.7%) and the increase in imports of food goods (16.2%). Imports of industrial capital goods, meanwhile, grew at a high rate (25%), in contrast to their contraction in 2012. A closer analysis of the import structure reveals significant growth in petroleum product imports in the first half of 2013 (90.2%) 2 relative to the same half of last year. This confirms the upward trend in this area over the past two years, correlative to imports of vehicles (tourist, commercial and other). Imports of services excluding factor income stabilised in the first half of 2013 compared to the same period last year, mainly due to an increase in imports of maritime transport, insurance, technical and other services, offset by the sharp contraction (-39.8%) in imports of services under "building and public works". On a quarterly basis in 2013, imports of services stabilized at 2.9 billion, while exports of services edged up in the second quarter. This favourable trend contributed to the stabilization of the deficit in services excluding factor revenues to 3.7 billion in the first half of 2013. As a result of a widening of the "factor income" deficit and a decrease in net transfers, combined with the sharp contraction of the trade surplus, the current account of the external balance of payments recorded a deficit of 1.2 billion in the first half of 2013 compared to a surplus of 10 billion in the first half of 2012. With reference to the first half of 2009, this can be interpreted as a shock to the external balance of payments in 2013. As a result, and despite the stabilization of foreign (net) direct investment and the improvement in the capital account, the overall balance of payments recorded a slight deficit (-0.15 billion) in the first half of 2013. This underperformance is inherent in the external current account deficit of the second quarter of 2013 estimated at 1.78 billion against a surplus of 0.53 billion in the first quarter of 2013. It confirms the vulnerability of the external balance of payments to the external shock, especially since the first half of 2012 recorded a large surplus in the global external balance (8.90 billion). As a result, with the flow of reserves and the negative valuation effect, the stock of foreign exchange reserves (excluding gold) is estimated at 189.750 billion at the end of June 2013 compared to 189.768 billion at the end of March 2013 and 190.661 billion at the end of December 2012. This stability in the level of external assets reinforces the soundness of Algeria's net international financial position, which is historically low in external debt. This is estimated at only 3.435 billion at the end of June 2013 against 3.637 billion at the end of December 2012. 3 In the first half of 2013, the Bank of Algeria continued the prudent management of official foreign exchange reserves by increasingly emphasizing rigorous monitoring and risk management, including through appropriate prudent measures to protect investment capital from any loss, while achieving an acceptable level of return given the persistence of the environment of low global interest rates. At the end of June 2013, 10-year government bonds in the United States had a yield of 2.5% compared to 1.71% for German government securities of the same maturity. For the record, the investments made by the Bank of Algeria in the sovereign securities of the countries of the euro zone are in the least risky securities, while deposits are directed more towards central banks to stem any counterparty risk. The prudent management of official foreign exchange reserves by the Bank of Algeria contributes to external financial stability, in the context of flexible conduct of the policy of stabilization of the effective exchange rate of the dinar. The Intervention of the Bank of Algeria in the interbank foreign exchange market has helped to mitigate the impact of financial volatility on the national economy, while it has resulted in risks to financial stability in several emerging countries. Increased volatility in foreign exchange markets has led to the depreciation of the currencies of several emerging countries. It is in such a context of volatility in the exchange rates of the main currencies that the average exchange rate of the dinar against the US dollar for the semester under review recorded a depreciation of 4.11% compared to the first half of 2012, while it appreciated by 1.54% compared to the second half of 2012. The average price was USD 78.4781/DZD in the first half of 2013 compared to USD 79.7082/DZD recorded in the second half of 2012 and USD 75.3791/DZD in the first half of 2012. At the same time, the average exchange rate of the dinar against the euro was EUR 103.0376/DZD in the first half of 2013, a slight depreciation both compared to the first half of 2012 (EUR 102.169/DZD) and in the second half of 2012, 0.85% and 0.86% respectively. As a result, and under the effect of the narrowing of the inflation differential between Algeria and its 15 main trading partner countries, i.e. to 4.43% in June 2013 against 6.23% in December 2012, and the increase in relative prices, the real effective exchange rate 4 of the dinar depreciated by 1.28% on average in the first half of 2013 compared to the same period of 2012. It appreciated by 0.90% compared to the second half of 2012, after an appreciation of 5.89%, on an annual average, in the same year. Despite the balance of payments deficit in the second quarter of 2013, it remains appreciated by around 7% in June 2013 compared to its equilibrium level determined by fundamentals. 2. Monetary developments The deceleration in the pace of monetary expansion that characterized 2012, with an increase in the monetary aggregate M2 of only 10.92% against 19.91% for 2011, is confirmed in the first half of the current year when the growth rate of M2 is estimated at only 2.23% (3.19% in the first quarter of 2013) against 7.02% for the first half of 2012. With such a deceleration in its pace and a contraction in the second quarter of 2013, the monetary expansion recorded during the semester under review is weak, with its outstanding amount rising from 11013.39 billion dinars at the end of 2012 to 11258.97 billion dinars at the end of June 2013, given the significant growth in loans to the economy in the context of moderate growth in net foreign assets in the aggregate monetary situation. Despite the deceleration in the pace of growth, i.e. 1.66% in the first half of 2013 against 5.99% for the same period last year, net foreign assets, which reached 14755.73 billion dinars at the end of June 2013, play an important role in the consolidated monetary situation, especially since this aggregate has greatly fuelled the excess liquidity on the money market between 2004 and 2008. Nevertheless, sterilization by the Treasury through the sustained accumulation of resources in the revenue regulation fund has helped to contain this excess liquidity. In addition, after a quasi-stabilization of the State's net financial position in the monetary situation between the end of 2011 and the end of March 2013, the second quarter of 2013 recorded an improvement in this area, i.e. about 8% for the first half of 2013 against a decrease of nearly 2% in 2012. The improvement in the State's net financial position in the first half of 2013 was combined with the deceleration in the growth rate of CCP and Treasury deposits to 9.09% from 24.84% in the first half of last year (30.46% in 2012). Thus, the financial position of the State as a net creditor vis-a-vis the banking system remains appreciable compared to 5 the aggregate credits to the economy. It is important to note that the Treasury's stock of financial savings, namely the savings in its accounts opened at the Bank of Algeria, increased by 288.58 billion dinars in the first half of 2013. Indeed, the overall outstanding amount of the Treasury accounts (current account, revenue regulation fund) amounted to 6002.04 billion dinars at the end of June 2013 against 5816.8 billion dinars at the end of March 2013 and 5713.46 billion dinars at the end of December 2012, in the context of relative stabilization of the overall outstanding issues of Treasury securities, by way of auction on the money market. This outstanding amount increased from 600.85 billion dinars at the end of December 2012 to 592.2 billion dinars at the end of March 2013, to close the half-year under review at 599.39 billion dinars. As a result, the main determinant of monetary expansion in the first half of 2013 is represented by the strong pace of growth in loans to the economy (14.05%), almost double that recorded in the same half of last year (7.76%). The dynamism of bank loans to the economy, supported by the facilitation and support measures taken by the public authorities at the beginning of the year, is such that the rate reached in the first half of 2013 is very close to the rate of expansion in this area for the whole of 2012 (15.35%). At the end of March 2013, bank loans to the economy reached 4568.05 billion dinars, corresponding to an increase of 6.27% compared to December 2012 (4298.45 billion dinars). Indeed, the dynamism of bank loans was more sustained in the second quarter of the current year (7.3%), since the outstanding amount reached 4902.50 billion dinars at the end of June 2013. On this date, loans to private companies reached 2160.96 billion dinars (2037.91 billion dinars at the end of March 2013) against 1940.32 billion dinars at the end of 2012, so that loans to the private sector (including households) (2489.07 billion dinars) exceed the outstanding loans to the public sector (2413.43 billion dinars). In addition, the first half of 2013 was marked by an increase in both private and public sector loans. In parallel with the very strong growth in loans to the economy in the first half of 2013, the analysis of the structure of loans to the economy by maturity confirms the increase in the relative share of medium- and long-term loans to 71.12% at the end of June (70.40% at the end of March 2013, 68.31% at the end of 2012 and 63.41% at the end of 2011). The dynamism of bank loans to the economy reflects the improvement in the structure and conditions of financing (extension of maturity and reduction of cost), correlative to the significant financial support provided by the State to SMEs from the fourth quarter of 2011. In addition, 6 Facilitation measures taken at the beginning of 2013 made the State's support system more effective in the context of the development of healthy credits to SMEs. Household loans increased by 7.1% in the first half of 2013, mainly for mortgage loans. After this broad review of the counterparties of the M2 money supply and particularly the increased role of the credit aggregate, the analysis of the structure of M2 provides information on the financial saving behaviour of economic agents and its impact on the banks' means of action. Excluding hydrocarbon deposits, which suffered a very sharp contraction in the first half of 2013 (-38.85%), due to the external shock in the second quarter, the growth rate of M2 fell to 4.76% during the semester under review against 11.03% in the first half of last year. At the same time, the ratio of loans to the economy to M2 (excluding hydrocarbon deposits) increased to 45.11% at the end of June 2013, after stabilizing in 2012 at 41%, indicating a boost in bank intermediation in terms of credit allocation, while resource mobilization dried up. Dinar deposits collected by banks increased slightly in the first half of 2013 (0.89%), due to a contraction in the second quarter that affected demand deposits (- 8,57 %). Indeed, the growth of deposits in the hydrocarbons (4.9%) in the first quarter was largely offset by the very sharp contraction in the second quarter (-41.71%) due in particular to self-financing the sectoral investment programme and imports of petroleum products. As demand and term deposits in dinars of public enterprises (excluding the hydrocarbons), they increased by 7.3% during the half-year under review, mainly in the first quarter (5.3%). However, this flow of increase is good below the contraction in hydrocarbon deposits, so that the sector the public did not contribute to the development of the banks' means of action in the first semester 2013. It is in such a context that the demand and term deposits in dinars of the private businesses and households grew slightly in the first half of 2013 (2.9%), after a significant expansion recorded in 2012 (14.7%) in relation to the household income effect. In addition, the foreign currency deposits of the latter represent 65.6% of outstanding foreign currency deposits mobilized by banks at the end of June 2013. Their total amount increased by 7% in the first half of 2013, an annual rate higher than the previous year (11.5%). As for deposits in ccPs and the Consolidated Revenue Fund, which are mainly the work of households, they continued their increase in the first half of 2013 (9.09%), in a slower pace compared to first half of 2012 (24.84%). 7 In total, the evolution of the structure of resources collected by banks (including foreign currency deposits and excluding investment funds) indicates a slight increase in the share of the private sector and households to 60.91% at the end of June 2013, while this ratio had increased from 54.82% at the end of 2011 to 59.01% at the end of 2012. As a result, the relative share of the public sector in banks' means of action is decreasing, due in particular to the contraction of deposits in the hydrocarbon sector. As a result of the evolution of dinar term deposits and foreign currency deposits, the quasi-currency aggregate grew at a higher rate (7.59%) than that of the M2 (2.23%) and M2 (excluding hydrocarbon deposits) (4.76%) money supply, but at a slower pace than in the first half of 2012. This confirms the deceleration of monetary expansion in the first half of 2013, especially since the M1 money supply has barely stabilized (-0.10%) in the face of the decline in demand deposits at the level of banks whose rate is estimated at 4.88%. This last phenomenon already recorded in 2012 is linked to the profile of deposits in the hydrocarbon sector, which seem to decrease further in 2013. However, banks' resource base is now less vulnerable to an external shock affecting this sector. As a result, the structure of M2 at the end of June 2013 indicates a decrease in the relative share of bank demand deposits, an increase in that of deposits in the CCP and Treasury as well as that of quasi-money, in a situation of stabilization of the relative share of cash circulation. Indeed, after recording strong monthly net outflows during 2012 with the exception of November and December, cash circulation increased by only 1.18% in the first half of 2013 against 9.15% in the same half of the previous year (14.81% in 2012). As a result of the outflow of fiat money through the Algeria Post network, fiat money increased again in January and February, and then recorded moderate rates of growth in March and April 2013. The months of May and June 2013 recorded a contraction in this area, with the rate of growth of fiat money for the six months under review (1.18%) even slower than the pace recorded in the first quarter (1.45%). Finally, the stabilization of fiat circulation relative to the monetary aggregate M2, the slight decline in the money supply M1 and the contraction of cash circulation in the second quarter of 2013 indicate a stability in the demand for financial savings and household cash, in the context of a deceleration in consumer price inflation. 8 However, given the high level of inflation recorded over the past year, the Bank of Algeria introduced in mid-January 2013 a new monetary policy instrument, namely the recovery of liquidity at six months at a rate of remuneration of 1.50%. This strengthening of monetary policy instruments came after the measures taken in April 2012  increasing the amount of liquidity recoveries by 250 billion dinars to 1350 billion dinars  and May 2012, namely the increase of two percentage points (from 9% to 11%) in the rate of constitution of minimum reserves. The extension of the maturity of liquidity recoveries from January 2013 aims to absorb more stable liquidity from banks and thereby better manage excess liquidity on the money market. Bank liquidity, which remained stable in the first quarter of 2013, contracted in the second quarter to 2542.49 billion dinars at the end of June 2013 against 2865.94 billion dinars at the end of March 2013 and 2876.26 billion dinars at the end of December 2012. The excess liquidity was effectively absorbed by liquidity recovery instruments (1350 billion dinars), in a situation of lower use by banks of the 24-hour deposit facility (163.98 billion dinars at the end of June 2013 against 838.08 billion dinars at the end of December 2012). The banks have also, within the framework of the minimum reserves, increased their holdings in accounts with the Bank of Algeria. In addition, while the interbank money market remained almost inactive in the first quarter of 2013, due to the spread of excess liquidity, interbank lending and borrowing resumed in May and June 2013 with interest rates formed on the interbank market close to 2%. Finally, the preservation of macroeconomic stability remains a primary objective. Monetary policy, underpinned by the flexible conduct of exchange rate policy, plays an active role, especially since the Bank of Algeria consolidated its instruments for reducing excess liquidity at the beginning of the year, with the aim of stemming the inflationary phenomenon. Trend towards deceleration in inflation After a long period of moderate inflation following structural adjustment, inflationary emerged particularly acutely in 2012, following the domestic price shock of some commodities in early 2011 and the acceleration of inflation in the second half of the same year. In 2012, the inflationary phenomenon was essentially endogenous in nature, anchored on a very limited number of fresh products whose prices soared in the first quarter of 2012. Indeed, as early as January 2012, the overall consumer price index of Greater Algiers showed a sudden and sudden increase (2.31%), equivalent to 5.5 times the average monthly increase in this index for 2011. Indeed, the annual average inflation rate was 8.07% in March 2013 compared to 8.89%, 8.91% and 8.56% respectively in December 2012, January and February 2013. This confirms the high impact of food prices; a situation similar to that of the previous year when the average annual increase at June 2012 was 8.8%. In addition, their contribution in June 2013 (61.0%), 10 up 5.7 points in one year, far exceeds their weighting (43.1%) in the consumer price index. With regard to the impact of imported inflation, it should be noted that the domestic prices of imported agricultural products do not sufficiently reflect the downward trend in their world prices, especially since they benefit from implicit subsidies such as exemptions from taxes and customs duties. As a result, domestic price levels are almost always well above those of world prices, although they are expected to move in tandem with both upwards and downwards. In addition, the trend among Algeria's main economic partners is towards disinflation, with the year-on-year pace being less than two percent in June 2013, i.e. 1.8% for the United States and 1.6% for the euro zone. Within the food group, fresh agricultural products experienced double-digit inflation and also increased from 12.9% in June 2012 to 14.8% in June 2013. These products, which represent only 16.9% of the index, generated almost half of inflation in June 2013 (48.6%) compared to 36.5% a year earlier, while the increase in industrial food prices was relatively moderate. Their inflation is estimated at only 3.3% in June 2013 compared to 5.5% a year earlier and, moreover, their contribution fell by 6.4 points to 12.3%, for a weighting of 26.2%. Judging by their contribution to the sharp rise in prices of the food group, two subgroups - vegetables, meat and sheep offal - which together account for 24.0% of the index, generated 64.0% of the inflation of this group in June 2013. In addition, this contribution has increased by 21 percentage points since June 2012. Price inflation for manufactured goods is relatively moderate, at 4.3% as at June 2013, down 2.5 percentage points, while their contribution fell by 10.6 points to 24.1%. In addition, services price inflation accelerated from 4.2% in June 2012 to 5.8% in June 2013, with a contribution to inflation (15.0%) up 4.9 points since June 2012. In terms of structural or core inflation, the disinflation trend that began in August 2012 (5.93%) continued steadily to reach 4.5% in June 2013. 11 Forecasts made in June 2013 indicate that inflation in 2013, on an annual average, would be within the medium-term objective set by the Currency and Credit Council. The moderation of disbursements from the State budget, in a context of monetary deceleration and the continuation of regulatory and market organization actions, contributed to disinflation in 2013. As a result, the trend towards disinflation was confirmed in the first half of 2013 both on an annual average and on a year-on-year basis. However, the still high level of prices makes it necessary to maintain the effort to control liquidity and the expansion of demand and to ensure that supply increases. Finally, in the context of the development of healthy and widely disseminated credit to the economy, aimed at stimulating domestic production, the bank credit channel remains potentially important in terms of financing both productive investment by SMEs and promotional housing (mortgage loans). In support of this important objective, the gradual absorption of excess liquidity in the money market must be accompanied by sustained efforts by commercial banks to mobilize the forward financial savings of businesses and households. Thus, the mobilization of household financial savings by banks, driven by adequate remuneration in real terms, will be a powerful lever in the fight against the inflationary phenomenon. 12
